abstract: We investigate the behavior of different learning algorithms for networks of neuron-like units. As test cases we use simple pat(cid:173) tern association problems, such as the XOR-problem and symmetry de(cid:173) tection problems. The algorithms considered are either versions of the Boltzmann machine learning rule or based on the backpropagation of errors. We also propose and analyze a generalized delta rule for linear threshold units. We find that the performance of a given learning algorithm depends strongly on the type of units used. In particular, we observe that networks with ±1 units quite generally exhibit a significantly better learning behavior than the correspon(cid:173) ding 0,1 versions. We also demonstrate that an adaption of the weight-structure to the symmetries of the problem can lead to a drastic increase in learning speed.

paragraphs: The paper compares learning algorithms on simple pattern association tasks, including XOR and symmetry detection. It examines variants of Boltzmann machine learning and error backpropagation, and also proposes a generalized delta rule for linear threshold units. The aim is to understand how learning behavior changes with the ingredients of the network.

A central finding is that the type of neuron-like unit strongly affects an algorithm's performance. Networks whose units use values of minus one and plus one generally learn substantially better than corresponding networks using zero and one. This means that choosing a learning rule alone does not determine how effectively a network will learn; the representation used by its units also matters.

The authors further show that adapting the weight structure to the symmetries of the task can greatly accelerate learning. This makes the organization of connections another important part of the comparison. Taken together, the results emphasize the interaction among the learning algorithm, unit values, and task structure when designing networks for pattern association.
summary.tldr: Learning performance depends strongly on neuron values and connection structure, with bipolar units and task-aligned symmetries improving learning in the studied tasks.

title: Analysis and Comparison of Different Learning Algorithms for Pattern Association Problems

abstract: The interaction of a set of tropisms is sufficient in many cases to explain the seemingly complex behavioral responses exhibited by varied classes of biological systems to combinations of stimuli. It can be shown that a straightforward generalization of the tropism phenomenon allows the efficient implementation of effective algorithms which appear to respond "intelligently" to changing environmental conditions. Examples of the utilization of tropistic processing techniques will be presented in this paper in applications entailing simulated behavior synthesis, path-planning, pattern analysis (clustering), and engineering design optimization.
originalAbstract: The interaction of a set of tropisms is sufficient in many cases to explain the seemingly complex behavioral responses exhibited by varied classes of biological systems to combinations of stimuli. It can be shown that a straightforward generalization of the tropism phenomenon allows the efficient implementation of effective algorithms which appear to respond "intelligently" to changing environmental conditions. Examples of the utilization of tropistic processing techniques will be presented in this paper in applications entailing simulated behavior synthesis, path-planning, pattern analysis (clustering), and engineering design optimization.

paragraphs: The paper starts from the observation that interactions among tropisms can explain apparently complex biological behavior. A tropism is a response tendency associated with a stimulus. When several such tendencies act together, their combined effect can produce responses to combinations of environmental signals that seem much more elaborate than the individual tendencies.

The authors propose generalizing this idea into a computational approach called tropistic processing. The abstract states that this generalization supports efficient implementations of effective algorithms that respond to changing environmental conditions. The central design idea is to build useful behavior from interacting response tendencies.

The paper presents applications in simulated behavior synthesis, path planning, clustering, and engineering design optimization. These examples connect the same processing idea to generating actions, organizing patterns, and searching for designs. Their breadth is part of the motivation: a principle drawn from biological responses is presented as a reusable algorithmic approach. The stated contribution is the generalization and its applications, with intelligent-looking adaptation explained through the interaction of simpler responses.
summary.tldr: Tropistic processing builds adaptive algorithms from interacting stimulus-response tendencies, with applications from path planning to design optimization.

title: On Tropistic Processing and Its Applications

abstract: Inspired by the information theoretic idea of minimum description length, we add a term to the back propagation cost function that penalizes network complexity. We give the details of the procedure, called weight-elimination, describe its dynamics, and clarify the meaning of the parameters involved. From a Bayesian perspective, the complexity term can be usefully interpreted as an assumption about prior distribution of the weights. We use this procedure to predict the sunspot time series and the notoriously noisy series of currency exchange rates.
originalAbstract: Inspired by the information theoretic idea of minimum description length, we add a term to the back propagation cost function that penalizes network complexity. We give the details of the procedure, called weight-elimination, describe its dynamics, and clarify the meaning of the parameters involved. From a Bayesian perspective, the complexity term can be usefully interpreted as an assumption about prior distribution of the weights. We use this procedure to predict the sunspot time series and the notoriously noisy series of currency exchange rates.

paragraphs: This paper introduces weight-elimination, a training procedure that adds a network-complexity penalty to the usual backpropagation objective. The method is motivated by minimum description length, an information-theoretic idea that favors economical explanations of data. Training therefore takes account of both fit to the examples and the complexity of the resulting network.

The paper explains the procedure's dynamics and the meaning of its parameters. It also gives a Bayesian interpretation: the added complexity term can express a prior distribution over weights. This connects a practical modification of the training objective to an explicit assumption about which weight configurations are preferred before considering the observed data.

The authors apply weight-elimination to forecasting sunspot activity and currency exchange rates, with the latter described as particularly noisy. These applications place complexity control in settings where the network must predict a time series. The contribution is a method for making simplicity part of learning itself, together with two forecasting applications and complementary information-theoretic and Bayesian explanations of the penalty.
summary.tldr: Weight-elimination adds a complexity penalty to backpropagation and applies the resulting training procedure to sunspot and exchange-rate forecasting.

title: Generalization by Weight-Elimination with Application to Forecasting

abstract: A three-layered neural network model was used to explore the organization of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR). The dynamic model was trained using recurrent back-propagation to produce compensatory, long duration eye muscle motoneuron outputs in response to short duration vestibular afferent head velocity inputs. The network learned to produce this response prolongation, known as velocity storage, by developing complex, lateral inhibitory interac(cid:173) tions among the interneurons. These had the low baseline, long time constant, rectified and skewed responses that are characteristic of real VOR inter(cid:173) neurons. The model suggests that all of these features are interrelated and result from lateral inhibition. 1 SIGNAL PROCESSING IN THE VOR The VOR stabilizes the visual image by producing eye rotations that are nearly equal and opposite to head rotations (Wilson and Melvill Jones 1979). The VOR utilizes head rotational velocity signals, which originate in the semicircular canal receptors of the inner ear, to control contractions of the extraocular muscles. The reflex is coor(cid:173) dinated by brainstem interneurons in the vestibular nuclei (VN), that relay signals from canal afferent sensory neurons to eye muscle motoneurons. 32 A Recurrent Neural Network Model of Velocity Storage 33 The VN intemeurons, however, do more than just relay signals. Among other func(cid:173) tions, the VN neurons process the canal afferent signals, stretching out their time con(cid:173) stants by about four times before transmitting this signal to the motoneurons. This time constant prolongation, which is one of the clearest examples of signal processing in motor neurophysiology, has been termed velocity storage (Raphan et al. 1979). The neural mechanisms underlying velocity storage, however, remain unidentified. The VOR is bilaterally symmetric (Wilson and Melvill Jones 1979). The semicircular canals operate in push-pull pairs, and the extraocular muscles are arranged in agonist/antagonist pairs. The VN are also arranged bilaterally and interact via in(cid:173) hibitory commissural connections. The commissures are necessary for velocity storage, which is eliminated by cutting the commissures in monkeys (Blair and Gavin 1981). When the overall V OR fails to compensate for head rotations, the visual image is not stabilized but moves across the retina at a velocity that is equal to the amount of VOR error. This 'retinal slip' signal is transmitted back to the VN, and is known to modify VOR operation (Wilson and Melvill Jones 1979). Thus the VOR can be modeled beautifully as a three-layered neural network, complete with recurrent connections and error signal back-propagation at the VN level. By modeling the VOR as a neural net(cid:173) work, insight can be gained into the global organization of this reflex. Figure 1: Architecture of the Horizontal VOR Neural Network Model. lhc and rhc, left and right horizontal canal afferents; Ivn and rvn, left and right VN neurons; lr and mr, lateral and medial rectus motoneurons of the left eye. This and all subsequent figures are redrawn from Anastasio (1991), with permission.

title: A Recurrent Neural Network Model of Velocity Storage in the Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex

abstract: We have created new networks to unmix signals which have been mixed either with time delays or via filtering. We first show that a subset of the Herault-Jutten learning rules fulfills a principle of minimum output power. We then apply this principle to extensions of the Herault-Jutten network which have delays in the feedback path. Our networks perform well on real speech and music signals that have been mixed using time delays or filtering.
originalAbstract: We have created new networks to unmix signals which have been mixed either with time delays or via filtering. We first show that a subset of the Herault-Jutten learning rules fulfills a principle of minimum output power. We then apply this principle to extensions of the Herault-Jutten network which have delays in the feedback path. Our networks perform well on real speech and music signals that have been mixed using time delays or filtering.

paragraphs: This paper develops networks for recovering source signals from mixtures involving time delays or filtering. In these settings, the observed mixture reflects more than the simultaneous addition of source values: timing and signal transformations also affect what reaches the separator. The aim is to recover the component signals despite those effects.

The authors first show that a subset of the Herault–Jutten learning rules satisfies a minimum-output-power principle. They then use that principle to guide extensions of the Herault–Jutten network with delays in the feedback path. The theoretical connection gives the extended architecture a common objective linking its learning behavior to the original rules.

The resulting networks perform well on real speech and music signals mixed using delays or filtering. These examples support the approach for signals with the temporal structure relevant to the stated separation problem. The contribution combines an interpretation of existing learning rules with an architectural extension, showing how a shared optimization principle can guide networks toward handling more complicated mixtures.
summary.tldr: Networks with delayed feedback use a minimum-output-power principle to separate speech and music mixtures involving delays or filtering.

title: Networks for the Separation of Sources that are Superimposed and Delayed
Processing of Visual and Auditory Space and Its Modification by Experience

abstract: Jeffrey L. Elman Center for Research on Language Department of Cognitive Science University of California at San Diego LaJolla, CA 92093-0126 U.S.A. elman@crl.ucsd.edu The non-linear complexities of neural networks make network solutions difficult to understand. Sanger's contribution analysis is here extended to the analysis of networks automatically generated by the cascade(cid:173) correlation learning algorithm. Because such networks have cross connections that supersede hidden layers, standard analyses of hidden unit activation patterns are insufficient. A contribution is defined as the product of an output weight and the associated activation on the sending unit, whether that sending unit is an input or a hidden unit, multiplied by the sign of the output target for the current input pattern. Intercorrelations among contributions, as gleaned from the matrix of contributions x input patterns, can be subjected to principal components analysis (PCA) to extract the main features of variation in the contributions. Such an analysis is applied to three problems, continuous XOR, arithmetic comparison, and distinguishing between two interlocking spirals. In all three cases, this technique yields useful insights into network solutions that are consistent across several networks.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to interpret networks built by cascade-correlation learning. These networks contain connections that cut across a conventional hidden-layer organization. Looking only at hidden-unit activations can therefore miss how units actually influence the output, making ordinary activation-based analysis insufficient.

The method extends contribution analysis. For each input pattern, a unit's contribution combines its activation, its connection weight to the output, and the sign of the desired output. This relates a unit's activity to the direction and strength of its output influence. Contributions are collected across patterns, and principal components analysis extracts their main shared variations.

The authors apply the analysis to continuous XOR, arithmetic comparison, and separating two interlocking spirals. In all three problems, it produces useful interpretations that remain consistent across several networks. The result suggests that examining coordinated output contributions can reveal common features of learned solutions even when the architecture lacks a simple layer-by-layer structure and individual activations are difficult to interpret.
summary.tldr: Contribution analysis and principal components analysis reveal consistent patterns in how cross-connected networks solve three classification problems.

title: Analyzing Cross-Connected Networks

abstract: This paper presents NeuroChess, a program which learns to play chess from the final outcome of games. NeuroChess learns chess board evaluation functions, represented by artificial neural networks. It integrates inductive neural network learning, temporal differencing, and a variant of explanation-based learning. Performance results illustrate some of the strengths and weaknesses of this approach.
originalAbstract: This paper presents NeuroChess, a program which learns to play chess from the final outcome of games. NeuroChess learns chess board evaluation functions, represented by artificial neural networks. It integrates inductive neural network learning, temporal differencing, and a variant of explanation-based learning. Performance results illustrate some of the strengths and weaknesses of this approach.

paragraphs: The paper presents NeuroChess, a program that learns from the final outcomes of chess games. Its learned component is a board evaluation function represented by an artificial neural network. Such a function assigns an assessment to a board position, making position evaluation the concrete target of the learning process.

NeuroChess combines inductive neural network learning, temporal differencing, and a variant of explanation-based learning. These ingredients bring together learning from examples, learning across successive positions, and an explanation-based component. Their integration addresses the challenge posed by the training signal: the final outcome belongs to an entire game, while the evaluation function must assess positions encountered within it.

The paper reports performance results illustrating both strengths and weaknesses of this approach. The stated contribution is a working combination of learning methods for acquiring chess evaluations from game outcomes. It frames chess learning around improving the judgment of board positions and examines what that combination can achieve through the program's observed performance.
summary.tldr: NeuroChess learns neural board evaluations from game outcomes by combining temporal differencing, inductive learning, and explanation-based learning.

title: Learning to Play the Game of Chess

abstract: We introduce and analyze a mixture model for supervised learning of probabilistic transducers. We devise an online learning algorithm that efficiently infers the structure and estimates the parameters of each model in the mixture. Theoretical analysis and comparative simulations indicate that the learning algorithm tracks the best model from an arbitrarily large (possibly infinite) pool of models. We also present an application of the model for inducing a noun phrase recognizer.
originalAbstract: We introduce and analyze a mixture model for supervised learning of probabilistic transducers. We devise an online learning algorithm that efficiently infers the structure and estimates the parameters of each model in the mixture. Theoretical analysis and comparative simulations indicate that the learning algorithm tracks the best model from an arbitrarily large (possibly infinite) pool of models. We also present an application of the model for inducing a noun phrase recognizer.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a mixture model for supervised learning of probabilistic transducers. A transducer represents a mapping from inputs to outputs, with probabilities describing uncertainty in that mapping. A mixture allows several such models to participate, making the learning problem include both the component models and their combination.

The authors devise an online algorithm that learns as examples arrive. It efficiently infers each component's structure as well as estimating its parameters. This distinction matters: estimating parameter values presumes a model structure, whereas learning structure also determines the form of the model used to explain the examples.

Theoretical analysis and comparative simulations indicate that the algorithm tracks the best model in an arbitrarily large, potentially infinite pool. This is a claim about adapting competitively among candidate models, rather than needing to settle on a small fixed collection beforehand. The paper also applies the approach to learning a noun phrase recognizer, connecting its general sequence-modeling formulation with a concrete language-processing task.
summary.tldr: An online mixture algorithm learns probabilistic transducer structures and parameters while tracking the best model in a potentially infinite pool.

title: Adaptive Mixture of Probabilistic Transducers
Strong Unimodality and Exact Learning of Constant Depth µ-Perceptron Networks

abstract: A latent variable generative model with finite noise is used to de(cid:173) scribe several different algorithms for Independent Components Anal(cid:173) ysis (lCA). In particular, the Fixed Point ICA algorithm is shown to be equivalent to the Expectation-Maximization algorithm for maximum likelihood under certain constraints, allowing the conditions for global convergence to be elucidated. The algorithms can also be explained by their generic behavior near a singular point where the size of the opti(cid:173) mal generative bases vanishes. An expansion of the likelihood about this singular point indicates the role of higher order correlations in determin(cid:173) ing the features discovered by ICA. The application and convergence of these algorithms are demonstrated on a simple illustrative example.
originalAbstract: A latent variable generative model with finite noise is used to de(cid:173) scribe several different algorithms for Independent Components Anal(cid:173) ysis (lCA). In particular, the Fixed Point ICA algorithm is shown to be equivalent to the Expectation-Maximization algorithm for maximum likelihood under certain constraints, allowing the conditions for global convergence to be elucidated. The algorithms can also be explained by their generic behavior near a singular point where the size of the opti(cid:173) mal generative bases vanishes. An expansion of the likelihood about this singular point indicates the role of higher order correlations in determin(cid:173) ing the features discovered by ICA. The application and convergence of these algorithms are demonstrated on a simple illustrative example.

paragraphs: This paper uses a generative model with hidden variables and finite noise to explain several algorithms for independent component analysis, or ICA. The common model provides a way to compare procedures that might otherwise appear to be separate computational recipes. It also connects the features they discover to the statistical structure of the data.

A central result links Fixed Point ICA to expectation-maximization for maximum-likelihood learning under particular constraints. The equivalence is conditional, and it helps clarify the conditions for global convergence. Framing the algorithm this way gives its updates an interpretation in terms of fitting a probabilistic model.

The authors also examine behavior near a singular point where the optimal generative basis elements shrink to zero. Expanding the likelihood around that point reveals how higher-order correlations help determine which features ICA discovers. A simple illustrative example demonstrates the algorithms' application and convergence. Together, these analyses connect algorithmic behavior, convergence conditions, and the statistics responsible for learned features.
summary.tldr: A noisy generative model connects ICA algorithms to constrained expectation-maximization and explains the role of higher-order correlations in learned features.

title: Algorithms for Independent Components Analysis and Higher Order Statistics

paragraphs: Policy-gradient reinforcement learning relies on estimating how policy changes affect performance. This paper studies two choices involved in those estimates: representing state-action values with function approximation and including a bias term in their estimation. The focus is the rate at which performance-gradient estimates converge, rather than only the form of the value representation.

The first theoretical result shows that linear function approximation can slow convergence relative to estimating the gradient without that approximation. The stated comparison depends on the number of basis functions. The second result shows that a nonzero bias term can improve convergence, with the stated relationship involving the number of possible actions. The supplied abstract has damaged formulas, so exact factors cannot be recovered from it.

Experiments show significant improvements in policy-gradient convergence when the theoretical findings are used. Together, the results show that approximation and bias choices can materially affect gradient estimation. In particular, the reported benefit of a nonzero bias term makes convergence behavior an important consideration when selecting how state-action values enter the learning procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper shows that linear value approximation can slow policy-gradient convergence, while a nonzero bias term can improve it.

title: Rates of Convergence of Performance Gradient Estimates Using Function Approximation and Bias in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analy- sis and factor analysis are used to discover a linear mapping between high dimensional data samples and points in a lower dimensional subspace. In [6], Jojic and Frey introduced mixture of transformation-invariant component analyzers (MTCA) that can account for global transforma- tions such as translations and rotations, perform clustering and learn lo- cal appearance deformations by dimensionality reduction. However, due to enormous computational requirements of the EM algorithm for learn- ing the model, O( is the dimensionality of a data sample, MTCA was not practical for most applications. In this paper, we demon- strate how fast Fourier transforms can reduce the computation to the or- . With this speedup, we show the effectiveness of MTCA der of in various applications - tracking, video textures, clustering video se- quences, object recognition, and object detection in images.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction represents high-dimensional samples through a smaller set of coordinates. For visual data, the task becomes more complicated when appearance also changes through translations or rotations. Mixtures of transformation-invariant component analyzers address these changes while also clustering samples and learning local appearance deformations through dimensionality reduction.

The obstacle addressed here is the computational burden of learning that model with EM. The paper introduces fast Fourier transforms as a way to reduce the required computation. This targets the practical cost of fitting a model that already combines several useful capabilities, making its treatment of transformations and appearance variation more usable.

With the resulting speedup, the authors demonstrate the model in tracking, video textures, clustering video sequences, object recognition, and object detection in images. These applications illustrate the range of visual tasks that can benefit from the accelerated computation. The stated contribution is both an algorithmic acceleration and evidence that the faster model is effective across these applications.
summary.tldr: Fast Fourier transforms accelerate transformation-invariant factor analysis, enabling demonstrations across several visual learning tasks.

title: Fast Transformation-Invariant Factor Analysis

abstract: We propose a new linear method for dimension reduction to identify nonGaussian components in high dimensional data. Our method, NGCA (non-Gaussian component analysis), uses a very general semi-parametric framework. In contrast to existing projection methods we define what is uninteresting (Gaussian): by projecting out uninterestingness, we can estimate the relevant non-Gaussian subspace. We show that the estimation error of finding the non-Gaussian components tends to zero at a parametric rate. Once NGCA components are identified and extracted, various tasks can be applied in the data analysis process, like data visualization, clustering, denoising or classification. A numerical study demonstrates the usefulness of our method.

paragraphs: Non-Gaussian component analysis is a linear dimensionality reduction method built around a particular definition of irrelevant structure: Gaussian components are treated as uninteresting. The method seeks a lower-dimensional subspace containing the non-Gaussian components of high-dimensional data. This makes the choice of what to discard central to how the representation is constructed.

The authors formulate the problem in a general semi-parametric framework. By projecting out the Gaussian structure, they estimate the relevant non-Gaussian subspace. They also show that the estimation error tends to zero at a parametric rate, providing a statistical convergence result for recovering those components within the proposed framework.

Once extracted, the components can be used for visualization, clustering, denoising, or classification. A numerical study demonstrates the method's usefulness. The approach matters because it offers a common preprocessing representation for several analysis tasks, with relevance defined through departures from Gaussian structure and supported by a theoretical result about the accuracy of subspace estimation.
summary.tldr: NGCA estimates a non-Gaussian subspace by removing Gaussian structure and establishes parametric-rate convergence of its estimation error.

title: Non-Gaussian Component Analysis: a Semi-parametric Framework for Linear Dimension Reduction

abstract: We examine the problem of predicting local sentiment flow in documents, and its application to several areas of text analysis. Formally, the problem is stated as predicting an ordinal sequence based on a sequence of word sets. In the spirit of isotonic regression, we develop a variant of conditional random fields that is well suited to handle this problem. Using the Mobius transform, we express the model as a simple convex optimization problem. Experiments demonstrate the model and its applications to sentiment prediction, style analysis, and text summarization.

In the spirit of isotonic regression, we develop a variant of conditional random fields that is well suited to handle this problem. Using the Mobius transform, we express the model as a simple convex optimization problem. Experiments demonstrate the model and its applications to sentiment prediction, style analysis, and text summarization.

paragraphs: A document can change sentiment as it unfolds, so describing its local sentiment requires a sequence of predictions. This paper frames that task as predicting an ordinal sequence from a sequence of word sets. The ordinal formulation captures the fact that sentiment labels have an ordering, giving the model structure to use in its predictions.

The authors develop a variant of conditional random fields inspired by isotonic regression. This brings an order-aware approach to a model designed for sequence prediction. Using the Möbius transform, they express the model as a simple convex optimization problem, providing a computational formulation for learning the proposed sentiment-flow model.

Experiments demonstrate the model in sentiment prediction, style analysis, and text summarization. These applications show how a representation of sentiment across a document can be useful beyond a single overall sentiment judgment. The central contribution is the combination of ordered outputs, sequence modeling, and convex optimization in a framework specifically aimed at predicting local sentiment flow.
summary.tldr: An order-aware conditional random field models sentiment changes through documents using a convex optimization formulation.

title: Isotonic Conditional Random Fields and Local Sentiment Flow

abstract: Bayesian inference has become increasingly important in statistical machine learning. Exact Bayesian calculations are often not feasible in practice, however. A number of approximate Bayesian methods have been proposed to make such calculations practical, among them the variational Bayesian (VB) approach. The VB approach, while useful, can nevertheless suffer from slow convergence to the approximate solution. To address this problem, we propose Parameter-eXpanded Variational Bayesian (PX-VB) methods to speed up VB. The new algorithm is inspired by parameter-expanded expectation maximization (PX-EM) and parameterexpanded data augmentation (PX-DA). Similar to PX-EM and -DA, PX-VB expands a model with auxiliary variables to reduce the coupling between variables in the original model. We analyze the convergence rates of VB and PX-VB and demonstrate the superior convergence rates of PX-VB in variational probit regression and automatic relevance determination.

To address this problem, we propose Parameter-eXpanded Variational Bayesian (PX-VB) methods to speed up VB. The new algorithm is inspired by parameter-expanded expectation maximization (PX-EM) and parameterexpanded data augmentation (PX-DA). Similar to PX-EM and -DA, PX-VB expands a model with auxiliary variables to reduce the coupling between variables in the original model. We analyze the convergence rates of VB and PX-VB and demonstrate the superior convergence rates of PX-VB in variational probit regression and automatic relevance determination.

paragraphs: Variational Bayesian methods make otherwise impractical Bayesian calculations approachable by seeking an approximate solution. However, reaching that approximation can itself be slow. This paper targets that convergence problem, proposing parameter-expanded variational Bayesian methods, abbreviated PX-VB, to accelerate the learning procedure.

The approach expands a model with auxiliary variables to reduce coupling among its original variables. It draws inspiration from parameter expansion in expectation maximization and data augmentation. The key idea is to change the representation used during computation so that the approximate inference procedure can progress more quickly toward its solution.

The authors analyze convergence rates for ordinary VB and PX-VB. They demonstrate superior convergence rates for PX-VB in variational probit regression and automatic relevance determination. These results support parameter expansion as a way to improve the speed of variational computation in the demonstrated settings. The improvement concerns how rapidly the approximation is reached; the method remains within the variational Bayesian approach to making Bayesian inference practical.
summary.tldr: Parameter expansion reduces variable coupling and accelerates variational Bayesian convergence in two demonstrated applications.

title: Parameter Expanded Variational Bayesian Methods

abstract: We consider the problem of bounding from above the log-partition function corresponding to second-order Ising models for binary distributions. We introduce a new bound, the cardinality bound, which can be computed via convex optimization. The corresponding error on the logpartition function is bounded above by twice the distance, in model parameter space, to a class of "standard" Ising models, for which variable inter-dependence is described via a simple mean field term. In the context of maximum-likelihood, using the new bound instead of the exact log-partition function, while constraining the distance to the class of standard Ising models, leads not only to a good approximation to the log-partition function, but also to a model that is parsimonious, and easily interpretable. We compare our bound with the log-determinant bound introduced by Wainwright and Jordan (2006), and show that when the l1 -norm of the model parameter vector is small enough, the latter is outperformed by the new bound.

paragraphs: The paper studies a quantity needed to normalize probabilities in binary Ising models: the log-partition function. It focuses on models with pairwise interactions and introduces the cardinality bound, an upper approximation that can be computed through convex optimization. This makes the approximation itself an optimization problem with useful mathematical structure.

The authors also give an explicit guarantee on approximation error. The error is no greater than twice the model’s parameter-space distance from a particular class of standard Ising models. In that class, a simple mean-field term describes dependence among variables. The guarantee therefore links accuracy to proximity to a simpler model family.

For maximum-likelihood learning, the authors combine the bound with a constraint keeping the learned model close to that family. They describe the resulting models as parsimonious and interpretable while retaining a good log-partition approximation. They also establish an advantage over the log-determinant bound when the parameter vector’s absolute values sum to a sufficiently small amount; the comparison is conditional on that regime.
summary.tldr: A convexly computable bound approximates binary Ising models’ log-partition function, with error controlled by distance to a simpler model family.

title: A Convex Upper Bound on the Log-Partition Function for Binary Distributions

abstract: We propose a novel non-parametric adaptive anomaly detection algorithm for high dimensional data based on score functions derived from nearest neighbor graphs on n-point nominal data. Anomalies are declared whenever the score of a test sample falls below q, which is supposed to be the desired false alarm level. The resulting anomaly detector is shown to be asymptotically optimal in that it is uniformly most powerful for the specified false alarm level, q, for the case when the anomaly density is a mixture of the nominal and a known density. Our algorithm is computationally efficient, being linear in dimension and quadratic in data size. It does not require choosing complicated tuning parameters or function approximation classes and it can adapt to local structure such as local change in dimensionality. We demonstrate the algorithm on both artificial and real data sets in high dimensional feature spaces.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an anomaly detector that learns from examples of nominal, or ordinary, behavior. It constructs nearest-neighbor graphs from these examples and derives a score for a new observation. A test sample is declared anomalous when its score falls below a threshold q, intended to represent the desired false-alarm level.

The method is non-parametric and can adapt to local structure, including changes in local dimensionality. It does not require selecting complicated tuning parameters or a class of functions for approximation. Its computational cost grows linearly with the number of dimensions and quadratically with the number of nominal examples, making these two aspects of scale affect the workload differently.

The theoretical guarantee is asymptotic and assumes the anomaly density is a mixture of the nominal density and a known density. In that setting, the detector is uniformly most powerful at the specified false-alarm level. The authors also demonstrate it on artificial and real high-dimensional datasets. The guarantee therefore supplies a precise conditional foundation for a detector that is also examined empirically.
summary.tldr: Nearest-neighbor graph scores enable adaptive anomaly detection with an asymptotic optimality guarantee under a specified anomaly-mixture model.

title: Anomaly Detection with Score functions based on Nearest Neighbor Graphs

abstract: Despite the ubiquity of clustering as a tool in unsupervised learning, there is not yet a consensus on a formal theory, and the vast majority of work in this direction has focused on unsupervised clustering. We study a recently proposed framework for supervised clustering where there is access to a teacher. We give an improved generic algorithm to cluster any concept class in that model. Our algorithm is query-efficient in the sense that it involves only a small amount of interaction with the teacher. We also present and study two natural generalizations of the model. The model assumes that the teacher response to the algorithm is perfect. We eliminate this limitation by proposing a noisy model and give an algorithm for clustering the class of intervals in this noisy model. We also propose a dynamic model where the teacher sees a random subset of the points. Finally, for datasets satisfying a spectrum of weak to strong properties, we give query bounds, and show that a class of clustering functions containing Single-Linkage will find the target clustering under the strongest property.

paragraphs: Clustering is usually framed as an unsupervised task, but a teacher can provide information about the grouping a learner should recover. This paper studies a formal supervised-clustering framework with that kind of interaction. It gives an improved generic algorithm for any concept class within the model, emphasizing how little interaction with the teacher is needed.

The authors also extend the framework in two directions. The original model assumes perfect teacher responses; a noisy version relaxes this assumption, with an algorithm provided for the class of intervals. A separate dynamic model lets the teacher see a random subset of the points. These extensions distinguish different ways that access to supervision can be restricted.

Finally, the paper derives query bounds for datasets satisfying properties that range from weak to strong. Under the strongest property, a class of clustering functions that includes Single-Linkage finds the target clustering. The results connect the amount of supervision required to dataset structure, while keeping the broad generic result separate from the more specialized guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper improves query-efficient supervised clustering and develops noisy and dynamic teacher models with additional conditional guarantees.

title: Supervised Clustering

abstract: Being able to predict the course of arbitrary chemical reactions is essential to the theory and applications of organic chemistry. Previous approaches are not high-throughput, are not generalizable or scalable, or lack sufficient data to be effective. We describe single mechanistic reactions as concerted electron movements from an electron orbital source to an electron orbital sink. We use an existing rule-based expert system to derive a dataset consisting of 2,989 productive mechanistic steps and 6.14 million non-productive mechanistic steps. We then pose identifying productive mechanistic steps as a ranking problem: rank potential orbital interactions such that the top ranked interactions yield the major products. The machine learning implementation follows a two-stage approach, in which we first train atom level reactivity filters to prune 94.0% of non-productive reactions with less than a 0.1% false negative rate. Then, we train an ensemble of ranking models on pairs of interacting orbitals to learn a relative productivity function over single mechanistic reactions in a given system. Without the use of explicit transformation patterns, the ensemble perfectly ranks the productive mechanisms at the top 89.1% of the time, rising to 99.9% of the time when top ranked lists with at most four non-productive reactions are considered. The final system allows multi-step reaction prediction. Furthermore, it is generalizable, making reasonable predictions over reactants and conditions which the rule-based expert system does not handle.

paragraphs: The paper treats chemical reaction prediction as a problem of ranking possible electron movements. Each mechanistic step connects an electron orbital source to an orbital sink. An existing rule-based expert system supplies training data containing 2,989 productive steps and 6.14 million nonproductive steps, giving the learning system examples of both useful and unsuccessful possibilities.

Prediction proceeds in two stages. Atom-level reactivity filters first remove 94.0% of nonproductive reactions with a false negative rate below 0.1%. The final system supports multistep prediction and produces reasonable predictions for some reactants and conditions beyond those handled by its rule-based data source.
summary.tldr: A two-stage system filters and ranks orbital interactions to predict productive reaction mechanisms and support multistep chemical prediction.

title: A Machine Learning Approach to Predict Chemical Reactions

abstract: We study the problem of online learning Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) when both the transition distributions and loss functions are chosen by an adversary. We present an algorithm that, under a mixing assumption, achieves $O(\sqrt{T\log|\Pi|}+\log|\Pi|)$ regret with respect to a comparison set of policies $\Pi$. The regret is independent of the size of the state and action spaces. When expectations over sample paths can be computed efficiently and the comparison set $\Pi$ has polynomial size, this algorithm is efficient. We also consider the episodic adversarial online shortest path problem. Here, in each episode an adversary may choose a weighted directed acyclic graph with an identified start and finish node. The goal of the learning algorithm is to choose a path that minimizes the loss while traversing from the start to finish node. At the end of each episode the loss function (given by weights on the edges) is revealed to the learning algorithm. The goal is to minimize regret with respect to a fixed policy for selecting paths. This problem is a special case of the online MDP problem. For randomly chosen graphs and adversarial losses, this problem can be efficiently solved. We show that it also can be efficiently solved for adversarial graphs and randomly chosen losses. When both graphs and losses are adversarially chosen, we present an efficient algorithm whose regret scales linearly with the number of distinct graphs. Finally, we show that designing efficient algorithms for the adversarial online shortest path problem (and hence for the adversarial MDP problem) is as hard as learning parity with noise, a notoriously difficult problem that has been used to design efficient cryptographic schemes.

paragraphs: The paper studies online decision-making when an adversary chooses both losses and state-transition distributions. Under a mixing assumption, its algorithm achieves regret O(√(T log|Π|) + log|Π|) against a comparison set of policies Π. This bound does not depend on the sizes of the state and action spaces.

Computational efficiency requires additional conditions: expectations over trajectories must be efficiently computable, and the policy comparison set must have polynomial size. The authors also examine an episodic shortest-path problem, where each episode supplies a directed acyclic graph and edge losses are revealed after the path is traversed.

Efficient solutions are available when graphs are random and losses adversarial, or when graphs are adversarial and losses random. When both are adversarial, the proposed efficient algorithm has regret growing linearly with the number of distinct graphs. Finally, a hardness result connects efficient algorithms for the general adversarial problem to learning parity with noise. The results therefore separate favorable regret guarantees from the additional conditions needed to achieve them efficiently.
summary.tldr: Adversarial MDP learning admits state-space-independent regret under mixing, while efficient computation depends on additional conditions and faces a hardness barrier.

title: Online Learning in Markov Decision Processes with Adversarially Chosen Transition Probability Distributions

abstract: This paper examines the question: What kinds of distributions can be efficiently represented by Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs)? We characterize the RBM's unnormalized log-likelihood function as a type of neural network (called an RBM network), and through a series of simulation results relate these networks to types that are better understood. We show the surprising result that RBM networks can efficiently compute any function that depends on the number of 1's in the input, such as parity. We also provide the first known example of a particular type of distribution which provably cannot be efficiently represented by an RBM (or equivalently, cannot be efficiently computed by an RBM network), assuming a realistic exponential upper bound on the size of the weights. By formally demonstrating that a relatively simple distribution cannot be represented efficiently by an RBM our results provide a new rigorous justification for the use of potentially more expressive generative models, such as deeper ones.

paragraphs: The paper studies which probability distributions restricted Boltzmann machines can represent efficiently. The issue is representational cost: a model may be capable of expressing a distribution in principle while requiring an impractically large representation. The authors recast an RBM's unnormalized log-likelihood as a particular neural network, creating a way to analyze its expressive abilities.

By relating these RBM networks to better-understood network types, they establish an expressive strength: RBM networks efficiently compute any function depending only on the number of ones in the input. Parity is one example. This demonstrates that the model can compactly handle a broad family of functions defined by a global property of the input.

The authors also exhibit a distribution that provably lacks an efficient RBM representation, assuming an exponential upper bound on weight sizes. This conditional impossibility result shows that even a relatively simple distribution can challenge the architecture. Together, the positive and negative results sharpen its expressive boundaries and motivate considering potentially more expressive generative models, including deeper ones.
summary.tldr: The paper proves expressive strengths and a weight-bounded limitation of restricted Boltzmann machines, motivating potentially richer generative models.

title: On the Representational Efficiency of Restricted Boltzmann Machines

abstract: POMDPs provide a principled framework for planning under uncertainty, but are computationally intractable, due to the “curse of dimensionality” and the “curse of history”. This paper presents an online lookahead search algorithm that alleviates these difficulties by limiting the search to a set of sampled scenarios. The execution of all policies on the sampled scenarios is summarized using a Determinized Sparse Partially Observable Tree (DESPOT), which is a sparsely sampled belief tree. Our algorithm, named Regularized DESPOT (R-DESPOT), searches the DESPOT for a policy that optimally balances the size of the policy and the accuracy on its value estimate obtained through sampling. We give an output-sensitive performance bound for all policies derived from the DESPOT, and show that R-DESPOT works well if a small optimal policy exists. We also give an anytime approximation to R-DESPOT. Experiments show strong results, compared with two of the fastest online POMDP algorithms.

This paper presents an online lookahead search algorithm that alleviates these difficulties by limiting the search to a set of sampled scenarios. paragraphs: Planning in a partially observable environment requires reasoning about uncertainty and many possible observation histories. These sources of complexity make POMDP planning computationally difficult. This paper reduces the search burden by planning over sampled scenarios, using a sparse belief tree called DESPOT to summarize how policies execute on those scenarios.

The proposed R-DESPOT algorithm searches this tree while balancing policy size against the accuracy of its value estimate from samples. This regularization makes the complexity of the chosen policy part of the planning objective. The authors provide an output-sensitive performance bound for policies derived from the tree and establish favorable behavior when a small optimal policy exists.

The paper also develops an anytime approximation, allowing planning to produce an approximate result within available computation. Experiments report strong results against two fast online POMDP algorithms. The contribution combines scenario-based search with explicit control of policy complexity; its stated theoretical success depends in particular on whether a compact optimal policy is available.
summary.tldr: R-DESPOT balances policy complexity and sampled value estimates to make online POMDP planning effective when a small optimal policy exists.

title: DESPOT: Online POMDP Planning with Regularization

abstract: A long term goal of Interactive Reinforcement Learning is to incorporate non-expert human feedback to solve complex tasks. State-of-the-art methods have approached this problem by mapping human information to reward and value signals to indicate preferences and then iterating over them to compute the necessary control policy. In this paper we argue for an alternate, more effective characterization of human feedback: Policy Shaping. We introduce Advise, a Bayesian approach that attempts to maximize the information gained from human feedback by utilizing it as direct labels on the policy. We compare Advise to state-of-the-art approaches and highlight scenarios where it outperforms them and importantly is robust to infrequent and inconsistent human feedback.

paragraphs: Interactive reinforcement learning aims to use feedback from people who need not be experts to help an agent learn complex tasks. Existing approaches described in this paper translate that feedback into reward or value signals, then use those signals to compute a control policy. The authors propose interpreting the feedback more directly.

Their method, Advise, uses a Bayesian approach to treat human feedback as labels on the policy itself. This is the idea of policy shaping: human input informs the agent's action-selection behavior directly. The approach attempts to extract as much information as possible from the feedback, making its interpretation a central part of the learning method.

Comparisons with state-of-the-art approaches identify scenarios in which Advise performs better. The reported results also highlight robustness when feedback arrives infrequently or inconsistently, conditions relevant to relying on human guidance. The findings support policy shaping as an effective alternative in those scenarios. They do not imply that direct policy labels universally outperform reward-based interpretations, but show that how feedback is represented can materially affect its usefulness.
summary.tldr: Advise treats human feedback as Bayesian policy labels and outperforms comparison methods in scenarios with sparse or inconsistent guidance.

title: Policy Shaping: Integrating Human Feedback with Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We consider a popular problem in finance, option pricing, through the lens of an online learning game between Nature and an Investor. In the Black-Scholes option pricing model from 1973, the Investor can continuously hedge the risk of an option by trading the underlying asset, assuming that the asset's price fluctuates according to Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM). We consider a worst-case model, in which Nature chooses a sequence of price fluctuations under a cumulative quadratic volatility constraint, and the Investor can make a sequence of hedging decisions. Our main result is to show that the value of our proposed game, which is the regret'' of hedging strategy, converges to the Black-Scholes option price. We use significantly weaker assumptions than previous work---for instance, we allow large jumps in the asset price---and show that the Black-Scholes hedging strategy is near-optimal for the Investor even in this non-stochastic framework."

paragraphs: This paper studies option pricing as an online game between an investor and an adversarial Nature. In the standard Black-Scholes setting, asset prices follow geometric Brownian motion and the investor continuously trades to hedge an option. The authors ask what remains valid when price movements are chosen adversarially instead.

Their game allows Nature to choose a sequence of price changes subject to a cumulative quadratic volatility constraint. The investor responds with a sequence of hedging decisions. This replaces a specified random price process with a worst-case model, while retaining a restriction on cumulative volatility. The assumptions are weaker than those of previous work and permit large price jumps.

The main result shows that the game's value, expressed through hedging regret, converges to the Black-Scholes option price. The Black-Scholes hedging strategy is also near-optimal for the investor in this non-stochastic setting. These conclusions provide a minimax interpretation of the pricing rule within the proposed constrained game, extending its justification beyond the original stochastic model.
summary.tldr: Under a cumulative quadratic volatility constraint, an adversarial hedging game's value converges to the Black-Scholes price and its hedging strategy remains near-optimal.

title: How to Hedge an Option Against an Adversary: Black-Scholes Pricing is Minimax Optimal

abstract: This paper presents foundational theoretical results on distributed parameter estimation for undirected probabilistic graphical models. It introduces a general condition on composite likelihood decompositions of these models which guarantees the global consistency of distributed estimators, provided the local estimators are consistent.
originalAbstract: This paper presents foundational theoretical results on distributed parameter estimation for undirected probabilistic graphical models. It introduces a general condition on composite likelihood decompositions of these models which guarantees the global consistency of distributed estimators, provided the local estimators are consistent.

paragraphs: This paper investigates when parameter estimation for an undirected probabilistic graphical model can be distributed across local estimation problems. The central concern is statistical correctness: breaking an estimation task into parts should still allow the overall procedure to recover the intended model parameters as the amount of data grows.

The authors introduce a general condition on composite likelihood decompositions. Such a decomposition organizes the estimation objective into component likelihood contributions. Their result connects how these components are chosen with the consistency of the resulting distributed estimator. Under the proposed condition, consistency of the local estimators is sufficient to guarantee consistency at the global level.

The distinction between local and global correctness is the main point of the contribution. Reliable estimation within each component carries through to the whole model when the decomposition satisfies the stated condition. The guarantee therefore has two linked requirements: an appropriate decomposition and consistent local estimation. It provides a theoretical basis for assessing whether a distributed construction preserves the statistical goal of parameter estimation.
summary.tldr: A condition on composite likelihood decompositions guarantees globally consistent distributed estimation when the local estimators are consistent.

title: Distributed Parameter Estimation in Probabilistic Graphical Models

abstract: We propose a new variational inference method based on the Kullback-Leibler (KL) proximal term. We make two contributions towards improving efficiency of variational inference. Firstly, we derive a KL proximal-point algorithm and show its equivalence to gradient descent with natural gradient in stochastic variational inference. Secondly, we use the proximal framework to derive efficient variational algorithms for non-conjugate models. We propose a splitting procedure to separate non-conjugate terms from conjugate ones. We then linearize the non-conjugate terms and show that the resulting subproblem admits a closed-form solution. Overall, our approach converts a non-conjugate model to subproblems that involve inference in well-known conjugate models. We apply our method to many models and derive generalizations for non-conjugate exponential family. Applications to real-world datasets show that our proposed algorithms are easy to implement, fast to converge, perform well, and reduce computations.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a Bayesian posterior by optimizing within a chosen family of distributions. This paper develops a method using a Kullback-Leibler proximal term, which expresses the update in terms of divergence between distributions. The framework is intended to improve computational efficiency and handle models whose structure does not yield convenient conjugate calculations.

The first contribution connects two optimization perspectives: the authors derive a KL proximal-point algorithm and show its equivalence to natural-gradient descent in stochastic variational inference. The second contribution uses splitting to separate conjugate and nonconjugate terms. Linearizing the nonconjugate terms produces a subproblem with a closed-form solution, turning the original inference task into a sequence of tractable conjugate-model subproblems.

The paper applies the method to multiple models and derives extensions for nonconjugate exponential-family settings. On real-world datasets, the proposed algorithms are reported to converge quickly, reduce computation, and perform well while remaining easy to implement. The practical significance is that difficult model terms can be accommodated through structured updates that retain useful closed-form calculations.
summary.tldr: KL proximal updates connect natural-gradient inference with a splitting method that reduces nonconjugate inference to tractable conjugate subproblems.

title: Kullback-Leibler Proximal Variational Inference

abstract: This paper studies the generalization performance of multi-class classification algorithms, for which we obtain, for the first time, a data-dependent generalization error bound with a logarithmic dependence on the class size, substantially improving the state-of-the-art linear dependence in the existing data-dependent generalization analysis. The theoretical analysis motivates us to introduce a new multi-class classification machine based on lp-norm regularization, where the parameter p controls the complexity of the corresponding bounds. We derive an efficient optimization algorithm based on Fenchel duality theory. Benchmarks on several real-world datasets show that the proposed algorithm can achieve significant accuracy gains over the state of the art.
originalAbstract: This paper studies the generalization performance of multi-class classification algorithms, for which we obtain, for the first time, a data-dependent generalization error bound with a logarithmic dependence on the class size, substantially improving the state-of-the-art linear dependence in the existing data-dependent generalization analysis. The theoretical analysis motivates us to introduce a new multi-class classification machine based on lp-norm regularization, where the parameter p controls the complexity of the corresponding bounds. We derive an efficient optimization algorithm based on Fenchel duality theory. Benchmarks on several real-world datasets show that the proposed algorithm can achieve significant accuracy gains over the state of the art.

paragraphs: The paper studies how well multiclass classifiers generalize beyond their training examples. Its central theoretical contribution is a data-dependent generalization-error bound whose dependence on the number of classes is logarithmic. This improves on the linear class-count dependence in the existing data-dependent analysis identified by the authors, making the role of many classes less severe in the bound.

The analysis then informs the design of a new multiclass classification method using lp-norm regularization. The parameter p controls the complexity appearing in the corresponding bounds. This connects a choice in the learning objective to the theoretical analysis, rather than presenting the bound and the classifier as unrelated contributions.

To train the proposed classifier efficiently, the authors derive an optimization algorithm using Fenchel duality. Benchmarks on several real-world datasets show that the algorithm can achieve significant accuracy gains over state-of-the-art methods. The theoretical improvement concerns the error bound's dependence on class count, while the empirical results separately demonstrate benefits for classification accuracy in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A tighter multiclass generalization bound motivates an lp-regularized classifier that achieves accuracy gains on several real-world benchmarks.

title: Multi-class SVMs: From Tighter Data-Dependent Generalization Bounds to Novel Algorithms

abstract: High dimensional superposition models characterize observations using parameters which can be written as a sum of multiple component parameters, each with its own structure, e.g., sum of low rank and sparse matrices. In this paper, we consider general superposition models which allow sum of any number of component parameters, and each component structure can be characterized by any norm. We present a simple estimator for such models, give a geometric condition under which the components can be accurately estimated, characterize sample complexity of the estimator, and give non-asymptotic bounds on the componentwise estimation error. We use tools from empirical processes and generic chaining for the statistical analysis, and our results, which substantially generalize prior work on superposition models, are in terms of Gaussian widths of suitable spherical caps.

We present a simple estimator for such models, give a geometric condition under which the components can be accurately estimated, characterize sample complexity of the estimator, and give non-asymptotic bounds on the componentwise estimation error. paragraphs: A structured superposition model describes observations using parameters that are sums of differently structured components. One example is a matrix expressed as the sum of a low-rank matrix and a sparse matrix. The statistical task includes estimating the individual pieces, making their separate recoverability an important part of the problem.

This paper treats a general setting with any number of components, each described through a norm. The authors provide a simple estimator and a geometric condition under which the components can be estimated accurately. That condition ties the possibility of separating the components to the geometry of their structures, rather than restricting the analysis to a single predefined combination.

The analysis characterizes sample complexity and provides finite-sample bounds on the estimation error of each component. It uses empirical-process tools and generic chaining, with results expressed through Gaussian widths of suitable spherical caps. These geometric quantities organize the statistical guarantees. The resulting framework substantially generalizes earlier work on superposition models while retaining component-specific accuracy statements.
summary.tldr: A general estimator separates sums of norm-structured components under a geometric condition, with sample-complexity and componentwise error guarantees.

title: High Dimensional Structured Superposition Models

abstract: Computer vision has benefited from initializing multiple deep layers with weights pretrained on large supervised training sets like ImageNet. Natural language processing (NLP) typically sees initialization of only the lowest layer of deep models with pretrained word vectors. In this paper, we use a deep LSTM encoder from an attentional sequence-to-sequence model trained for machine translation (MT) to contextualize word vectors. We show that adding these context vectors (CoVe) improves performance over using only unsupervised word and character vectors on a wide variety of common NLP tasks: sentiment analysis (SST, IMDb), question classification (TREC), entailment (SNLI), and question answering (SQuAD). For fine-grained sentiment analysis and entailment, CoVe improves performance of our baseline models to the state of the art.

paragraphs: This paper transfers representations learned during machine translation to other language tasks. Its starting observation is that language models commonly initialize only their lowest layer with pretrained word vectors, whereas vision systems have benefited from transferring multiple pretrained layers. The authors investigate whether a deeper language encoder can likewise provide reusable information.

They take a deep LSTM encoder from an attentional sequence-to-sequence translation model and use it to produce contextualized word vectors, called CoVe. These vectors represent words in relation to their surrounding text. Adding them supplies downstream models with representations learned through the supervised translation task, alongside their existing word and character vectors.

Across sentiment analysis, question classification, entailment, and question answering, adding CoVe improves performance over using only unsupervised word and character representations. For fine-grained sentiment analysis and entailment, the additions bring the authors’ baseline models to state-of-the-art performance. The findings show that translation-trained context representations can transfer across a variety of language tasks, with the strongest stated result applying to those two task settings.
summary.tldr: CoVe transfers a translation-trained LSTM encoder’s contextual word representations to improve several downstream language tasks.

title: Learned in Translation: Contextualized Word Vectors

abstract: We provide the first information theoretical tight analysis for inference of latent community structure given a sparse graph along with high dimensional node covariates, correlated with the same latent communities. Our work bridges recent theoretical breakthroughs in detection of latent community structure without nodes covariates and a large body of empirical work using diverse heuristics for combining node covariates with graphs for inference. The tightness of our analysis implies in particular, the information theoretic necessity of combining the different sources of information. Our analysis holds for networks of large degrees as well as for a Gaussian version of the model.
originalAbstract: We provide the first information theoretical tight analysis for inference of latent community structure given a sparse graph along with high dimensional node covariates, correlated with the same latent communities. Our work bridges recent theoretical breakthroughs in detection of latent community structure without nodes covariates and a large body of empirical work using diverse heuristics for combining node covariates with graphs for inference. The tightness of our analysis implies in particular, the information theoretic necessity of combining the different sources of information. Our analysis holds for networks of large degrees as well as for a Gaussian version of the model.

paragraphs: Community inference seeks hidden groups in a network. This paper studies a setting with two sources of evidence: a sparse graph and high-dimensional attributes attached to its nodes. Both sources are correlated with the same underlying communities, raising the question of what can be inferred when their information is considered together.

The authors provide an information-theoretically tight analysis of this problem. Such an analysis concerns the information available for inference, rather than only the behavior of a particular heuristic. The work connects theoretical progress on graph-only community detection with empirical approaches that have combined graph connections and node attributes in diverse ways.

A consequence of the tight analysis is that combining the information sources is necessary in the information-theoretic sense captured by the model. This gives a formal basis for joint use of relationships and attributes. The stated scope of the analysis includes networks with large degrees and a Gaussian version of the model. Those conditions locate the result: the paper establishes sharp theoretical conclusions within these settings.
summary.tldr: A tight theoretical analysis explains why community inference can require jointly using graph connections and node attributes.

title: Contextual Stochastic Block Models

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel maximum causal Tsallis entropy (MCTE) framework for imitation learning which can efficiently learn a sparse multi-modal policy distribution from demonstrations. We provide the full mathematical analysis of the proposed framework. First, the optimal solution of an MCTE problem is shown to be a sparsemax distribution, whose supporting set can be adjusted. The proposed method has advantages over a softmax distribution in that it can exclude unnecessary actions by assigning zero probability. Second, we prove that an MCTE problem is equivalent to robust Bayes estimation in the sense of the Brier score. Third, we propose a maximum causal Tsallis entropy imitation learning (MCTEIL) algorithm with a sparse mixture density network (sparse MDN) by modeling mixture weights using a sparsemax distribution. In particular, we show that the causal Tsallis entropy of an MDN encourages exploration and efficient mixture utilization while Boltzmann Gibbs entropy is less effective. We validate the proposed method in two simulation studies and MCTEIL outperforms existing imitation learning methods in terms of average returns and learning multi-modal policies.

paragraphs: Expert demonstrations can contain several distinct ways to act successfully. This paper proposes an imitation-learning framework that can represent such multimodal behavior while assigning probability to only a selected set of actions. Its organizing objective is maximum causal Tsallis entropy, abbreviated MCTE.

The authors prove that the optimal solution has a sparsemax distribution with an adjustable supporting set. Unlike softmax, this distribution can assign exactly zero probability to unnecessary actions. They also establish an equivalence between the MCTE problem and robust Bayes estimation under the Brier score, giving the framework a second mathematical interpretation beyond its entropy-based formulation.

The practical MCTEIL algorithm uses a sparse mixture density network whose mixture weights follow sparsemax. The paper shows that causal Tsallis entropy encourages exploration and efficient use of mixture components, with Boltzmann–Gibbs entropy being less effective in this role. In two simulation studies, MCTEIL outperforms existing imitation-learning methods on average returns and learning multimodal policies. These results connect the theoretical sparsity property to demonstrated policy-learning benefits.
summary.tldr: MCTEIL uses Tsallis entropy and sparsemax mixture weights to learn sparse, multimodal policies, with improvements in two simulation studies.

title: Maximum Causal Tsallis Entropy Imitation Learning

abstract: Memory is an important aspect of intelligence and plays a role in many deep reinforcement learning models. However, little progress has been made in understanding when specific memory systems help more than others and how well they generalize. The field also has yet to see a prevalent consistent and rigorous approach for evaluating agent performance on holdout data. In this paper, we aim to develop a comprehensive methodology to test different kinds of memory in an agent and assess how well the agent can apply what it learns in training to a holdout set that differs from the training set along dimensions that we suggest are relevant for evaluating memory-specific generalization. To that end, we first construct a diverse set of memory tasks that allow us to evaluate test-time generalization across multiple dimensions. Second, we develop and perform multiple ablations on an agent architecture that combines multiple memory systems, observe its baseline models, and investigate its performance against the task suite.

paragraphs: Memory appears in many reinforcement-learning agents, but its presence alone does not explain when a particular memory system helps. This paper focuses on evaluating that question systematically. It asks how well agents transfer what they learn to held-out tasks that differ along dimensions relevant to memory use.

The authors construct a diverse suite of memory tasks designed to test generalization across multiple dimensions. This makes the relationship between training and evaluation an explicit part of the methodology. The intended assessment concerns whether learned behavior remains useful when the held-out setting changes in ways selected to probe memory-specific generalization.

The paper also develops an agent architecture combining multiple memory systems and studies it through several ablations and baseline models. Removing or changing components provides a way to investigate their contributions within the task suite. The stated contribution is an evaluation methodology and accompanying architectural investigation, giving researchers a structured way to study working and episodic memory rather than treating memory as a single undifferentiated capability.
summary.tldr: A diverse task suite and agent ablations provide a systematic methodology for evaluating how reinforcement-learning memory systems generalize.

title: Generalization of Reinforcement Learners with Working and Episodic Memory

abstract: Feature importance estimates that inform users about the degree to which given inputs influence the output of a predictive model are crucial for understanding, validating, and interpreting machine-learning models. However, providing fast and accurate estimates of feature importance for high-dimensional data, and quantifying the uncertainty of such estimates remain open challenges. Here, we frame the task of providing explanations for the decisions of machine-learning models as a causal learning task, and train causal explanation (CXPlain) models that learn to estimate to what degree certain inputs cause outputs in another machine-learning model. CXPlain can, once trained, be used to explain the target model in little time, and enables the quantification of the uncertainty associated with its feature importance estimates via bootstrap ensembling. We present experiments that demonstrate that CXPlain is significantly more accurate and faster than existing model-agnostic methods for estimating feature importance. In addition, we confirm that the uncertainty estimates provided by CXPlain ensembles are strongly correlated with their ability to accurately estimate feature importance on held-out data.
