paragraphs: Feature-importance methods help users understand how inputs influence a predictive model's output. For high-dimensional inputs, producing accurate explanations quickly is challenging, and the reliability of those explanations also matters. CXPlain approaches explanation as a causal learning task, training a separate model to estimate how inputs cause outputs within the predictive model being explained.

Once trained, the explanation model can provide feature-importance estimates quickly. The method also uses bootstrap ensembling to quantify uncertainty in those estimates. This adds information about how dependable an explanation may be, alongside the estimated importance of each input. The causal framing concerns the behavior of the target machine-learning model.

The reported experiments find CXPlain significantly faster and more accurate than existing model-agnostic feature-importance methods. They also find a strong correlation between the ensembles' uncertainty estimates and their ability to estimate importance accurately on held-out data. Together, these findings support learning an explanation model as a practical way to obtain both efficient explanations and useful signals about explanation reliability.
summary.tldr: CXPlain learns fast feature-importance explanations and uses bootstrap ensembles to estimate their uncertainty.

title: CXPlain: Causal Explanations for Model Interpretation under Uncertainty

abstract: In a series of papers [Lee et al 2016], [Panageas and Piliouras 2017], [Lee et al 2019], it was established that some of the most commonly used first order methods almost surely (under random initializations) and with step-size being small enough, avoid strict saddle points, as long as the objective function $f$ is $C^2$ and has Lipschitz gradient. The key observation was that first order methods can be studied from a dynamical systems perspective, in which instantiations of Center-Stable manifold theorem allow for a global analysis. The results of the aforementioned papers were limited to the case where the step-size $\alpha$ is constant, i.e., does not depend on time (and typically bounded from the inverse of the Lipschitz constant of the gradient of $f$). It remains an open question whether or not the results still hold when the step-size is time dependent and vanishes with time. In this paper, we resolve this question on the affirmative for gradient descent, mirror descent, manifold descent and proximal point. The main technical challenge is that the induced (from each first order method) dynamical system is time non-homogeneous and the stable manifold theorem is not applicable in its classic form. By exploiting the dynamical systems structure of the aforementioned first order methods, we are able to prove a stable manifold theorem that is applicable to time non-homogeneous dynamical systems and generalize the results in [Lee et al 2019] for time dependent step-sizes.

paragraphs: Previous results showed that several first-order optimization methods almost surely avoid strict saddle points under random initialization, sufficiently small constant steps, and smoothness assumptions. The assumptions described include a twice continuously differentiable objective with a Lipschitz gradient. This paper asks whether saddle avoidance can also hold when the step size changes over time and approaches zero.

The authors answer affirmatively for gradient descent, mirror descent, manifold descent, and the proximal point method in the settings they analyze. The proof difficulty is that changing step sizes produce a time-dependent dynamical system. Earlier arguments used a stable-manifold theorem whose classical form does not directly apply to this changing update process.

The main technical contribution is a stable-manifold theorem suited to time-nonhomogeneous systems, developed by exploiting the structure of these optimization methods. It extends the analysis of saddle avoidance beyond constant step sizes. The conclusion concerns almost-sure avoidance of strict saddles under the relevant setup; it should not be read as a claim that these methods necessarily find global minima or that every vanishing step-size schedule works.
summary.tldr: A new dynamical-systems theorem extends almost-sure strict-saddle avoidance results to several optimization methods with vanishing step sizes.

title: First-order methods almost always avoid saddle points: The case of vanishing step-sizes

abstract: We study a wide class of non-convex non-concave min-max games that generalizes over standard bilinear zero-sum games. In this class, players control the inputs of a smooth function whose output is being applied to a bilinear zero-sum game. This class of games is motivated by the indirect nature of the competition in Generative Adversarial Networks, where players control the parameters of a neural network while the actual competition happens between the distributions that the generator and discriminator capture. We establish theoretically, that depending on the specific instance of the problem gradient-descent-ascent dynamics can exhibit a variety of behaviors antithetical to convergence to the game theoretically meaningful min-max solution. Specifically, different forms of recurrent behavior (including periodicity and Poincar\'{e} recurrence) are possible as well as convergence to spurious (non-min-max) equilibria for a positive measure of initial conditions. At the technical level, our analysis combines tools from optimization theory, game theory and dynamical systems.

In this class, players control the inputs of a smooth function whose output is being applied to a bilinear zero-sum game. This class of games is motivated by the indirect nature of the competition in Generative Adversarial Networks, where players control the parameters of a neural network while the actual competition happens between the distributions that the generator and discriminator capture. We establish theoretically, that depending on the specific instance of the problem gradient-descent-ascent dynamics can exhibit a variety of behaviors antithetical to convergence to the game theoretically meaningful min-max solution. Specifically, different forms of recurrent behavior (including periodicity and Poincar\'{e} recurrence) are possible as well as convergence to spurious (non-min-max) equilibria for a positive measure of initial conditions. At the technical level, our analysis combines tools from optimization theory, game theory and dynamical systems.

paragraphs: The paper examines gradient descent-ascent in a broad class of non-convex, non-concave zero-sum games. Each player controls inputs to a smooth function, whose outputs participate in a bilinear game. This indirect competition is motivated by GANs, where players adjust network parameters while their competition concerns the distributions represented by those networks.

The authors prove that the dynamics can behave in several ways that fail to approach a meaningful min-max solution. Depending on the instance, trajectories may be periodic or exhibit Poincaré recurrence, returning arbitrarily close to earlier states. Other instances allow convergence to equilibria that are not min-max solutions.

The spurious-equilibrium behavior occurs for a positive-measure set of initial conditions, giving the result more scope than a single specially chosen starting point. The analysis combines optimization, game theory, and dynamical systems to characterize these possibilities. Its significance is that neither continued movement nor eventual convergence alone guarantees successful game solving: the dynamics and the quality of their destination both require attention in this class of problems.
summary.tldr: Gradient descent-ascent can cycle, recur, or converge to non-min-max equilibria in a broad class of indirectly parameterized zero-sum games.

title: Poincaré Recurrence, Cycles and Spurious Equilibria in Gradient-Descent-Ascent for Non-Convex Non-Concave Zero-Sum Games

abstract: In deep reinforcement learning, policy optimization methods need to deal with issues such as function approximation and the reuse of off-policy data. Standard policy gradient methods do not handle off-policy data well, leading to premature convergence and instability. This paper introduces a method to stabilize policy optimization when off-policy data are reused. The idea is to include a Bregman divergence between the behavior policy that generates the data and the current policy to ensure small and safe policy updates with off-policy data. The Bregman divergence is calculated between the state distributions of two policies, instead of only on the action probabilities, leading to a divergence augmentation formulation. Empirical experiments on Atari games show that in the data-scarce scenario where the reuse of off-policy data becomes necessary, our method can achieve better performance than other state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning algorithms.
originalAbstract: In deep reinforcement learning, policy optimization methods need to deal with issues such as function approximation and the reuse of off-policy data. Standard policy gradient methods do not handle off-policy data well, leading to premature convergence and instability. This paper introduces a method to stabilize policy optimization when off-policy data are reused. The idea is to include a Bregman divergence between the behavior policy that generates the data and the current policy to ensure small and safe policy updates with off-policy data. The Bregman divergence is calculated between the state distributions of two policies, instead of only on the action probabilities, leading to a divergence augmentation formulation. Empirical experiments on Atari games show that in the data-scarce scenario where the reuse of off-policy data becomes necessary, our method can achieve better performance than other state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning systems often need to reuse experience collected by an earlier or different policy. Such off-policy data can be valuable when new interactions are scarce, but standard policy gradient methods may handle it poorly. The paper focuses on the resulting instability and premature convergence when policy optimization combines data reuse with function approximation.

The proposed method adds a Bregman divergence between the behavior policy that collected the data and the current policy. Crucially, the comparison concerns the distributions of states associated with the policies, rather than only their probabilities of choosing actions. The added divergence is intended to keep updates small and controlled when learning from reused experience.

Experiments on Atari games show that the method can outperform other leading deep reinforcement learning algorithms in a data-scarce setting where off-policy reuse becomes necessary. The finding is tied to that evaluated scenario. Its significance is that controlling changes in state distributions offers a way to stabilize learning while still making use of previously collected data.
summary.tldr: Penalizing divergence between policies’ state distributions helps stabilize policy optimization when off-policy experience must be reused.

title: Divergence-Augmented Policy Optimization

abstract: Recently, attention based models have been used extensively in many sequence-to-sequence learning systems. Especially for image captioning, the attention based models are expected to ground correct image regions with proper generated words. However, for each time step in the decoding process, the attention based models usually use the hidden state of the current input to attend to the image regions. Under this setting, these attention models have a ``deviated focus'' problem that they calculate the attention weights based on previous words instead of the one to be generated, impairing the performance of both grounding and captioning. In this paper, we propose the Prophet Attention, similar to the form of self-supervision. In the training stage, this module utilizes the future information to calculate the ``ideal'' attention weights towards image regions. These calculated ``ideal'' weights are further used to regularize the ``deviated'' attention. In this manner, image regions are grounded with the correct words. The proposed Prophet Attention can be easily incorporated into existing image captioning models to improve their performance of both grounding and captioning. The experiments on the Flickr30k Entities and the MSCOCO datasets show that the proposed Prophet Attention consistently outperforms baselines in both automatic metrics and human evaluations. It is worth noticing that we set new state-of-the-arts on the two benchmark datasets and achieve the 1st place on the leaderboard of the online MSCOCO benchmark in terms of the default ranking score, i.e., CIDEr-c40.

The mechanism resembles self-supervision because the additional guidance comes from information available within the training sequence. It is designed to be incorporated into existing captioning models.

Experiments on Flickr30k Entities and MSCOCO show consistent improvements over baselines in automatic measurements and human evaluations. The authors report state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks and first place on the online MSCOCO leaderboard under its default CIDEr-c40 ranking. These results support using future-informed training targets to improve the connection between generated words and the image regions that should support them.
summary.tldr: Prophet Attention uses future information during training to guide image attention, improving reported word grounding and caption quality.

title: Prophet Attention: Predicting Attention with Future Attention

abstract: This paper considers the problem of designing optimal algorithms for reinforcement learning in two-player zero-sum games. We focus on self-play algorithms which learn the optimal policy by playing against itself without any direct supervision. In a tabular episodic Markov game with S states, A max-player actions and B min-player actions, the best existing algorithm for finding an approximate Nash equilibrium requires \tlO(S^2AB) steps of game playing, when only highlighting the dependency on (S,A,B). In contrast, the best existing lower bound scales as \Omega(S(A+B)) and has a significant gap from the upper bound. This paper closes this gap for the first time: we propose an optimistic variant of the Nash Q-learning algorithm with sample complexity \tlO(SAB), and a new Nash V-learning algorithm with sample complexity \tlO(S(A+B)). The latter result matches the information-theoretic lower bound in all problem-dependent parameters except for a polynomial factor of the length of each episode. In addition, we present a computational hardness result for learning the best responses against a fixed opponent in Markov games---a learning objective different from finding the Nash equilibrium.

paragraphs: The paper studies how efficiently an agent can learn through self-play in two-player zero-sum games. The setting is a tabular episodic Markov game, and the goal is to find an approximate Nash equilibrium without direct supervision. A central issue is how the required amount of game experience grows with the numbers of states and available actions.

Writing these counts as S states, A maximizing-player actions, and B minimizing-player actions, the authors improve the highlighted dependence from roughly S²AB to SAB using an optimistic Nash Q-learning variant. Their new Nash V-learning algorithm improves it further to S(A+B), with logarithmic factors suppressed. This replaces a product of the players’ action counts with their sum.

The Nash V-learning result matches the information-theoretic lower bound in the problem-dependent parameters except for a polynomial factor in episode length. The paper also establishes computational hardness for learning a best response to a fixed opponent. That is a distinct learning objective, so the hardness result addresses a different question from the near-optimal self-play guarantee.
summary.tldr: New self-play algorithms approach optimal sample complexity for finding approximate Nash equilibria in tabular episodic zero-sum Markov games.

title: Near-Optimal Reinforcement Learning with Self-Play

abstract: We study high-confidence behavior-agnostic off-policy evaluation in reinforcement learning, where the goal is to estimate a confidence interval on a target policy's value, given only access to a static experience dataset collected by unknown behavior policies. Starting from a function space embedding of the linear program formulation of the Q-function, we obtain an optimization problem with generalized estimating equation constraints. By applying the generalized empirical likelihood method to the resulting Lagrangian, we propose CoinDICE, a novel and efficient algorithm for computing confidence intervals. Theoretically, we prove the obtained confidence intervals are valid, in both asymptotic and finite-sample regimes. Empirically, we show in a variety of benchmarks that the confidence interval estimates are tighter and more accurate than existing methods.

paragraphs: CoinDICE addresses the problem of evaluating a reinforcement learning policy using an existing, fixed collection of experience. The policies that generated those experiences are unknown. Rather than returning only an estimated value for the target policy, the method computes a confidence interval, making uncertainty about that value part of the evaluation.

The construction begins with a linear programming formulation of the Q-function, which describes values associated with actions and states. The authors embed this formulation in a function space and obtain an optimization problem constrained by generalized estimating equations. They then apply generalized empirical likelihood to its Lagrangian. This sequence yields an algorithm for calculating confidence intervals without requiring knowledge of the behavior policies.

The paper proves interval validity in both finite-sample and asymptotic regimes. Across the evaluated benchmarks, the intervals are tighter and more accurate than those of existing methods. These findings combine theoretical support for the uncertainty estimates with empirical evidence that the resulting ranges can be more informative in practice.
summary.tldr: CoinDICE computes theoretically supported confidence intervals for policy values from fixed experience collected by unknown behavior policies.

title: CoinDICE: Off-Policy Confidence Interval Estimation

abstract: Reconciling symbolic and distributed representations is a crucial challenge that can potentially resolve the limitations of current deep learning. Remarkable advances in this direction have been achieved recently via generative object-centric representation models. While learning a recognition model that infers object-centric symbolic representations like bounding boxes from raw images in an unsupervised way, no such model can provide another important ability of a generative model, i.e., generating (sampling) according to the structure of learned world density. In this paper, we propose Generative Neurosymbolic Machines, a generative model that combines the benefits of distributed and symbolic representations to support both structured representations of symbolic components and density-based generation. These two crucial properties are achieved by a two-layer latent hierarchy with the global distributed latent for flexible density modeling and the structured symbolic latent map. To increase the model flexibility in this hierarchical structure, we also propose the StructDRAW prior. In experiments, we show that the proposed model significantly outperforms the previous structured representation models as well as the state-of-the-art non-structured generative models in terms of both structure accuracy and image generation quality.

paragraphs: Object-centered generative models can learn structured descriptions, such as bounding boxes, from images without supervision. The paper identifies a further capability that existing models of this kind lacked: sampling images according to the structure of the learned world distribution. Recognizing symbolic components and generating coherent samples from a learned density are related but distinct goals.

Generative Neurosymbolic Machines combine symbolic and distributed representations through a two-layer latent hierarchy. A global distributed latent representation provides flexible density modeling, while a structured symbolic latent map represents components explicitly. The authors also introduce the StructDRAW prior to increase flexibility within this hierarchy. The design gives the model a place for both global statistical information and structured symbolic content.

Experiments show significant improvements over previous structured representation models and state-of-the-art non-structured generative models in structure accuracy and image generation quality. These findings support the proposed hierarchy as a way to serve both objectives together. The contribution is a generative architecture whose learned representation can expose symbolic structure while also supporting sampling from a flexible model of the image distribution.
summary.tldr: Generative Neurosymbolic Machines combine global distributed latents with symbolic structure to improve both structured representation and image generation.

title: Generative Neurosymbolic Machines

abstract: This paper introduces a new method to build linear flows, by taking the exponential of a linear transformation. This linear transformation does not need to be invertible itself, and the exponential has the following desirable properties: it is guaranteed to be invertible, its inverse is straightforward to compute and the log Jacobian determinant is equal to the trace of the linear transformation. An important insight is that the exponential can be computed implicitly, which allows the use of convolutional layers. Using this insight, we develop new invertible transformations named convolution exponentials and graph convolution exponentials, which retain the equivariance of their underlying transformations. In addition, we generalize Sylvester Flows and propose Convolutional Sylvester Flows which are based on the generalization and the convolution exponential as basis change. Empirically, we show that the convolution exponential outperforms other linear transformations in generative flows on CIFAR10 and the graph convolution exponential improves the performance of graph normalizing flows. In addition, we show that Convolutional Sylvester Flows improve performance over residual flows as a generative flow model measured in log-likelihood.

paragraphs: This paper builds invertible linear transformations by taking the exponential of a linear operator. The original operator need not be invertible: its exponential is guaranteed to be, has a straightforward inverse, and has a log Jacobian determinant equal to the original operator’s trace. These properties make it useful for constructing generative flows.

A key observation is that the exponential can be computed implicitly, allowing convolutional operators to be used. The authors develop convolution exponentials and graph convolution exponentials that preserve the equivariance of their underlying transformations. They also generalize Sylvester flows and use the convolution exponential as a change of basis in a new convolutional version.

Experiments show that convolution exponentials outperform other linear transformations in generative flows on CIFAR10, while graph convolution exponentials improve graph normalizing flows. Convolutional Sylvester Flows also improve log-likelihood over residual flows in the reported evaluation. The paper combines guaranteed invertibility and tractable determinant calculations with empirical improvements from transformations that preserve convolutional structure.
summary.tldr: Exponentiating convolutional operators creates invertible, equivariant transformations that improve the reported performance of generative flows.

title: The Convolution Exponential and Generalized Sylvester Flows

abstract: We address the question of characterizing and finding optimal representations for supervised learning. Traditionally, this question has been tackled using the Information Bottleneck, which compresses the inputs while retaining information about the targets, in a decoder-agnostic fashion. In machine learning, however, our goal is not compression but rather generalization, which is intimately linked to the predictive family or decoder of interest (e.g. linear classifier). We propose the Decodable Information Bottleneck (DIB) that considers information retention and compression from the perspective of the desired predictive family. As a result, DIB gives rise to representations that are optimal in terms of expected test performance and can be estimated with guarantees. Empirically, we show that the framework can be used to enforce a small generalization gap on downstream classifiers and to predict the generalization ability of neural networks.

paragraphs: A representation can retain useful information without making that information accessible to the predictor that will use it. This paper studies optimal representations for supervised learning with the downstream predictive family explicitly in view. It argues that representation quality should be tied to generalization and the chosen decoder, such as a linear classifier.

The Decodable Information Bottleneck adapts the information-bottleneck approach by measuring information retention and compression from that decoder's perspective. Traditional information bottlenecks compress inputs while preserving target information without accounting for a particular decoder. DIB instead links those goals to what the desired family of predictors can decode.

Within this framework, the authors characterize representations that are optimal for expected test performance and can be estimated with guarantees. Empirically, they show that DIB can encourage a small gap between training and test performance for downstream classifiers and help predict neural-network generalization. The contribution is a decoder-dependent account of useful representation learning, connecting the structure of learned information to the predictive model expected to use it.
summary.tldr: The Decodable Information Bottleneck defines useful representations relative to a chosen predictive family and connects them to expected test performance.

title: Learning Optimal Representations with the Decodable Information Bottleneck

abstract: Deep sparse networks (DSNs), of which the crux is exploring the high-order feature interactions, have become the state-of-the-art on the prediction task with high-sparsity features. However, these models suffer from low computation efficiency, including large model size and slow model inference, which largely limits these models' application value. In this work, we approach this problem with neural architecture search by automatically searching the critical component in DSNs, the feature-interaction layer. We propose a distilled search space to cover the desired architectures with fewer parameters. We then develop a progressive search algorithm for efficient search on the space and well capture the order-priority property in sparse prediction tasks. Experiments on three real-world benchmark datasets show promising results of PROFIT in both accuracy and efficiency. Further studies validate the feasibility of our designed search space and search algorithm.

paragraphs: Deep sparse networks predict from inputs containing many sparse features, with high-order feature interactions playing a central role. Such interactions let the model consider combinations of features, but the resulting networks can be large and slow at inference. This paper tackles that efficiency problem by automatically searching the architecture of the feature-interaction layer.

The proposed method, PROFIT, first defines a distilled search space intended to include desirable architectures with fewer parameters. It then uses a progressive search algorithm to explore that space efficiently. The search is designed to capture the order-priority property of sparse prediction tasks, making interaction order part of the architecture-search strategy.

Experiments on three real-world benchmark datasets show promising results for both accuracy and efficiency. Additional studies support the feasibility of the chosen search space and algorithm. The contribution is therefore a focused architecture-search approach to a central source of complexity in deep sparse networks. The reported results suggest that selecting feature interactions carefully can help preserve predictive value while improving the practicality of these models.
summary.tldr: PROFIT progressively searches compact feature-interaction layers to improve the accuracy-efficiency balance of deep sparse networks.

title: Progressive Feature Interaction Search for Deep Sparse Network

abstract: We present Long Short-term TRansformer (LSTR), a temporal modeling algorithm for online action detection, which employs a long- and short-term memory mechanism to model prolonged sequence data. It consists of an LSTR encoder that dynamically leverages coarse-scale historical information from an extended temporal window (e.g., 2048 frames spanning of up to 8 minutes), together with an LSTR decoder that focuses on a short time window (e.g., 32 frames spanning 8 seconds) to model the fine-scale characteristics of the data. Compared to prior work, LSTR provides an effective and efficient method to model long videos with fewer heuristics, which is validated by extensive empirical analysis. LSTR achieves state-of-the-art performance on three standard online action detection benchmarks, THUMOS'14, TVSeries, and HACS Segment. Code has been made available at: https://xumingze0308.github.io/projects/lstr.

paragraphs: Online action detection must identify actions as video unfolds, making both recent motion and earlier context relevant. The Long Short-Term Transformer, or LSTR, models these two timescales with separate memory mechanisms. Its design gives extended history and fine-grained recent information distinct roles in the same temporal model.

The encoder dynamically uses coarse information from a long historical window. The abstract gives an example of 2,048 frames spanning up to eight minutes. The decoder focuses on fine-scale characteristics within a short window, illustrated by 32 frames spanning eight seconds. These are examples of the temporal windows, showing how the architecture combines prolonged context with detailed recent observations.

Extensive empirical analysis supports the authors' claim that LSTR models long videos effectively and efficiently with fewer heuristics than prior work. It achieves reported state-of-the-art results on THUMOS'14, TVSeries, and HACS Segment. The findings support separating temporal processing by scale as a practical way to use long video histories for online action detection.
summary.tldr: LSTR combines coarse long-term video memory with detailed short-term processing to achieve strong online action-detection results.

title: Long Short-Term Transformer for Online Action Detection

abstract: Forecasting of time-series data requires imposition of inductive biases to obtain predictive extrapolation, and recent works have imposed Hamiltonian/Lagrangian form to preserve structure for systems with \emph{reversible} dynamics. In this work we present a novel parameterization of dissipative brackets from metriplectic dynamical systems appropriate for learning \emph{irreversible} dynamics with unknown a priori model form. The process learns generalized Casimirs for energy and entropy guaranteed to be conserved and nondecreasing, respectively. Furthermore, for the case of added thermal noise, we guarantee exact preservation of a fluctuation-dissipation theorem, ensuring thermodynamic consistency. We provide benchmarks for dissipative systems demonstrating learned dynamics are more robust and generalize better than either "black-box" or penalty-based approaches.

paragraphs: Forecasting a physical system beyond observed data benefits from a model that respects its governing structure. Prior approaches imposed Hamiltonian or Lagrangian forms suited to reversible dynamics. This paper develops a structure-preserving approach for irreversible processes, where dissipation must be represented even when the model's functional form is not known beforehand.

The authors introduce a parameterization of dissipative brackets within metriplectic dynamical systems. The learned structure includes generalized Casimirs associated with energy and entropy, guaranteeing energy conservation and nondecreasing entropy, respectively. These properties are built into the representation of the dynamics, so learning operates within a form that already enforces the stated physical behavior.

When thermal noise is added, the method also guarantees exact preservation of a fluctuation-dissipation theorem, maintaining thermodynamic consistency in that setting. Benchmarks on dissipative systems show greater robustness and better generalization than black-box or penalty-based approaches. The findings support using structural constraints as part of the model itself when forecasting irreversible dynamics from time-series data.
summary.tldr: The paper learns irreversible dynamics using a structure that guarantees energy conservation, nondecreasing entropy, and thermodynamic consistency under added thermal noise.

title: Machine learning structure preserving brackets for forecasting irreversible processes

abstract: Silicon-photonics-based optical neural network (ONN) is a promising hardware platform that could represent a paradigm shift in efficient AI with its CMOS-compatibility, flexibility, ultra-low execution latency, and high energy efficiency. In-situ training on the online programmable photonic chips is appealing but still encounters challenging issues in on-chip implementability, scalability, and efficiency. In this work, we propose a closed-loop ONN on-chip learning framework L2ight to enable scalable ONN mapping and efficient in-situ learning. L2ight adopts a three-stage learning flow that first calibrates the complicated photonic circuit states under challenging physical constraints, then performs photonic core mapping via combined analytical solving and zeroth-order optimization. A subspace learning procedure with multi-level sparsity is integrated into L2ight to enable in-situ gradient evaluation and fast adaptation, unleashing the power of optics for real on-chip intelligence. Extensive experiments demonstrate our proposed L2ight outperforms prior ONN training protocols with 3-order-of-magnitude higher scalability and over 30x better efficiency, when benchmarked on various models and learning tasks. This synergistic framework is the first scalable on-chip learning solution that pushes this emerging field from intractable to scalable and further to efficient for next-generation self-learnable photonic neural chips. From a co-design perspective, L2ight also provides essential insights for hardware-restricted unitary subspace optimization and efficient sparse training. We open-source our framework at the link.

Hardware constraints complicate calibration, model mapping, and learning. L2ight addresses these connected problems through a closed-loop framework for scalable mapping and in-situ adaptation.

summary.tldr: L2ight combines calibration, photonic mapping, and sparse subspace learning to make on-chip optical-network training substantially more scalable and efficient in benchmarks.

title: L2ight: Enabling On-Chip Learning for Optical Neural Networks via Efficient in-situ Subspace Optimization

abstract: While reinforcement learning algorithms provide automated acquisition of optimal policies, practical application of such methods requires a number of design decisions, such as manually designing reward functions that not only define the task, but also provide sufficient shaping to accomplish it. In this paper, we view reinforcement learning as inferring policies that achieve desired outcomes, rather than as a problem of maximizing rewards. To solve this inference problem, we establish a novel variational inference formulation that allows us to derive a well-shaped reward function which can be learned directly from environment interactions. From the corresponding variational objective, we also derive a new probabilistic Bellman backup operator and use it to develop an off-policy algorithm to solve goal-directed tasks. We empirically demonstrate that this method eliminates the need to hand-craft reward functions for a suite of diverse manipulation and locomotion tasks and leads to effective goal-directed behaviors.

In this paper, we view reinforcement learning as inferring policies that achieve desired outcomes, rather than as a problem of maximizing rewards. To solve this inference problem, we establish a novel variational inference formulation that allows us to derive a well-shaped reward function which can be learned directly from environment interactions. From the corresponding variational objective, we also derive a new probabilistic Bellman backup operator and use it to develop an off-policy algorithm to solve goal-directed tasks. We empirically demonstrate that this method eliminates the need to hand-craft reward functions for a suite of diverse manipulation and locomotion tasks and leads to effective goal-directed behaviors.

A reward function must also provide a useful learning signal along the way, which can demand substantial manual design. This paper reframes goal-directed learning as inferring policies that produce desired outcomes, making the outcome itself central to the formulation.

The authors develop a variational inference objective for this policy-inference problem. From that objective, they derive a shaped reward function that can be learned through interactions with the environment. They also derive a probabilistic Bellman backup operator, connecting the inference formulation to a rule for updating the quantities used in learning.

These components lead to an off-policy algorithm for goal-directed tasks. In experiments spanning manipulation and locomotion, the method produces effective goal-reaching behavior without hand-crafted reward functions. The reported result shows how an inference-based formulation can supply both the reward signal and the learning update in those tasks. Its practical significance is reducing the need to manually engineer rewards that make a specified goal learnable.
summary.tldr: A variational inference formulation learns reward shaping from interaction and supports effective goal-directed behavior without hand-crafted rewards in the evaluated tasks.

title: Outcome-Driven Reinforcement Learning via Variational Inference

abstract: We introduce weak barycenters of a family of probability distributions, based on the recently developed notion of optimal weak transport of mass by Gozlan et al. (2017) and Backhoff-Veraguas et al. (2020). We provide a theoretical analysis of this object and discuss its interpretation in the light of convex ordering between probability measures. In particular, we show that, rather than averaging the input distributions in a geometric way (as the Wasserstein barycenter based on classic optimal transport does) weak barycenters extract common geometric information shared by all the input distributions, encoded as a latent random variable that underlies all of them. We also provide an iterative algorithm to compute a weak barycenter for a finite family of input distributions, and a stochastic algorithm that computes them for arbitrary populations of laws. The latter approach is particularly well suited for the streaming setting, i.e., when distributions are observed sequentially. The notion of weak barycenter and our approaches to compute it are illustrated on synthetic examples, validated on 2D real-world data and compared to standard Wasserstein barycenters.

title: A novel notion of barycenter for probability distributions based on optimal weak mass transport

abstract: Neural network robustness has become a central topic in machine learning in recent years. Most training algorithms that improve the model's robustness to adversarial and common corruptions also introduce a large computational overhead, requiring as many as ten times the number of forward and backward passes in order to converge. To combat this inefficiency, we propose BulletTrain, a boundary example mining technique to drastically reduce the computational cost of robust training. Our key observation is that only a small fraction of examples are beneficial for improving robustness. BulletTrain dynamically predicts these important examples and optimizes robust training algorithms to focus on the important examples. We apply our technique to several existing robust training algorithms and achieve a 2.2x speed-up for TRADES and MART on CIFAR-10 and a 1.7x speed-up for AugMix on CIFAR-10-C and CIFAR-100-C without any reduction in clean and robust accuracy.

BulletTrain targets this overhead so that robustness improvements require less training computation.

The results support selective allocation of robust training computation as a way to retain measured performance while reducing cost.
summary.tldr: BulletTrain focuses robust training on dynamically selected important examples, delivering reported speedups without accuracy loss in the tested settings.

title: BulletTrain: Accelerating Robust Neural Network Training via Boundary Example Mining

abstract: To achieve peak predictive performance, hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is a crucial component of machine learning and its applications. Over the last years, the number of efficient algorithms and tools for HPO grew substantially. At the same time, the community is still lacking realistic, diverse, computationally cheap, and standardized benchmarks. This is especially the case for multi-fidelity HPO methods. To close this gap, we propose HPOBench, which includes 7 existing and 5 new benchmark families, with a total of more than 100 multi-fidelity benchmark problems. HPOBench allows to run this extendable set of multi-fidelity HPO benchmarks in a reproducible way by isolating and packaging the individual benchmarks in containers. It also provides surrogate and tabular benchmarks for computationally affordable yet statistically sound evaluations. To demonstrate HPOBench’s broad compatibility with various optimization tools, as well as its usefulness, we conduct an exemplary large-scale study evaluating 13 optimizers from 6 optimization tools. We provide HPOBench here: https://github.com/automl/HPOBench.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization searches for model settings that improve predictive performance. Comparing optimization methods requires test problems that are realistic, varied, affordable, and consistent across studies. HPOBench addresses the shortage of such resources, particularly for multi-fidelity methods, which evaluate configurations at different levels of computational effort or fidelity.

The collection brings together seven existing benchmark families and five new ones, yielding more than 100 multi-fidelity problems. Each benchmark is isolated and packaged in a container to support reproducible execution. The framework is also extensible, allowing the collection to grow while retaining a shared way to run its problems.

HPOBench includes surrogate and tabular benchmarks to make evaluations computationally affordable while supporting statistically sound comparisons. To demonstrate compatibility and usefulness, the authors conduct a large study involving 13 optimizers from six optimization tools. That study illustrates how the framework can compare methods from different software ecosystems on a common collection of problems, providing infrastructure for more consistent optimization research.
summary.tldr: HPOBench packages more than 100 multi-fidelity hyperparameter optimization problems for reproducible and computationally affordable comparisons.

title: HPOBench: A Collection of Reproducible Multi-Fidelity Benchmark Problems for HPO

abstract: Time series outlier detection has been extensively studied with many advanced algorithms proposed in the past decade. Despite these efforts, very few studies have investigated how we should benchmark the existing algorithms. In particular, using synthetic datasets for evaluation has become a common practice in the literature, and thus it is crucial to have a general synthetic criterion to benchmark algorithms. This is a non-trivial task because the existing synthetic methods are very different in different applications and the outlier definitions are often ambiguous. To bridge this gap, we propose a behavior-driven taxonomy for time series outliers and categorize outliers into point- and pattern-wise outliers with clear context definitions. Following the new taxonomy, we then present a general synthetic criterion and generate 35 synthetic datasets accordingly. We further identify 4 multivariate real-world datasets from different domains and benchmark 9 algorithms on the synthetic and the real-world datasets. Surprisingly, we observe that some classical algorithms could outperform many recent deep learning approaches. The datasets, pre-processing and synthetic scripts, and the algorithm implementations are made publicly available at https://github.com/datamllab/tods/tree/benchmark

paragraphs: Time series outlier detection has many proposed algorithms, but comparing them depends on what counts as an outlier and how test data is constructed. The paper identifies ambiguity in existing definitions and substantial variation in synthetic data generation across applications. These differences make a shared basis for evaluation especially important.

The authors propose a behavior-based taxonomy that separates point-level outliers from pattern-level outliers and explicitly defines their context. They use this taxonomy to establish a general criterion for synthetic data generation, producing 35 datasets. They also select four multivariate real-world datasets from different domains, extending the comparison beyond generated examples.

Nine algorithms are evaluated across the synthetic and real-world collections. Some classical methods can outperform many recent deep learning approaches in these experiments, challenging an assumption that newer model families necessarily provide stronger results. The release includes datasets, preprocessing and generation scripts, and algorithm implementations, linking clearer task definitions with a reproducible way to investigate which methods work under different outlier conditions.
summary.tldr: A clearer outlier taxonomy and shared benchmark reveal cases where classical methods outperform recent deep learning approaches.

title: Revisiting Time Series Outlier Detection: Definitions and Benchmarks

abstract: Coordinate-based networks, usually in the forms of MLPs, have been successfully applied to the task of predicting high-frequency but low-dimensional signals using coordinate inputs. To scale them to model large-scale signals, previous works resort to hybrid representations, combining a coordinate-based network with a grid-based representation, such as sparse voxels. However, such approaches lack a compact global latent representation in its grid, making it difficult to model a distribution of signals, which is important for generalization tasks. To address the limitation, we propose the Levels-of-Experts (LoE) framework, which is a novel coordinate-based representation consisting of an MLP with periodic, position-dependent weights arranged hierarchically. For each linear layer of the MLP, multiple candidate values of its weight matrix are tiled and replicated across the input space, with different layers replicating at different frequencies. Based on the input, only one of the weight matrices is chosen for each layer. This greatly increases the model capacity without incurring extra computation or compromising generalization capability. We show that the new representation is an efficient and competitive drop-in replacement for a wide range of tasks, including signal fitting, novel view synthesis, and generative modeling.

paragraphs: Coordinate-based neural networks represent signals by mapping positions to signal values. Scaling them to larger signals often involves combining a network with a spatial grid. The paper identifies a difficulty with that approach: the grid lacks a compact global latent representation, complicating the task of modeling distributions of signals for generalization.

Levels-of-Experts, or LoE, instead builds position-dependent weights into a multilayer perceptron. Each linear layer has several candidate weight matrices arranged periodically across the input space. Different layers repeat their patterns at different frequencies, creating a hierarchy. For any input coordinate, the network selects just one candidate matrix at each layer.

This selection scheme increases the available model capacity while retaining a single active matrix per layer. The authors report that it achieves this without extra computation or sacrificing generalization capability. Across signal fitting, novel view synthesis, and generative modeling, LoE serves as an efficient and competitive replacement for existing representations. The contribution is a way to add spatial specialization within the coordinate network itself.
summary.tldr: LoE increases coordinate-network capacity through hierarchical, position-dependent weight selection while keeping one active weight matrix per layer.

title: Implicit Neural Representations with Levels-of-Experts

abstract: In this paper, we study a large-scale multi-agent minimax optimization problem, which models many interesting applications in statistical learning and game theory, including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The overall objective is a sum of agents' private local objective functions. We focus on the federated setting, where agents can perform local computation and communicate with a central server. Most existing federated minimax algorithms either require communication per iteration or lack performance guarantees with the exception of Local Stochastic Gradient Descent Ascent (SGDA), a multiple-local-update descent ascent algorithm which guarantees convergence under a diminishing stepsize. By analyzing Local SGDA under the ideal condition of no gradient noise, we show that generally it cannot guarantee exact convergence with constant stepsizes and thus suffers from slow rates of convergence. To tackle this issue, we propose FedGDA-GT, an improved Federated (Fed) Gradient Descent Ascent (GDA) method based on Gradient Tracking (GT). When local objectives are Lipschitz smooth and strongly-convex-strongly-concave, we prove that FedGDA-GT converges linearly with a constant stepsize to global $\epsilon$-approximation solution with $\mathcal{O}(\log (1/\epsilon))$ rounds of communication, which matches the time complexity of centralized GDA method. Then, we analyze the general distributed minimax problem from a statistical aspect, where the overall objective approximates a true population minimax risk by empirical samples. We provide generalization bounds for learning with this objective through Rademacher complexity analysis. Finally, we numerically show that FedGDA-GT outperforms Local SGDA.

paragraphs: This paper studies federated minimax optimization, where agents jointly optimize competing minimization and maximization objectives while keeping local objective functions private. Agents can compute locally and communicate with a central server. The challenge is to reduce communication while retaining a reliable path to an accurate global solution.

The authors first analyze Local Stochastic Gradient Descent Ascent under the idealized condition of noiseless gradients. They show that constant step sizes generally cannot guarantee exact convergence, helping explain why shrinking step sizes and slower convergence arise. Their proposed method, FedGDA-GT, adds gradient tracking to federated gradient descent ascent.

Reaching an epsilon-accurate solution requires communication rounds logarithmic in inverse accuracy, matching the stated centralized iteration complexity. The paper also gives generalization bounds using Rademacher complexity and reports numerical improvements over Local SGDA. Its fast convergence guarantee depends on the specified objective assumptions.
summary.tldr: FedGDA-GT uses gradient tracking to obtain fast, communication-efficient federated minimax optimization under smoothness and strong convexity–concavity assumptions.

title: A Communication-efficient Algorithm with Linear Convergence for Federated Minimax Learning

abstract: We study the constrained reinforcement learning problem, in which an agent aims to maximize the expected cumulative reward subject to a constraint on the expected total value of a utility function. In contrast to existing model-based approaches or model-free methods accompanied with a `simulator’, we aim to develop the first \emph{model-free}, \emph{simulator-free} algorithm that achieves a sublinear regret and a sublinear constraint violation even in \emph{large-scale} systems. To this end, we consider the episodic constrained Markov decision processes with linear function approximation, where the transition dynamics and the reward function can be represented as a linear function of some known feature mapping. We show that $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{d^3H^3T})$ regret and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{d^3H^3T})$ constraint violation bounds can be achieved, where $d$ is the dimension of the feature mapping, $H$ is the length of the episode, and $T$ is the total number of steps. Our bounds are attained without explicitly estimating the unknown transition model or requiring a simulator, and they depend on the state space only through the dimension of the feature mapping. Hence our bounds hold even when the number of states goes to infinity. Our main results are achieved via novel adaptations of the standard LSVI-UCB algorithms. In particular, we first introduce primal-dual optimization into the LSVI-UCB algorithm to balance between regret and constraint violation. More importantly, we replace the standard greedy selection with respect to the state-action function with a soft-max policy. This turns out to be key in establishing uniform concentration (a critical step for provably efficient model-free exploration) for the constrained case via its approximation-smoothness trade-off. Finally, we also show that one can achieve an even zero constraint violation for large enough $T$ by trading the regret a little bit but still maintaining the same order with respect to $T$.

summary.tldr: Under linear feature assumptions, a simulator-free reinforcement learning algorithm achieves sublinear regret and constraint violation.

title: Provably Efficient Model-Free Constrained RL with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: Multi-modal learning is essential for understanding information in the real world. Jointly learning from multi-modal data enables global integration of both shared and modality-specific information, but current strategies often fail when observa- tions from certain modalities are incomplete or missing for part of the subjects. To learn comprehensive representations based on such modality-incomplete data, we present a semi-supervised neural network model called CLUE (Cross-Linked Unified Embedding). Extending from multi-modal VAEs, CLUE introduces the use of cross-encoders to construct latent representations from modality-incomplete observations. Representation learning for modality-incomplete observations is common in genomics. For example, human cells are tightly regulated across multi- ple related but distinct modalities such as DNA, RNA, and protein, jointly defining a cell’s function. We benchmark CLUE on multi-modal data from single cell measurements, illustrating CLUE’s superior performance in all assessed categories of the NeurIPS 2021 Multimodal Single-cell Data Integration Competition. While we focus on analysis of single cell genomic datasets, we note that the proposed cross-linked embedding strategy could be readily applied to other cross-modality representation learning problems.

paragraphs: Multimodal data combine shared information with details specific to each measurement type, but many samples lack one or more modalities. CLUE, or Cross-Linked Unified Embedding, is a semisupervised neural model designed to learn useful representations from these incomplete observations.

The method extends multimodal variational autoencoders with cross-encoders that construct latent representations when modalities are missing. The paper focuses on single-cell measurements, where DNA, RNA, and protein provide related but distinct views of cellular function.

Benchmarks show superior performance in all assessed categories of the NeurIPS 2021 Multimodal Single-cell Data Integration Competition. The abstract does not provide category-level scores or quantify missing-data patterns. Although the cross-linked strategy is proposed as applicable to other multimodal tasks, the reported evidence is from single-cell genomics; broader applicability remains a plausible extension rather than an experimentally established result in every domain.
summary.tldr: CLUE learns cross-modal representations even when some measurements are missing.

title: Cross-Linked Unified Embedding for cross-modality representation learning

abstract: Lipschitz constrained networks have gathered considerable attention in the deep learning community, with usages ranging from Wasserstein distance estimation to the training of certifiably robust classifiers. However they remain commonly considered as less accurate, and their properties in learning are still not fully understood. In this paper we clarify the matter: when it comes to classification 1-Lipschitz neural networks enjoy several advantages over their unconstrained counterpart. First, we show that these networks are as accurate as classical ones, and can fit arbitrarily difficult boundaries. Then, relying on a robustness metric that reflects operational needs we characterize the most robust classifier: the WGAN discriminator. Next, we show that 1-Lipschitz neural networks generalize well under milder assumptions. Finally, we show that hyper-parameters of the loss are crucial for controlling the accuracy-robustness trade-off. We conclude that they exhibit appealing properties to pave the way toward provably accurate, and provably robust neural networks.

paragraphs: Lipschitz constraints limit how much a network's outputs can change as its inputs change. Such networks are used in robustness and distribution comparison, but are often regarded as less accurate classifiers. This paper examines that perception and argues that 1-Lipschitz networks have several useful classification properties.

The authors show that these networks can match classical networks in accuracy and fit arbitrarily difficult decision boundaries. They also characterize the most robust classifier under a robustness metric chosen to reflect operational needs, identifying it with the WGAN discriminator. That characterization depends on the chosen metric; it specifies what robustness means for the result.

The paper further establishes favorable generalization under milder assumptions and emphasizes that loss-function hyperparameters control the balance between accuracy and robustness. The practical message is that evaluating a Lipschitz constraint in isolation misses an important part of the learning setup. The loss and its settings influence which balance is obtained, while the theoretical results support the potential for classifiers with provable accuracy and robustness.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes classification advantages of 1-Lipschitz networks and shows that loss hyperparameters are crucial to their accuracy–robustness trade-off.

title: Pay attention to your loss : understanding misconceptions about Lipschitz neural networks

abstract: In recent years, neural implicit surface reconstruction methods have become popular for multi-view 3D reconstruction. In contrast to traditional multi-view stereo methods, these approaches tend to produce smoother and more complete reconstructions due to the inductive smoothness bias of neural networks. State-of-the-art neural implicit methods allow for high-quality reconstructions of simple scenes from many input views. Yet, their performance drops significantly for larger and more complex scenes and scenes captured from sparse viewpoints. This is caused primarily by the inherent ambiguity in the RGB reconstruction loss that does not provide enough constraints, in particular in less-observed and textureless areas. Motivated by recent advances in the area of monocular geometry prediction, we systematically explore the utility these cues provide for improving neural implicit surface reconstruction. We demonstrate that depth and normal cues, predicted by general-purpose monocular estimators, significantly improve reconstruction quality and optimization time. Further, we analyse and investigate multiple design choices for representing neural implicit surfaces, ranging from monolithic MLP models over single-grid to multi-resolution grid representations. We observe that geometric monocular priors improve performance both for small-scale single-object as well as large-scale multi-object scenes, independent of the choice of representation.
originalAbstract: In recent years, neural implicit surface reconstruction methods have become popular for multi-view 3D reconstruction. In contrast to traditional multi-view stereo methods, these approaches tend to produce smoother and more complete reconstructions due to the inductive smoothness bias of neural networks. State-of-the-art neural implicit methods allow for high-quality reconstructions of simple scenes from many input views. Yet, their performance drops significantly for larger and more complex scenes and scenes captured from sparse viewpoints. This is caused primarily by the inherent ambiguity in the RGB reconstruction loss that does not provide enough constraints, in particular in less-observed and textureless areas. Motivated by recent advances in the area of monocular geometry prediction, we systematically explore the utility these cues provide for improving neural implicit surface reconstruction. We demonstrate that depth and normal cues, predicted by general-purpose monocular estimators, significantly improve reconstruction quality and optimization time. Further, we analyse and investigate multiple design choices for representing neural implicit surfaces, ranging from monolithic MLP models over single-grid to multi-resolution grid representations. We observe that geometric monocular priors improve performance both for small-scale single-object as well as large-scale multi-object scenes, independent of the choice of representation.

paragraphs: Neural implicit methods reconstruct 3D surfaces from multiple images and often produce smooth, complete results. Their performance can deteriorate for complex scenes or sparse viewpoints because matching image colors leaves the geometry ambiguous. Areas with little texture or few observations are particularly weakly constrained by that objective.

MonoSDF systematically investigates adding depth and surface-normal cues predicted by general-purpose monocular estimators. These cues provide geometric information beyond the RGB reconstruction signal. The authors also compare several ways of representing the surface, including a single multilayer perceptron, a single grid, and grids at multiple resolutions.

The study finds that monocular depth and normal cues significantly improve reconstruction quality and optimization time. Benefits appear for both small scenes containing one object and larger scenes containing multiple objects, across the investigated representation choices. This matters because the useful addition is geometric guidance that works with several surface models. The results support using monocular predictions to constrain ambiguities that image-color matching alone does not adequately resolve.
summary.tldr: MonoSDF shows that predicted monocular depth and normals improve neural surface reconstruction quality and optimization time across several representations.

title: MonoSDF: Exploring Monocular Geometric Cues for Neural Implicit Surface Reconstruction

abstract: We propose a general and efficient framework to control auto-regressive generation models with NeurAlly-Decomposed Oracle (NADO). Given a pre-trained base language model and a sequence-level boolean oracle function, we aim to decompose the oracle function into token-level guidance to steer the base model in text generation. Specifically, the token-level guidance is provided by NADO, a neural model trained with examples sampled from the base model, demanding no additional auxiliary labeled data. Based on posterior regularization, we present the close-form optimal solution to incorporate the decomposed token-level guidance into the base model for controllable generation. We further discuss how the neural approximation affects the quality of the solution. These experiments conducted on two different applications: (1) text generation with lexical constraints and (2) machine translation with formality control demonstrate that our framework efficiently guides the base model towards the given oracle while keeping high generation quality.

paragraphs: A rule for judging a completed text does not directly tell a language model which token to generate next. This paper addresses that gap with NADO, a neural model that turns a sequence-level yes-or-no oracle into token-level guidance. The goal is to steer an existing autoregressive language model toward outputs that satisfy the oracle.

NADO is trained using examples sampled from the base language model, without requiring an additional auxiliary labeled dataset. The authors use posterior regularization to derive a closed-form optimal way to incorporate the decomposed guidance into generation. They also examine how approximating the guidance with a neural network affects the quality of that solution.

Experiments cover lexical constraints in text generation and formality control in machine translation. In these applications, the framework efficiently steers outputs toward the oracle while retaining high generation quality. The approach matters because it connects a criterion defined over complete outputs to the incremental decisions a language model must make while producing them.
summary.tldr: NADO learns token-level guidance from a whole-sequence oracle to control a pretrained language model without additional auxiliary labeled data.

title: Controllable Text Generation with Neurally-Decomposed Oracle

abstract: The success of style-based generators largely benefits from style modulation,which helps take care of the cross-instance variation within data. However, theinstance-wise stochasticity is typically introduced via regular convolution, wherekernels interact with features at some fixed locations, limiting its capacity formodeling geometric variation. To alleviate this problem, we equip the generatorin generative adversarial networks (GANs) with a plug-and-play module, termedas modulated transformation module (MTM). This module predicts spatial offsetsunder the control of latent codes, based on which the convolution operation canbe applied at variable locations for different instances, and hence offers the modelan additional degree of freedom to handle geometry deformation. Extensiveexperiments suggest that our approach can be faithfully generalized to variousgenerative tasks, including image generation, 3D-aware image synthesis, andvideo generation, and get compatible with state-of-the-art frameworks withoutany hyper-parameter tuning. It is noteworthy that, towards human generation onthe challenging TaiChi dataset, we improve the FID of StyleGAN3 from 21.36 to13.60, demonstrating the efficacy of learning modulated geometry transformation.Code and models are available at https://github.com/limbo0000/mtm.

paragraphs: Style-based generators use modulation to capture differences between generated examples. However, ordinary convolution still processes features at fixed spatial locations, restricting how directly it can represent geometric variation. This paper adds a mechanism that lets the generator change where convolution operates according to the particular example being generated.

The proposed modulated transformation module predicts spatial offsets under the control of latent codes. Those offsets allow convolution to access variable locations for different instances. This gives the generator an additional way to express geometric deformation, complementing the variation already handled by style modulation. The module is designed to plug into existing GAN generators.

Experiments suggest that the approach transfers across image generation, 3D-aware image synthesis, and video generation, and works with leading frameworks without hyperparameter tuning. For human generation on TaiChi, it reduces StyleGAN3’s FID from 21.36 to 13.60. This concrete improvement supports the usefulness of learning spatial transformations, while the broader experiments indicate compatibility across the evaluated generation tasks.
summary.tldr: A plug-in GAN module learns latent-controlled spatial offsets so convolution can better model geometric variation.

title: Learning Modulated Transformation in GANs

abstract: Locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) based frameworks have been used efficiently to select weight vectors in a dense hidden layer with high cosine similarity to an input, enabling dynamic pruning. While this type of scheme has been shown to improve computational training efficiency, existing algorithms require repeated randomized projection of the full layer weight, which is impractical for computational- and memory-constrained devices. In a distributed setting, deferring LSH analysis to a centralized host is (i) slow if the device cluster is large and (ii) requires access to input data which is forbidden in a federated context. Using a new family of hash functions, we develop the first private, personalized, and memory-efficient on-device LSH framework.Our framework enables privacy and personalization by allowing each device to generate hash tables, without the help of a central host, using device-specific hashing hyper-parameters (e.g., number of hash tables or hash length).Hash tables are generated with a compressed set of the full weights, and can be serially generated and discarded if the process is memory-intensive.This allows devices to avoid maintaining (i) the fully-sized model and (ii) large amounts of hash tables in local memory for LSH analysis. We prove several statistical and sensitivity properties of our hash functions, and experimentally demonstrate that our framework is competitive in training large scale recommender networks compared to other LSH frameworks which assume unrestricted on-device capacity.

paragraphs: Locality-sensitive hashing can select hidden-layer weight vectors that closely match an input, enabling dynamic pruning during training. However, repeatedly projecting an entire layer’s weights is expensive for devices with limited memory and computation. Moving that work to a central host also creates scaling problems and requires input access that conflicts with the federated setting considered here.

The authors introduce a family of hash functions that lets devices construct their own hash tables from compressed weights. Each device can choose settings such as table count and hash length. Tables can also be constructed and discarded sequentially when memory is tight. Consequently, the hashing analysis does not require storing either the full-sized model or many tables locally.

The paper proves statistical and sensitivity properties of its hash functions and evaluates large-scale recommender training. The framework remains competitive with other hashing approaches that assume unrestricted device capacity. Its practical contribution is to make hashing-based selection compatible with local input handling, device-specific configuration, and constrained memory, without relying on a central host to perform the analysis.
summary.tldr: A new on-device hashing framework enables personalized dynamic pruning from compressed weights without centralized input access or unrestricted device memory.

title: Large-Scale Distributed Learning via Private On-Device LSH

abstract: Most of the literature on learning in games has focused on the restrictive setting where the underlying repeated game does not change over time. Much less is known about the convergence of no-regret learning algorithms in dynamic multiagent settings. In this paper, we characterize the convergence of optimistic gradient descent (OGD) in time-varying games. Our framework yields sharp convergence bounds for the equilibrium gap of OGD in zero-sum games parameterized on natural variation measures of the sequence of games, subsuming known results for static games. Furthermore, we establish improved second-order variation bounds under strong convexity-concavity, as long as each game is repeated multiple times. Our results also apply to time-varying general-sum multi-player games via a bilinear formulation of correlated equilibria, which has novel implications for meta-learning and for obtaining refined variation-dependent regret bounds, addressing questions left open in prior papers. Finally, we leverage our framework to also provide new insights on dynamic regret guarantees in static games.

paragraphs: Learning in games is often analyzed with an unchanged game repeated over time. This paper studies optimistic gradient descent when the game itself changes. The question is how close the learning dynamics remain to equilibrium as the environment varies, extending convergence analysis beyond the static setting.

For zero-sum games, the authors derive sharp bounds on the equilibrium gap in terms of measures of variation across the sequence of games. These bounds include known static-game results as a special case. They also obtain improved second-order variation bounds under strong convexity-concavity, provided that each game is repeated multiple times. Both requirements are part of that stronger result.

A bilinear formulation of correlated equilibria extends the framework to changing general-sum games with multiple players. The authors derive implications for meta-learning and more refined variation-dependent regret bounds, addressing questions from prior work. The same framework also gives insights into dynamic regret in static games. Overall, the analysis makes the amount and structure of environmental change explicit in learning guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds optimistic gradient descent’s equilibrium gap in changing games using measures of how much the games vary.

title: On the Convergence of No-Regret Learning Dynamics in Time-Varying Games

abstract: Generalization bounds are valuable both for theory and applications. On the one hand, they shed light on the mechanisms that underpin the learning processes; on the other, they certify how well a learned model performs against unseen inputs. In this work we build upon a recent breakthrough in compression theory to develop a new framework yielding tight generalization bounds of wide practical applicability. The core idea is to embed any given learning algorithm into a suitably-constructed meta-algorithm (here called Pick-to-Learn, P2L) in order to instill desirable compression properties. When applied to the MNIST classification dataset and to a synthetic regression problem, P2L not only attains generalization bounds that compare favorably with the state of the art (test-set and PAC-Bayes bounds), but it also learns models with better post-training performance.
