paragraphs: ReStraV detects generated videos by examining how their visual representations change over time. Its starting point is the perceptual straightening hypothesis: trajectories from real-world videos tend to become straighter when expressed in a neural representation space. The paper investigates whether departures from that geometric pattern can help distinguish synthetic videos from natural ones.

The method uses the pretrained self-supervised vision transformer DINOv2 to represent video content. It then measures temporal curvature and the distances between successive representations. These quantities describe how sharply the representation trajectory turns and how far it moves. Statistical and signal descriptors summarize those measurements for each video, and a lightweight classifier learns to distinguish the resulting patterns.

The authors report significant differences between real and generated videos in both curvature and distance patterns. On VidProM, ReStraV achieves 97.17% accuracy and 98.63% AUROC, outperforming the compared image- and video-based detectors. The reported computational efficiency makes representation geometry a promising low-cost detection signal, with the demonstrated performance tied to the evaluations described.
summary.tldr: ReStraV detects AI-generated videos using differences in the curvature and movement of their neural representations over time.

title: AI-Generated Video Detection via Perceptual Straightening

abstract: Text-to-video generative models convert textual prompts into dynamic visual content, offering wide-ranging applications in film production, gaming, and education. However, their real-world performance often falls short of user expectations. One key reason is that these models have not been trained on videos related to some topics users want to create. In this paper, we propose VideoUFO, the first Video dataset specifically curated to align with Users' FOcus in real-world scenarios. Beyond this, our VideoUFO also features: (1) minimal (0.29\%) overlap with existing video datasets, and (2) videos searched exclusively via YouTube's official API under the Creative Commons license. These two attributes provide future researchers with greater freedom to broaden their training sources. The VideoUFO comprises over 1.09 million video clips, each paired with both a brief and a detailed caption (description). Specifically, through clustering, we first identify 1,291 user-focused topics from the million-scale real text-to-video prompt dataset, VidProM. Then, we use these topics to retrieve videos from YouTube, split the retrieved videos into clips, and generate both brief and detailed captions for each clip. After verifying the clips with specified topics, we are left with about 1.09 million video clips. Our experiments reveal that (1) current 16 text-to-video models do not achieve consistent performance across all user-focused topics; and (2) a simple model trained on VideoUFO outperforms others on worst-performing topics. The dataset and code are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/WenhaoWang/VideoUFO and https://github.com/WangWenhao0716/BenchUFO under the CC BY 4.0 License.

paragraphs: VideoUFO addresses a mismatch between the videos used to train text-to-video models and the topics people actually request. A model may perform unevenly because its training material does not cover some desired subjects. The dataset therefore starts from real user prompts to guide which videos are collected.

The authors cluster the million-scale VidProM prompt collection into 1,291 user-focused topics. They retrieve Creative Commons videos through YouTube’s official API, divide them into clips, generate short and detailed captions, and verify topic relevance. The resulting collection contains over 1.09 million clips and has a reported overlap of only 0.29% with existing video datasets.

Tests of 16 text-to-video models reveal inconsistent performance across the user-focused topics. A simple model trained on VideoUFO outperforms other models on the worst-performing topics in the experiments. These findings support the value of choosing training data around observed user interests, particularly for topics existing systems handle poorly. The paper contributes both a large captioned video collection and evidence connecting topic coverage to generation performance.
summary.tldr: VideoUFO collects over 1.09 million captioned clips around real user interests to improve coverage of difficult text-to-video topics.

title: VideoUFO: A Million-Scale User-Focused Dataset for Text-to-Video Generation

abstract: Federated continual learning (FCL) aims to maintain the model's performance on old tasks (i.e., stability) while enhancing its ability to acquire knowledge from current tasks (i.e., plasticity). With the development of pre-trained models (PTMs), fine-tuning PTMs on clients has become a promising approach to leveraging their extensive knowledge in FCL. In this paper, we propose MultiFCL, a novel FCL framework that fine-tunes PTMs to adapt to FCL while preserving their strong generalization capabilities. Specifically, to ensure the stability, MultiFCL introduces lightweight adapters for task adaption, which are subsequently frozen to prevent catastrophic forgetting. Moreover, by utilizing the semantic features of old tasks, MultiFCL performs multi-modal initialization of new task class prototypes. To enhance the plasticity, MultiFCL employs a multi-expert training mechanism that integrates multi-scale feature learning with multi-teacher dynamic self-distillation. Through intra-client and inter-client expert communication, MultiFCL facilitates cross-task and cross-client knowledge fusion. Experimental results demonstrate that MultiFCL achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets and settings, showcasing its effectiveness in FCL scenarios.

paragraphs: Federated continual learning must keep useful knowledge from earlier tasks while learning new tasks across clients. These goals are often described as stability and plasticity. MultiFCL builds on pretrained models, aiming to adapt their knowledge to this setting while retaining their generalization capabilities through a coordinated set of lightweight adaptation and knowledge-sharing mechanisms.

For stability, the framework learns task adapters and then freezes them to prevent catastrophic forgetting. It also uses semantic features from older tasks to initialize new class prototypes through multiple modalities. This gives new tasks a starting representation informed by previous knowledge while protecting the learned adapters associated with earlier tasks.

For plasticity, MultiFCL combines learning at multiple feature scales with dynamic self-distillation from multiple teachers. Experts communicate within and across clients, supporting knowledge fusion across both tasks and clients. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets and settings. The findings support coordinating protected task-specific knowledge with active expert communication as an effective way to address the competing demands of federated continual learning.
summary.tldr: MultiFCL combines frozen task adapters with communicating experts to preserve old knowledge and learn new tasks across federated clients.

title: Federated Continual Learning via Orchestrating Multi-Scale Expertise

abstract: Effective trajectory stitching for long-horizon planning is a significant challenge in robotic decision-making. While diffusion models have shown promise in planning, they are limited to solving tasks similar to those seen in their training data. We propose CompDiffuser, a novel generative approach that can solve new tasks by learning to compositionally stitch together shorter trajectory chunks from previously seen tasks. Our key insight is modeling the trajectory distribution by subdividing it into overlapping chunks and learning their conditional relationships through a single bidirectional diffusion model. This allows information to propagate between segments during generation, ensuring physically consistent connections. We conduct experiments on benchmark tasks of various difficulties, covering different environment sizes, agent state dimension, trajectory types, training data quality, and show that CompDiffuser significantly outperforms existing methods.

paragraphs: Long-horizon robotic planning requires useful short movements to fit together into a coherent longer trajectory. Diffusion planners can struggle when a new task differs from the tasks represented in training. CompDiffuser addresses this problem by learning to compose shorter trajectory chunks from previously seen tasks into solutions for new ones.

The method divides trajectories into overlapping segments and uses one bidirectional diffusion model to learn conditional relationships between them. During generation, information can propagate between segments, allowing neighboring parts to influence each other. The overlap and conditional modeling support physically consistent connections, making the compatibility of the segments part of the generation process itself.

The experiments cover benchmark tasks with differences in environment size, agent state dimension, trajectory type, and training-data quality. Across these evaluations, the authors report substantial improvements over existing methods. The findings support composition as a route to solving tasks beyond the particular complete trajectories seen during training, with the ability to coordinate connections between chunks serving as the central mechanism.
summary.tldr: CompDiffuser generates plans for new tasks by jointly stitching overlapping trajectory chunks with a bidirectional diffusion model.

title: Generative Trajectory Stitching through Diffusion Composition

abstract: Sampling multiple outputs from a Large Language Model (LLM) and selecting the most frequent (Self-consistency) or highest-scoring (Best-of-N) candidate is a popular approach to achieve higher accuracy in tasks with discrete final answers. Best-of-N (BoN) selects the output with the highest reward, and with perfect rewards, it often achieves near-perfect accuracy. With imperfect rewards from reward models, however, BoN fails to reliably find the correct answer and its performance degrades drastically. We consider the distribution of BoN’s outputs and highlight that, although the correct answer does not usually have a probability close to one under imperfect rewards, it is often the most likely outcome. This suggests that the mode of this distribution can be more reliably correct than a sample from it. Based on this idea, we propose Majority-of-the-Bests (MoB), a novel selection mechanism that estimates the output distribution of BoN via bootstrapping and selects its mode. Experimental results across five benchmarks, three different base LLMs, and two reward models demonstrate consistent improvements over BoN in 25 out of 30 setups. We also provide theoretical results for the consistency of the bootstrapping. MoB serves as a simple, yet strong alternative to BoN and self-consistency, and more broadly, motivates further research in more nuanced selection mechanisms.

paragraphs: Best-of-N improves language-model answers by generating several candidates and choosing the one with the highest reward score. Its reliability depends on the reward model: an imperfect scorer can elevate an incorrect answer. This paper examines the distribution of answers that Best-of-N selects, rather than relying on a single winning candidate.

The key observation is that the correct answer can remain the most likely Best-of-N outcome even when its probability is far below one. Majority-of-the-Bests estimates that outcome distribution through bootstrapping and selects its most frequent answer. This combines reward-based selection with a vote over the resulting selections, aiming to make imperfect reward judgments more dependable.

Across five benchmarks, three base language models, and two reward models, the method improves on Best-of-N in 25 of 30 setups. The authors also provide theoretical consistency results for the bootstrapping procedure. The findings support a stronger selection mechanism for discrete-answer tasks, while the reported success rate makes clear that the improvement is not universal across evaluated configurations.
summary.tldr: Majority-of-the-Bests bootstraps Best-of-N selections and chooses their most frequent answer, improving results in 25 of 30 tested setups.

title: Majority of the Bests: Improving Best-of-N via Bootstrapping

abstract: Reward shaping in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) for complex tasks remains a significant challenge. Existing approaches often fail to find optimal solutions or cannot efficiently handle such tasks. We propose HYPRL, a specification-guided reinforcement learning framework that learns control policies w.r.t. hyperproperties expressed in HyperLTL. Hyperproperties constitute a powerful formalism for specifying objectives and constraints over sets of execution traces across agents. To learn policies that maximize the satisfaction of a HyperLTL formula $\varphi$, we apply Skolemization to manage quantifier alternations and define quantitative robustness functions to shape rewards over execution traces of a Markov decision process with unknown transitions. A suitable RL algorithm is then used to learn policies that collectively maximize the expected reward and, consequently, increase the probability of satisfying $\varphi$. We evaluate HYPRL on a diverse set of benchmarks, including safety-aware planning, Deep Sea Treasure, and the Post Correspondence Problem. We also compare with specification-driven baselines to demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of HYPRL.

paragraphs: Some control objectives concern relationships among several possible executions or among agents, making reward design difficult. HYPRL addresses this using hyperproperties expressed in HyperLTL. These formal specifications describe objectives and constraints over sets of execution traces, providing a structured way to state what the learned policies should collectively achieve.

The framework applies Skolemization to manage alternations between quantifiers in the specification. It then defines quantitative robustness functions that turn trace-level satisfaction into a reward signal. A suitable reinforcement learning algorithm learns policies for a Markov decision process whose transitions are unknown, using these rewards to guide behavior toward the formal objective.

The goal is to maximize expected reward and thereby increase the probability of satisfying the HyperLTL formula. The abstract does not claim that every learned policy satisfies the specification with certainty. Evaluations span safety-aware planning, Deep Sea Treasure, and the Post Correspondence Problem, with comparisons against specification-driven baselines demonstrating effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution connects expressive multi-execution requirements to a usable reward-shaping procedure.
summary.tldr: HYPRL converts formal requirements over multiple execution traces into rewards that guide policies toward a higher probability of satisfying those requirements.

title: HypRL: Reinforcement Learning of Control Policies for Hyperproperties

abstract: This paper introduces **ReservoirTTA**, a novel plug–in framework designed for prolonged test–time adaptation (TTA) in scenarios where the test domain continuously shifts over time, including cases where domains recur or evolve gradually. At its core, ReservoirTTA maintains a reservoir of domain-specialized models—an adaptive test-time model ensemble—that both detects new domains via online clustering over style features of incoming samples and routes each sample to the appropriate specialized model, and thereby enables domain-specific adaptation. This multi-model strategy overcomes key limitations of single model adaptation, such as catastrophic forgetting, inter-domain interference, and error accumulation, ensuring robust and stable performance on sustained non-stationary test distributions. Our theoretical analysis reveals key components that bound parameter variance and prevent model collapse, while our plug–in TTA module mitigates catastrophic forgetting of previously encountered domains. Extensive experiments on scene-level corruption benchmarks (ImageNet-C, CIFAR-10/100-C), object-level style shifts (DomainNet-126, PACS), and semantic segmentation (Cityscapes→ACDC) — covering recurring and continuously evolving domain shifts — show that ReservoirTTA substantially improves adaptation accuracy and maintains stable performance across prolonged, recurring shifts, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/LTS5/ReservoirTTA.

summary.tldr: ReservoirTTA routes incoming samples to domain-specialized models to sustain adaptation across recurring and evolving test conditions.

title: ReservoirTTA: Prolonged Test-time Adaptation for Evolving and Recurring Domains

abstract: We study the regret in stochastic Multi-Armed Bandits (MAB) with multiple agents that communicate over an arbitrary connected communication graph. We analyzed a variant of Cooperative Successive Elimination algorithm, $\texttt{Coop-SE}$, and show an individual regret bound of ${O}(\mathcal{R} / m + A^2 + A \sqrt{\log T})$ and a nearly matching lower bound. Here $A$ is the number of actions, $T$ the time horizon, $m$ the number of agents, and $\mathcal{R} = \sum_{\Delta_i > 0}\log(T)/\Delta_i$ is the optimal single agent regret, where $\Delta_i$ is the sub-optimality gap of action $i$. Our work is the first to show an individual regret bound in cooperative stochastic MAB that is independent of the graph's diameter. When considering communication networks there are additional considerations beyond regret, such as message size and number of communication rounds. First, we show that our regret bound holds even if we restrict the messages to be of logarithmic size. Second, for logarithmic number of communication rounds, we obtain a regret bound of ${O}(\mathcal{R} / m+A \log T)$.

Its focus is the regret experienced by each individual agent, so the guarantee describes personal learning costs rather than only the group's combined performance.

For a variant of Cooperative Successive Elimination, the authors bound individual regret by O(R/m + A² + A√log T). Here R is the optimal single-agent regret expression, m is the number of agents, A is the number of actions, and T is the time horizon. The leading R/m term captures a benefit from cooperation, while the remaining terms represent additional costs. A nearly matching lower bound supports the strength of this guarantee.

Crucially, the bound does not depend on the graph's diameter, a first for individual regret in this setting according to the authors. It remains valid with logarithmic-size messages. A separate result restricts communication to logarithmically many rounds and obtains O(R/m + A log T), clarifying how learning guarantees interact with communication constraints.
summary.tldr: A cooperative bandit algorithm achieves individual regret guarantees independent of communication-graph diameter, including under communication restrictions.

title: Individual Regret in Cooperative Stochastic Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: We introduce Support Vector Generation (SVG), a kernel-based framework that converts a frozen language model into an interpretable, training-free classifier for zero- and few-shot learning. SVG operates by combining Metropolis–Hastings sampling with support vector machine optimization in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) induced by the language model's embedding. Each classification decision is based on a weighted combination of at most 32 natural-language sentences, which serve as explicit support vectors and provide faithful rationales. Our theoretical analysis proves that SVG minimizes the empirical hinge loss over the span of the supports and admits a generalization bound independent of the language model size. Experiments on the GLUE benchmark show that SVG matches or surpasses prompting-based zero-shot baselines in accuracy across multiple tasks—without any fine-tuning or GPU acceleration. Notably, our CPU-only implementation completes training in under three minutes per task, and maintains competitive inference speed. These results suggest that SVG offers a viable path toward efficient, interpretable NLP systems under compute constraints.

title: Support Vector Generation: Kernelizing Large Language Models for Efficient Zero‑Shot NLP

abstract: We study reinforcement learning in non-stationary communicating MDPs whose transition drift admits a low-rank plus sparse structure. We propose SVUCRL (Structured Variation UCRL) and prove the dynamic-regret bound $ \widetilde{\mathcal O}\bigl( D_{\max}S\sqrt{A T} +D_{\max}\sqrt{(B_r+B_p)K S T} +D_{\max}\,\delta_B\,B_p \bigr). $ where $S$ is the number of states, $A$ the number of actions, $T$ the horizon, $D_{\max}$ the MDP diameter, $B_r$/$B_p$ the total reward/transition variation budgets, and $K SA$ the rank of the structured drift. The first term is the statistical price of learning in stationary problems; the second is the \emph{non-stationarity price}, which scales with $\sqrt{K}$ rather than $\sqrt{SA}$ when drift is low-rank. This matches the $\sqrt{T}$ rate (up to logs) and improves on prior $T^{3/4}$-type guarantees. SVUCRL combines: (i) online low-rank tracking with explicit Frobenius guarantees, (ii) incremental RPCA to separate structured drift from sparse shocks, (iii) adaptive confidence widening via a bias-corrected local-variation estimator, and (iv) factor forecasting with an optimal shrinkage center.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes harder when an environment changes during learning. This paper studies communicating Markov decision processes whose transition changes have a low-rank component together with sparse changes. That structural assumption allows the algorithm to exploit coordinated variation instead of treating every transition change as independent.

The proposed SVUCRL algorithm tracks low-rank variation online and uses incremental robust principal component analysis to separate structured drift from sparse shocks. It also adjusts confidence ranges using a bias-corrected estimate of local variation and forecasts factors with a shrinkage center. These components connect estimates of environmental change to the learner's uncertainty.

For low-rank drift, the non-stationarity contribution scales with the square root of the structural parameter K rather than the square root of the state-action count. The stated bound achieves square-root time scaling up to logarithms, improving on prior three-quarter-power guarantees under the studied structure.
summary.tldr: SVUCRL exploits low-rank and sparse transition changes to obtain improved regret guarantees in non-stationary reinforcement learning.

title: Optimal Regret Bounds via Low-Rank Structured Variation in Non-Stationary Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Improving robustness of the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to input degradations is critical for its deployment in high-stakes applications such as autonomous driving and robotics. Our approach to this challenge prioritizes three key aspects: first, parameter efficiency to maintain the inherent generalization capability of SAM; second, fine-grained and input-aware robustification to precisely address the input corruption; and third, adherence to standard training protocols for ease of training. To this end, we propose gated-rank adaptation (GaRA). GaRA introduces lightweight adapters into intermediate layers of the frozen SAM, where each adapter dynamically adjusts the effective rank of its weight matrix based on the input by selectively activating (rank-1) components of the matrix using a learned gating module. This adjustment enables fine-grained and input-aware robustification without compromising the generalization capability of SAM. Our model, GaRA-SAM, significantly outperforms prior work on all robust segmentation benchmarks. In particular, it surpasses the previous best IoU score by up to 21.3%p on ACDC, a challenging real corrupted image dataset.

title: GaRA-SAM: Robustifying Segment Anything Model with Gated-Rank Adaptation

abstract: We propose a novel functorial graph coarsening method that preserves inner products between node features, a property often overlooked by existing approaches focusing primarily on structural fidelity. By treating node features as functions on the graph and preserving their inner products, our method retains both structural and feature relationships, facilitating substantial benefits for downstream tasks. To formalize this, we introduce the Inner Product Error (IPE), which quantifies how the inner products between node features are preserved. Leveraging the underlying geometry of the problem on the Grassmann manifold, we formulate an optimization objective that minimizes the IPE, also for unseen smooth functions. We show that minimizing the IPE improves standard coarsening metrics, and illustrate our method’s properties through visual examples that highlight its clustering ability. Empirical results on benchmarks for graph coarsening and node classification show that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Graph coarsening creates a smaller representation of a graph while trying to retain useful information. This paper argues that preserving structural relationships alone overlooks relationships among node features. Its method treats those features as functions on the graph and explicitly seeks to preserve their inner products during coarsening.

The authors introduce Inner Product Error, or IPE, to quantify how much those relationships change. They formulate an optimization objective using the geometry of the Grassmann manifold and minimize IPE, including for unseen smooth functions. This makes feature relationships a direct target of the coarsening procedure alongside the graph's structural information.

The paper shows that reducing IPE also improves standard coarsening metrics, connecting its proposed objective to established measures of graph preservation. Visual examples illustrate the method's clustering behavior, and experiments on graph-coarsening and node-classification benchmarks show gains over the compared state-of-the-art approaches. These results support preserving feature interactions as a useful principle for constructing smaller graphs that remain effective for downstream learning.
summary.tldr: The method coarsens graphs by preserving inner products among node features, improving both coarsening measures and node-classification results.

title: Spectral Graph Coarsening Using Inner Product Preservation and the Grassmann Manifold

abstract: Decision-making across various fields, such as medicine, heavily relies on conditional average treatment effects (CATEs). Practitioners commonly make decisions by checking whether the estimated CATE is positive, even though the decision-making performance of modern CATE estimators is poorly understood from a theoretical perspective. In this paper, we study optimal decision-making based on two-stage CATE estimators (e.g., DR-learner), which are considered state-of-the-art and widely used in practice. We prove that, while such estimators may be optimal for estimating CATE, they can be suboptimal when used for decision-making. Intuitively, this occurs because such estimators prioritize CATE accuracy in regions far away from the decision boundary, which is ultimately irrelevant to decision-making. As a remedy, we propose a novel two-stage learning objective that retargets the CATE to balance CATE estimation error and decision performance. We then propose a neural method that optimizes an adaptively-smoothed approximation of our learning objective. Finally, we confirm the effectiveness of our method both empirically and theoretically. In sum, our work is the first to show how state-of-the-art CATE estimators can be adapted for optimal decision-making.

paragraphs: Conditional average treatment effects estimate how an intervention's average impact varies with observed characteristics. A common decision rule chooses the intervention when its estimated effect is positive. This paper shows that an estimator can be optimal at predicting treatment-effect values yet still be suboptimal for making decisions with that rule.

The analysis focuses on two-stage estimators such as the DR-learner. Their estimation objectives can prioritize accuracy far from the decision boundary, where changing the estimated magnitude may leave the chosen action unchanged. Errors near the boundary matter differently because they can change which action is selected. This creates a mismatch between accurate effect estimation and good decision performance.

The authors propose a two-stage learning objective that retargets treatment-effect estimation to balance these concerns. A neural method optimizes an adaptively smoothed approximation of the objective. The paper supports the method both theoretically and empirically. Its central implication is that the purpose of an estimate should shape its training objective: when estimates drive decisions, optimizing numerical accuracy alone may not produce the best choices.
summary.tldr: Treatment-effect estimators can make suboptimal decisions despite optimal estimation accuracy; a retargeted objective better balances both goals.

title: Treatment Effect Estimation for Optimal Decision-Making

abstract: The theory of training deep networks has become a central question of modern machine learning and has inspired many practical advancements. In particular, the gradient descent (GD) optimization algorithm has been extensively studied in recent years. A key assumption about GD has appeared in several recent works: the \emph{GD map is non-singular} --- it preserves sets of measure zero under preimages. Crucially, this assumption has been used to prove that GD avoids saddle points and maxima, and to establish the existence of a computable quantity that determines the convergence to global minima (both for GD and stochastic GD). However, the current literature either assumes the non-singularity of the GD map or imposes restrictive assumptions, such as Lipschitz smoothness of the loss (for example, Lipschitzness does not hold for deep ReLU networks with the cross-entropy loss) and restricts the analysis to GD with small step-sizes. In this paper, we investigate the neural network map as a function on the space of weights and biases. We also prove, for the first time, the non-singularity of the gradient descent (GD) map on the loss landscape of realistic neural network architectures (with fully connected, convolutional, or softmax attention layers) and piecewise analytic activations (which includes sigmoid, ReLU, leaky ReLU, etc.) for almost all step-sizes. Our work significantly extends the existing results on the convergence of GD and SGD by guaranteeing that they apply to practical neural network settings and has the potential to unlock further exploration of learning dynamics.

paragraphs: Several analyses of neural-network training rely on a property called non-singularity of the gradient descent map. Here, this means that the preimage of a measure-zero set also has measure zero. The property has been used in results about avoiding saddles and maxima and in characterizations of convergence to global minima.

Previous work often assumes non-singularity or obtains it using restrictive smoothness conditions and small step sizes. Its activation class includes piecewise analytic functions such as ReLU, leaky ReLU, and sigmoid.

The guarantee holds for almost all step sizes, extending the scope beyond analyses restricted to small steps. This supplies a previously assumed ingredient for convergence results in more practical neural-network settings. The result establishes a structural property of the update map; its significance lies in broadening the applicability of existing analyses of gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent.
summary.tldr: The paper proves gradient descent map non-singularity for practical neural architectures with piecewise analytic activations at almost all step sizes.

title: Non-Singularity of the Gradient Descent Map for Neural Networks with Piecewise Analytic Activations

abstract: We analyze task orderings in continual learning for linear regression, assuming joint realizability of training data. We focus on orderings that greedily maximize dissimilarity between consecutive tasks, a concept briefly explored in prior work but still surrounded by open questions. Using tools from the Kaczmarz method literature, we formalize such orderings and develop geometric and algebraic intuitions around them. Empirically, we demonstrate that greedy orderings converge faster than random ones in terms of the average loss across tasks, both for linear regression with random data and for linear probing on CIFAR-100 classification tasks. Analytically, in a high-rank regression setting, we prove a loss bound for greedy orderings analogous to that of random ones. However, under general rank, we establish a repetition-dependent separation. Specifically, while prior work showed that for random orderings, with or without replacement, the average loss after $k$ iterations is bounded by $\\mathcal{O}(1/\\sqrt{k})$—we prove that single-pass greedy orderings may fail catastrophically, whereas those allowing repetition converge at rate $\\mathcal{O}(1/\\sqrt[3]{k})$. Overall, we reveal nuances within and between greedy and random orderings.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether choosing a deliberately different task at each step helps continual learning more than choosing tasks randomly. It studies linear regression under joint realizability: the training tasks admit a shared solution. The authors formalize greedy orderings that maximize dissimilarity between consecutive tasks, using tools from the Kaczmarz literature to explain their geometry and algebra.

Experiments show faster convergence of average task loss for greedy orderings on random regression data and on linear probing tasks using CIFAR-100. The theory gives a more conditional picture. In a high-rank regression setting, the authors establish a greedy-ordering loss bound analogous to the bound for random orderings.

For general rank, allowing tasks to repeat becomes crucial. Single-pass greedy orderings can fail catastrophically, whereas greedy orderings with repetition converge with a bound proportional to the inverse cube root of the iteration count. Prior random-ordering bounds decrease as the inverse square root. Thus, the observed empirical advantage does not translate into a uniformly stronger theoretical guarantee; task repetition and rank materially affect the comparison.
summary.tldr: Greedy task ordering can accelerate learning empirically, but its theoretical behavior depends strongly on task rank and repetition.

title: Are Greedy Task Orderings Better Than Random in Continual Linear Regression?

abstract: Neural networks offer a promising data-driven approach to tackle computationally challenging optimization problems. In this work, we introduce neural approximation frameworks for a family of geometric "extent measure" problems, including shape-fitting descriptors (e.g. minimum enclosing ball or annulus). Central to our approach is the \textit{alignment} of our neural model with a new variant of the classical $\varepsilon$-kernel technique from computational geometry. In particular, we develop a new relaxed-$\varepsilon$-kernel theory that maintains the approximation guarantees of the classical $\varepsilon$-kernels but with the crucial benefit that it can be easily implemented with \textit{bounded model complexity} (i.e, constant number of parameters) by the simple SumFormer neural network. This leads to a simple neural model to approximate objects such as the directional width of any input point set, and empirically shows excellent out-of-distribution generalization. Many geometric extent measures, such as the minimum enclosing spherical shell, cannot be directly captured by $\varepsilon$-kernels. To this end, we show that an encode-process-decode framework with our kernel approximating NN used as the ``process'' module can approximate such extent measures, again, with bounded model complexity where parameters scale only with the approximation error $\varepsilon$ and not the size of the input set. Empirical results on diverse point‐cloud datasets demonstrate the practical performance of our models.

In particular, we develop a new relaxed-$\varepsilon$-kernel theory that maintains the approximation guarantees of the classical $\varepsilon$-kernels but with the crucial benefit that it can be easily implemented with \textit{bounded model complexity} (i.e, constant number of parameters) by the simple SumFormer neural network. Many geometric extent measures, such as the minimum enclosing spherical shell, cannot be directly captured by $\varepsilon$-kernels. To this end, we show that an encode-process-decode framework with our kernel approximating NN used as the ``process'' module can approximate such extent measures, again, with bounded model complexity where parameters scale only with the approximation error $\varepsilon$ and not the size of the input set. Empirical results on diverse point‐cloud datasets demonstrate the practical performance of our models.

paragraphs: Geometric extent problems describe how a point set spreads through space, including finding enclosing balls or annuli. This paper develops neural approximations for these computationally challenging problems by aligning the network with a geometric approximation technique. The goal is to retain approximation guarantees while keeping the model's parameter count independent of the input set's size.

The authors introduce a relaxed version of the classical epsilon-kernel technique that preserves its approximation guarantees and can be implemented by a simple SumFormer network with bounded model complexity. This produces a neural model for quantities such as directional width. Experiments also show strong generalization to inputs outside the training distribution.

Some extent measures, including the minimum enclosing spherical shell, cannot be captured directly by epsilon-kernels. For these, the paper places its kernel-approximating network inside an encode-process-decode framework. The resulting parameter count scales with the requested approximation error rather than the number of input points. Evaluations on diverse point-cloud datasets demonstrate practical performance alongside the theoretical approximation results.
summary.tldr: Geometry-aligned neural networks approximate point-set extent measures with guarantees and parameter counts independent of input size.

title: Effective Neural Approximations for Geometric Optimization Problems

abstract: Pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit significant vulnerability to imperceptible adversarial perturbations. Current advanced defense strategies typically employ adversarial prompt tuning to improve the adversarial robustness of VLMs, which struggle to simultaneously maintain generalization across both natural and adversarial examples under different benchmarks and downstream tasks. We propose a collaborative adversarial prompt tuning (CoAPT) approach from pre-trained VLMs to target robust VLMs. Inspired by the image mask modeling, we adopt an improved real-time total variation algorithm to suppress and eliminate high-frequency details from images while preserving edge structures, thereby disrupting the adversarial perturbation space. Subsequently, guided by the high-level image and text representations in the latent space of the pre-trained VLMs, the corrupted natural features are restored while inheriting the superior generalization capability. Experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate that CoAPT achieves an excellent trade-off among natural generalization, adversarial robustness, and task-specific adaptation compared to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Pretrained vision-language models can be disrupted by adversarial image changes that are difficult to perceive. Improving resistance to these changes can also make it harder to preserve performance on ordinary inputs and across downstream tasks. CoAPT addresses this balance through collaborative adversarial prompt tuning that draws guidance from the original pretrained model.

The approach first uses an improved real-time total variation algorithm to suppress high-frequency image details while retaining edge structure. This step is intended to disrupt the space in which adversarial perturbations operate. It then restores natural features damaged by the processing, guided by high-level image and text representations in the pretrained model's latent space.

These two stages connect perturbation suppression with recovery of useful visual information. Experiments on four benchmarks report a strong trade-off among ordinary-input generalization, adversarial robustness, and task-specific adaptation compared with state-of-the-art methods. The findings support using pretrained latent representations as a guide for robust learning while retaining the generalization capabilities that make those models useful.
summary.tldr: CoAPT suppresses adversarial image details and restores useful features using pretrained representations, improving the tested balance between robustness and generalization.

title: Learning Robust Vision-Language Models from Natural Latent Spaces

abstract: Recently, text-to-image diffusion models have been widely used for style mimicry and personalized customization through methods such as DreamBooth and Textual Inversion. This has raised concerns about intellectual property protection and the generation of deceptive content. Recent studies, such as Glaze and Anti-DreamBooth, have proposed using adversarial noise to protect images from these attacks. However, recent purification-based methods, such as DiffPure and Noise Upscaling, have successfully attacked these latest defenses, showing the vulnerabilities of these methods. Moreover, present methods show limited transferability across models, making them less effective against unknown text-to-image models. To address these issues, we propose a novel anti-mimicry method, StyleGuard. We propose a novel style loss that optimizes the style-related features in the latent space to make it deviate from the original image, which improves model-agnostic transferability. Additionally, to enhance the perturbation's ability to bypass diffusion-based purification, we designed a novel upscale loss that involves ensemble purifiers and upscalers during training. Extensive experiments on the WikiArt and CelebA datasets demonstrate that StyleGuard outperforms existing methods in robustness against various transformations and purifications, effectively countering style mimicry in various models. Moreover, StyleGuard is effective on different style mimicry methods, including DreamBooth and Textual Inversion. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/PolyLiYJ/StyleGuard}.

paragraphs: Protective image perturbations aim to make it harder for text-to-image models to imitate an image’s style. Existing defenses can be weakened by purification methods and may transfer poorly to unfamiliar models. StyleGuard targets both problems by designing perturbations around style-related internal features and the transformations used to remove protective noise.

Its style loss pushes latent style features away from those of the original image, with the goal of improving transfer across models. An additional upscale loss incorporates an ensemble of purifiers and upscalers during training. This trains the perturbations to better withstand diffusion-based purification, addressing a specific route by which earlier defenses have been defeated.

The authors also report effectiveness across multiple models and style-mimicry methods, including DreamBooth and Textual Inversion. The findings support combining style-focused optimization with explicit exposure to purification operations to strengthen anti-mimicry protection in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: StyleGuard designs style-focused image perturbations that better transfer across models and resist tested purification-based mimicry attacks.

title: StyleGuard: Preventing Text-to-Image-Model-based Style Mimicry Attacks by Style Perturbations

abstract: Graph classification has long assumed a closed-world setting, limiting its applicability to real-world scenarios where new categories often emerge. To address this limitation, we introduce Graph-Level Novel Category Discovery (GLNCD), a new task aimed at identifying unseen graph categories without supervision from novel classes. We first adapt classical Novel Category Discovery (NCD) methods for images to the graph domain and evaluate these baseline methods on four diverse graph datasets curated for the GLNCD task. Our analysis reveals that these methods suffer a notable performance degradation compared to their image-based counterparts, due to two key challenges: (1) insufficient utilization of structural information in graph self-supervised learning (SSL), and (2) ineffective pseudo-labeling strategies based on ranking statistics (RS) that neglect graph structure. To alleviate these issues, we propose ProtoFGW-NCD, a framework consisting of two core components: ProtoFGW-CL, a novel graph SSL framework, and FGW-RS, a structure-aware pseudo-labeling method. Both components employ a differentiable Fused Gromov-Wasserstein (FGW) distance to effectively compare graphs by incorporating structural information. These components are built upon learnable prototype graphs, which enable efficient, parallel FGW-based graph comparisons and capture representative patterns within graph datasets. Experiments on four GLNCD benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ProtoFGW-NCD.

paragraphs: Graph classification commonly assumes that the relevant categories are already known. This paper introduces Graph-Level Novel Category Discovery, which asks models to identify previously unseen graph categories without supervision from those new classes. The authors curate four graph datasets to study this setting.

Adapting existing image-based category-discovery methods reveals substantial performance degradation. The analysis identifies two problems: self-supervised learning makes insufficient use of graph structure, and ranking-based pseudo-labeling also neglects that structure. Both weaknesses concern how graphs are compared and grouped, motivating a method that places structural information inside those operations.

The proposed ProtoFGW-NCD framework combines a graph self-supervised learning component with structure-aware pseudo-labeling. Both use a differentiable Fused Gromov-Wasserstein distance and learnable prototype graphs. The prototypes capture representative patterns and enable efficient parallel comparisons using that distance. Experiments on all four benchmarks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. The paper contributes both a new evaluation task and an approach that adapts category discovery to the structural information that distinguishes graphs from images.
summary.tldr: ProtoFGW-NCD uses graph prototypes and structure-aware comparisons to discover unseen graph categories without labels for those classes.

title: GLNCD: Graph-Level Novel Category Discovery

abstract: We consider an agent interacting with an environment in a single stream of actions, observations, and rewards, with no reset. This process is not assumed to be a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Rather, the agent has several representations (mapping histories of past interactions to a discrete state space) of the environment with unknown dynamics, only some of which result in an MDP. The goal is to minimize the average regret criterion against an agent who knows an MDP representation giving the highest optimal reward, and acts optimally in it. Recent regret bounds for this setting are of order O(T^2/3) with an additive term constant yet exponential in some characteristics of the optimal MDP. We propose an algorithm whose regret after T time steps is O(\sqrtT), with all constants reasonably small. This is optimal in T since O(\sqrtT) is the optimal regret in the setting of learning in a (single discrete) MDP.

paragraphs: The paper considers an agent learning from one uninterrupted sequence of actions, observations, and rewards, without resets. The environment itself need not be a Markov decision process. Instead, the agent has several ways to map its interaction history into discrete states, only some of which produce a valid Markov representation.

The learner must choose among these representations while also learning unknown dynamics. Its regret is measured against an agent that already knows a Markov representation with the highest optimal reward and acts optimally within it. This comparison combines the cost of discovering a useful state description with the cost of learning how to act.

The proposed algorithm achieves regret of order square root of T after T steps, improving on the earlier T-to-the-two-thirds rate described in the abstract. It also avoids the earlier bound's additive term exponential in characteristics of the optimal model, with constants described as reasonably small. The dependence on T is optimal because the same square-root rate is optimal even for learning within a single discrete Markov decision process.
summary.tldr: An algorithm selects among candidate state representations while learning to act, achieving regret with optimal square-root dependence on interaction length.

title: Optimal Regret Bounds for Selecting the State Representation in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We consider stochastic multi-armed bandit problems with complex actions over a set of basic arms, where the decision maker plays a complex action rather than a basic arm in each round. The reward of the complex action is some function of the basic arms’ rewards, and the feedback observed may not necessarily be the reward per-arm. For instance, when the complex actions are subsets of the arms, we may only observe the maximum reward over the chosen subset. Thus, feedback across complex actions may be coupled due to the nature of the reward function. We prove a frequentist regret bound for Thompson sampling in a very general setting involving parameter, action and observation spaces and a likelihood function over them. The bound holds for discretely-supported priors over the parameter space and without additional structural properties such as closed-form posteriors, conjugate prior structure or independence across arms. The regret bound scales logarithmically with time but, more importantly, with an improved constant that non-trivially captures the coupling across complex actions due to the structure of the rewards. As applications, we derive improved regret bounds for classes of complex bandit problems involving selecting subsets of arms, including the first nontrivial regret bounds for nonlinear MAX reward feedback from subsets. Using particle filters for computing posterior distributions which lack an explicit closed-form, we present numerical results for the performance of Thompson sampling for subset-selection and job scheduling problems.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes bandit problems where each decision combines basic arms into a complex action. Feedback may reveal only a function of their rewards, such as the maximum reward in a chosen subset. This creates coupling across actions, making their statistical relationship important to learning.

The authors prove a frequentist regret bound for Thompson sampling in a general framework of parameters, actions, observations, and likelihoods. The bound assumes a discretely supported prior, but does not require independent arms, conjugate priors, or closed-form posteriors. Regret grows logarithmically with time, with an improved constant that captures coupling induced by the reward structure.

Numerical studies examine subset selection and job scheduling, using particle filters when posterior distributions lack closed forms. The work connects a broad regret analysis with computation for problems whose feedback cannot be separated into individual arm rewards.
summary.tldr: Thompson sampling receives logarithmic regret bounds that account for coupled feedback in complex bandit actions under discretely supported priors.

title: Thompson Sampling for Complex Online Problems

abstract: Networks play a central role in modern data analysis, enabling us to reason about systems by studying the relationships between their parts. Most often in network analysis, the edges are given. However, in many systems it is difficult or impossible to measure the network directly. Examples of latent networks include economic interactions linking financial instruments and patterns of reciprocity in gang violence. In these cases, we are limited to noisy observations of events associated with each node. To enable analysis of these implicit networks, we develop a probabilistic model that combines mutually-exciting point processes with random graph models. We show how the Poisson superposition principle enables an elegant auxiliary variable formulation and a fully-Bayesian, parallel inference algorithm. We evaluate this new model empirically on several datasets.
originalAbstract: Networks play a central role in modern data analysis, enabling us to reason about systems by studying the relationships between their parts. Most often in network analysis, the edges are given. However, in many systems it is difficult or impossible to measure the network directly. Examples of latent networks include economic interactions linking financial instruments and patterns of reciprocity in gang violence. In these cases, we are limited to noisy observations of events associated with each node. To enable analysis of these implicit networks, we develop a probabilistic model that combines mutually-exciting point processes with random graph models. We show how the Poisson superposition principle enables an elegant auxiliary variable formulation and a fully-Bayesian, parallel inference algorithm. We evaluate this new model empirically on several datasets.

paragraphs: Network analysis often starts with known connections, but some systems reveal only events associated with their individual nodes. This paper addresses the problem of learning the hidden network from those noisy observations. Examples motivating the work include economic interactions between financial instruments and patterns of reciprocal gang violence, where direct measurements of connections may be unavailable.

The proposed probabilistic model combines mutually exciting point processes with random graph models. The point-process component represents how events can be associated with increased activity elsewhere, while the graph component represents the underlying connection structure. Combining them makes it possible to reason about the network through the event data rather than requiring its edges as input.

The authors use the Poisson superposition principle to introduce auxiliary variables and construct a fully Bayesian inference algorithm that supports parallel computation. This formulation connects a model of event activity with a practical procedure for estimating hidden structure. The model is evaluated empirically on several datasets, providing applications of the approach to observed event sequences.
summary.tldr: The paper combines event-process and random-graph models to infer hidden networks from noisy observations of activity at their nodes.

title: Discovering Latent Network Structure in Point Process Data

abstract: This paper presents a new technique for computing the barycenter of a set of distance or kernel matrices. These matrices, which define the inter-relationships between points sampled from individual domains, are not required to have the same size or to be in row-by-row correspondence. We compare these matrices using the softassign criterion, which measures the minimum distortion induced by a probabilistic map from the rows of one similarity matrix to the rows of another; this criterion amounts to a regularized version of the Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance between metric-measure spaces. The barycenter is then defined as a Fréchet mean of the input matrices with respect to this criterion, minimizing a weighted sum of softassign values. We provide a fast iterative algorithm for the resulting nonconvex optimization problem, built upon state-of- the-art tools for regularized optimal transportation. We demonstrate its application to the computation of shape barycenters and to the prediction of energy levels from molecular configurations in quantum chemistry.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to average distance or kernel matrices describing relationships within different collections of points. The matrices can have different sizes, and their rows need not come with matching identities. This makes the averaging problem about reconciling relational structures, rather than simply averaging corresponding matrix entries.

The comparison uses a probabilistic mapping between rows of two matrices and measures how much that mapping distorts their internal relationships. Called the softassign criterion, it is a regularized form of Gromov–Wasserstein distance. The average, or barycenter, minimizes a weighted sum of these comparison values, making it a Fréchet mean under the chosen criterion.

The resulting optimization problem is nonconvex. The authors provide a fast iterative algorithm built from regularized optimal-transport tools and demonstrate applications to shape barycenters and prediction of molecular energy levels. These examples show how a common relational representation can support both averaging objects and prediction from their configurations, even when direct point-by-point alignment is unavailable.
summary.tldr: A regularized Gromov–Wasserstein approach averages relational matrices without requiring equal sizes or predefined point correspondences.

title: Gromov-Wasserstein Averaging of Kernel and Distance Matrices

abstract: The purported “black box” nature of neural networks is a barrier to adoption in applications where interpretability is essential. Here we present DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures), a method for decomposing the output prediction of a neural network on a specific input by backpropagating the contributions of all neurons in the network to every feature of the input. DeepLIFT compares the activation of each neuron to its `reference activation’ and assigns contribution scores according to the difference. By optionally giving separate consideration to positive and negative contributions, DeepLIFT can also reveal dependencies which are missed by other approaches. Scores can be computed efficiently in a single backward pass. We apply DeepLIFT to models trained on MNIST and simulated genomic data, and show significant advantages over gradient-based methods. paragraphs: Understanding why a neural network produced a particular prediction is important when interpretability affects whether the model can be used. This paper introduces DeepLIFT, a method that assigns contribution scores to input features for a specific prediction. It traces contributions backward through the network's neurons to the original input.

The method compares each neuron's activation with a reference activation and bases its attribution on that difference. This makes the reference comparison central to the explanation. DeepLIFT can also treat positive and negative contributions separately, an option the authors show can reveal dependencies missed by other approaches.

Contribution scores require only a single backward pass, making the method computationally efficient. The authors apply it to models trained on MNIST and simulated genomic data, reporting significant advantages over gradient-based methods. These findings support activation differences as a useful basis for explaining individual predictions. The resulting scores describe how input features contribute through the network relative to the reference used by the method.
summary.tldr: DeepLIFT explains individual predictions by propagating contributions based on differences from reference neuron activations.

title: Learning Important Features Through Propagating Activation Differences

abstract: We develop the first Bayesian Optimization algorithm, BLOSSOM, which selects between multiple alternative acquisition functions and traditional local optimization at each step. This is combined with a novel stopping condition based on expected regret. This pairing allows us to obtain the best characteristics of both local and Bayesian optimization, making efficient use of function evaluations while yielding superior convergence to the global minimum on a selection of optimization problems, and also halting optimization once a principled and intuitive stopping condition has been fulfilled.
originalAbstract: We develop the first Bayesian Optimization algorithm, BLOSSOM, which selects between multiple alternative acquisition functions and traditional local optimization at each step. This is combined with a novel stopping condition based on expected regret. This pairing allows us to obtain the best characteristics of both local and Bayesian optimization, making efficient use of function evaluations while yielding superior convergence to the global minimum on a selection of optimization problems, and also halting optimization once a principled and intuitive stopping condition has been fulfilled.

paragraphs: BLOSSOM addresses two decisions in optimization: how to choose the next function evaluation and when to stop searching. It combines Bayesian optimization with traditional local optimization. At each step, the algorithm selects among multiple acquisition functions and the local optimization option, making the choice of search strategy part of the procedure.

Acquisition functions guide which evaluation to request, while local optimization provides another way to pursue improvement. Allowing the algorithm to switch between them is intended to capture useful characteristics of both approaches. A stopping condition based on expected regret complements that selection mechanism, giving the search a principled criterion for deciding when further optimization is no longer required.

On a selection of optimization problems, the authors report efficient use of function evaluations and superior convergence toward the global minimum. Those findings concern the evaluated problems. The contribution brings search and stopping together: BLOSSOM adapts how it searches and halts when its expected-regret condition is fulfilled, treating both decisions as parts of one optimization process.
summary.tldr: BLOSSOM switches between Bayesian and local optimization strategies and uses expected regret to decide when to stop.

title: Optimization, fast and slow: optimally switching between local and Bayesian optimization

abstract: Learning sparse linear models with two-way interactions is desirable in many application domains such as genomics. $\ell_1$-regularised linear models are popular to estimate sparse models, yet standard implementations fail to address specifically the quadratic explosion of candidate two-way interactions in high dimensions, and typically do not scale to genetic data with hundreds of thousands of features. Here we present WHInter, a working set algorithm to solve large $\ell_1$-regularised problems with two-way interactions for binary design matrices. The novelty of WHInter stems from a new bound to efficiently identify working sets while avoiding to scan all features, and on fast computations inspired from solutions to the maximum inner product search problem. We apply WHInter to simulated and real genetic data and show that it is more scalable and two orders of magnitude faster than the state of the art.

Here we present WHInter, a working set algorithm to solve large $\ell_1$-regularised problems with two-way interactions for binary design matrices. The novelty of WHInter stems from a new bound to efficiently identify working sets while avoiding to scan all features, and on fast computations inspired from solutions to the maximum inner product search problem. paragraphs: Sparse linear models with pairwise interactions can capture relationships that individual features alone do not express. However, the number of possible pairs grows quadratically with the number of features. This makes conventional ℓ1-regularized implementations difficult to scale to genetic datasets containing hundreds of thousands of features.

WHInter addresses this problem with a working-set algorithm for binary design matrices. It focuses optimization on selected variables, using a new bound to identify working sets efficiently without scanning all features. It also incorporates fast computations inspired by maximum inner product search. These components target the cost of finding relevant interactions within the enormous candidate space.

Tests on simulated and real genetic data show greater scalability and a reported speed improvement of two orders of magnitude over the state of the art. The method’s scope includes the stated binary-matrix setting. Its contribution is a computational strategy that makes large sparse interaction models more tractable by reducing the search work required to assemble and update useful working sets.
summary.tldr: WHInter efficiently selects working sets for sparse pairwise-interaction models on binary data, reporting substantially better scalability and roughly hundredfold speedups.

title: WHInter: A Working set algorithm for High-dimensional sparse second order Interaction models

abstract: We provide a comprehensive overview and tooling for GP modelling with non-Gaussian likelihoods using state space methods. The state space formulation allows for solving one-dimensonal GP models in O(n) time and memory complexity. While existing literature has focused on the connection between GP regression and state space methods, the computational primitives allowing for inference using general likelihoods in combination with the Laplace approximation (LA), variational Bayes (VB), and assumed density filtering (ADF) / expectation propagation (EP) schemes has been largely overlooked. We present means of combining the efficient O(n) state space methodology with existing inference methods. We also furher extend existing methods, and provide unifying code implementing all approaches.

The state space formulation allows for solving one-dimensonal GP models in O(n) time and memory complexity. While existing literature has focused on the connection between GP regression and state space methods, the computational primitives allowing for inference using general likelihoods in combination with the Laplace approximation (LA), variational Bayes (VB), and assumed density filtering (ADF) / expectation propagation (EP) schemes has been largely overlooked. We present means of combining the efficient O(n) state space methodology with existing inference methods. We also furher extend existing methods, and provide unifying code implementing all approaches.

paragraphs: State-space methods provide a way to solve one-dimensional Gaussian process models with time and memory costs that grow linearly with the number of observations. This paper focuses on extending that computational advantage to models with non-Gaussian likelihoods. Such likelihoods require inference machinery beyond the familiar connection between Gaussian process regression and state-space methods.

The authors present the computational building blocks needed to combine state-space calculations with several approximate-inference approaches. These include the Laplace approximation, variational Bayes, assumed density filtering, and expectation propagation. The contribution explains how these existing inference schemes can use the efficient state-space formulation, bringing multiple approaches into a common computational setting.

The paper also extends existing methods and provides unified code implementing all the approaches. Its significance lies in both organization and tooling: it makes the relationship between scalable state-space calculations and general-likelihood inference explicit and usable. The linear-complexity claim concerns the one-dimensional state-space GP methodology, giving a specific setting in which these computational benefits apply.
summary.tldr: The paper unifies methods and code for combining efficient one-dimensional state-space Gaussian processes with non-Gaussian likelihood inference.

title: State Space Gaussian Processes with Non-Gaussian Likelihood

abstract: We investigate the complexity of deep neural networks (DNN) that represent piecewise linear (PWL) functions. In particular, we study the number of linear regions, i.e. pieces, that a PWL function represented by a DNN can attain, both theoretically and empirically. We present (i) tighter upper and lower bounds for the maximum number of linear regions on rectifier networks, which are exact for inputs of dimension one; (ii) a first upper bound for multi-layer maxout networks; and (iii) a first method to perform exact enumeration or counting of the number of regions by modeling the DNN with a mixed-integer linear formulation. These bounds come from leveraging the dimension of the space defining each linear region. The results also indicate that a deep rectifier network can only have more linear regions than every shallow counterpart with same number of neurons if that number exceeds the dimension of the input.

paragraphs: A piecewise linear neural network divides its input space into regions, with a linear rule applying within each region. This paper studies how many such regions a network can represent. Counting these pieces gives a concrete way to investigate representational complexity and compare the effects of network structure.

The authors derive tighter upper and lower bounds for rectifier networks, with exact results when the input has one dimension. They also provide an upper bound for multilayer maxout networks. Their reasoning uses the dimension of the space defining each region. Alongside these theoretical results, they introduce exact region enumeration and counting through a mixed-integer linear formulation of the network.

The analysis also qualifies when depth can provide an advantage in region count. For a deep rectifier network to exceed every shallow counterpart with the same number of neurons, that neuron count must exceed the input dimension. This is a necessary condition for the stated advantage, not a guarantee that every network satisfying it will outperform its shallow counterparts.
summary.tldr: New bounds and exact counting methods clarify how network architecture and input dimension constrain the number of linear regions.

title: Bounding and Counting Linear Regions of Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Training complex machine learning models for prediction often requires a large amount of data that is not always readily available. Leveraging these external datasets from related but different sources is therefore an important task if good predictive models are to be built for deployment in settings where data can be rare. In this paper we propose a novel approach to the problem in which we use multiple GAN architectures to learn to translate from one dataset to another, thereby allowing us to effectively enlarge the target dataset, and therefore learn better predictive models than if we simply used the target dataset. We show the utility of such an approach, demonstrating that our method improves the prediction performance on the target domain over using just the target dataset and also show that our framework outperforms several other benchmarks on a collection of real-world medical datasets.

paragraphs: A target prediction task may have too little data to train a complex model well, even when related datasets exist elsewhere. Those external datasets come from different sources, so making them useful for the target setting is itself a learning problem. RadialGAN addresses this situation by learning translations between datasets.

The method uses multiple generative adversarial network architectures to map data from one dataset to another. These translations allow information from related sources to enlarge the target dataset effectively. The objective is to improve the predictive model for that specific target domain by making additional data useful in its setting.

On a collection of real-world medical datasets, the authors report better target-domain prediction than training with the target dataset alone. They also report improvements over several comparison methods. These results support learned dataset translation as a way to benefit from multiple related sources when target data are scarce, with the demonstrated gains belonging to the medical datasets evaluated.
summary.tldr: RadialGAN learns translations among related datasets to expand target-domain training data and improve prediction in reported medical-data experiments.

title: RadialGAN: Leveraging multiple datasets to improve target-specific predictive models using Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: We consider optimization of composite objective functions, i.e., of the form $f(x)=g(h(x))$, where $h$ is a black-box derivative-free expensive-to-evaluate function with vector-valued outputs, and $g$ is a cheap-to-evaluate real-valued function. While these problems can be solved with standard Bayesian optimization, we propose a novel approach that exploits the composite structure of the objective function to substantially improve sampling efficiency. Our approach models $h$ using a multi-output Gaussian process and chooses where to sample using the expected improvement evaluated on the implied non-Gaussian posterior on $f$, which we call expected improvement for composite functions (EI-CF). Although EI-CF cannot be computed in closed form, we provide a novel stochastic gradient estimator that allows its efficient maximization. We also show that our approach is asymptotically consistent, i.e., that it recovers a globally optimal solution as sampling effort grows to infinity, generalizing previous convergence results for classical expected improvement. Numerical experiments show that our approach dramatically outperforms standard Bayesian optimization benchmarks, reducing simple regret by several orders of magnitude.

While these problems can be solved with standard Bayesian optimization, we propose a novel approach that exploits the composite structure of the objective function to substantially improve sampling efficiency. Our approach models $h$ using a multi-output Gaussian process and chooses where to sample using the expected improvement evaluated on the implied non-Gaussian posterior on $f$, which we call expected improvement for composite functions (EI-CF). paragraphs: The paper studies objectives built in two stages: an expensive black-box function produces several outputs, and a cheap function converts them into a single score. Standard Bayesian optimization can search for the best score, but the authors show how explicitly modeling the intermediate outputs can make expensive evaluations more informative.

Their method places a multi-output Gaussian process over the expensive function. Passing its uncertain outputs through the cheap function produces a generally non-Gaussian distribution over the final score. The method chooses evaluations using expected improvement under that distribution. Because this acquisition rule has no closed-form calculation, the authors develop a stochastic gradient estimator for efficiently maximizing it.

The authors prove asymptotic consistency: with sampling effort growing without bound, the approach recovers a global optimum. This is a long-run guarantee rather than a finite-budget promise. In numerical experiments, it substantially outperforms standard Bayesian optimization benchmarks, reducing simple regret—the gap from the optimal objective value—by several orders of magnitude.
summary.tldr: Modeling an objective’s expensive intermediate outputs improves Bayesian optimization sampling efficiency, with asymptotic consistency and large empirical regret reductions.

title: Bayesian Optimization of Composite Functions

abstract: We define a unified information-based measure to provide quantitative explanations on how intermediate layers of deep Natural Language Processing (NLP) models leverage information of input words. Our method advances existing explanation methods by addressing issues in coherency and generality. Explanations generated by using our method are consistent and faithful across different timestamps, layers, and models. We show how our method can be applied to four widely used models in NLP and explain their performances on three real-world benchmark datasets.
originalAbstract: We define a unified information-based measure to provide quantitative explanations on how intermediate layers of deep Natural Language Processing (NLP) models leverage information of input words.
