We show how our method can be applied to four widely used models in NLP and explain their performances on three real-world benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: This paper examines how intermediate layers of deep language models use information from input words. Its goal is quantitative explanation: describing the role of word information inside a model in a way that supports consistent interpretation. The focus extends beyond the final prediction to the representations involved in producing it.

The authors define a unified information-based measure to address coherence and generality in existing explanation methods. They report that the resulting explanations remain consistent and faithful across time positions, layers, and different models. A common measure matters here because it provides a shared basis for examining information use across those different parts of a model and across architectures.

The method is applied to four widely used NLP models on three real-world benchmark datasets. The authors use its explanations to account for the models' performances on those tasks. The contribution is therefore an explanatory framework with applications across several models, connecting internal use of word information to observed performance rather than proposing a new predictive architecture.
summary.tldr: A unified information-based measure explains how language models use input words across time positions, layers, and architectures.

title: Towards a Deep and Unified Understanding of Deep Neural Models in NLP

abstract: In importance sampling (IS)-based reinforcement learning algorithms such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), IS weights are typically clipped to avoid large variance in learning. However, policy update from clipped statistics induces large bias in tasks with high action dimensions, and bias from clipping makes it difficult to reuse old samples with large IS weights. In this paper, we consider PPO, a representative on-policy algorithm, and propose its improvement by dimension-wise IS weight clipping which separately clips the IS weight of each action dimension to avoid large bias and adaptively controls the IS weight to bound policy update from the current policy. This new technique enables efficient learning for high action-dimensional tasks and reusing of old samples like in off-policy learning to increase the sample efficiency. Numerical results show that the proposed new algorithm outperforms PPO and other RL algorithms in various Open AI Gym tasks.

paragraphs: Importance-sampling weights help reinforcement-learning algorithms account for differences between policies. Algorithms such as PPO clip these weights to control variance, but the paper identifies a cost: clipping can introduce substantial bias when actions have many dimensions. It can also make older samples with large weights difficult to reuse effectively.

The proposed improvement clips the importance-sampling weight separately for each action dimension. It also adapts the weight control to bound the policy update relative to the current policy. The aim is to retain the stabilizing role of clipping while avoiding the large bias associated with the usual treatment of high-dimensional actions.

This adjustment enables learning on high-dimensional action tasks and reuse of older samples in a manner resembling off-policy learning. Reusing experience is central to the claimed improvement in sample efficiency, because previously collected interactions remain useful for training. Numerical experiments on various OpenAI Gym tasks show the resulting algorithm outperforming PPO and other reinforcement-learning algorithms included in the comparison.
summary.tldr: Clipping importance weights separately by action dimension improves PPO-style learning and enables more effective reuse of old samples.

title: Dimension-Wise Importance Sampling Weight Clipping for Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The well-known Gumbel-Max trick for sampling from a categorical distribution can be extended to sample $k$ elements without replacement. We show how to implicitly apply this ’Gumbel-Top-$k$’ trick on a factorized distribution over sequences, allowing to draw exact samples without replacement using a Stochastic Beam Search. Even for exponentially large domains, the number of model evaluations grows only linear in $k$ and the maximum sampled sequence length. The algorithm creates a theoretical connection between sampling and (deterministic) beam search and can be used as a principled intermediate alternative. In a translation task, the proposed method compares favourably against alternatives to obtain diverse yet good quality translations. We show that sequences sampled without replacement can be used to construct low-variance estimators for expected sentence-level BLEU score and model entropy.

paragraphs: Sampling several sequences can produce repeated outputs, while deterministic beam search follows a different selection procedure. This paper develops Stochastic Beam Search by extending the Gumbel-Max sampling trick to select k elements without replacement. It applies the resulting Gumbel-Top-k construction implicitly to distributions that factorize over sequences.

The method draws exact samples without replacement even when the sequence domain is exponentially large. Its number of model evaluations grows only linearly with k and with the maximum sampled sequence length. The construction also establishes a theoretical connection between sampling and deterministic beam search, providing a principled intermediate alternative between these procedures.

On a translation task, the authors report favorable results for obtaining outputs that combine diversity with good quality. They also show that sampling sequences without replacement can support low-variance estimates of expected sentence-level BLEU and model entropy. The contribution therefore serves both output generation and statistical estimation: the same sampling construction can produce distinct sequences and help estimate quantities defined over the model's sequence distribution.
summary.tldr: Stochastic Beam Search uses Gumbel-Top-k to sample sequences exactly without replacement with model evaluations scaling linearly in sample count and maximum length.

title: Stochastic Beams and Where To Find Them: The Gumbel-Top-k Trick for Sampling Sequences Without Replacement

abstract: In this paper, we propose a unified view of gradient-based algorithms for stochastic convex composite optimization by extending the concept of estimate sequence introduced by Nesterov. This point of view covers the stochastic gradient descent method, variants of the approaches SAGA, SVRG, and has several advantages: (i) we provide a generic proof of convergence for the aforementioned methods; (ii) we show that this SVRG variant is adaptive to strong convexity; (iii) we naturally obtain new algorithms with the same guarantees; (iv) we derive generic strategies to make these algorithms robust to stochastic noise, which is useful when data is corrupted by small random perturbations. Finally, we show that this viewpoint is useful to obtain new accelerated algorithms in the sense of Nesterov.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we propose a unified view of gradient-based algorithms for stochastic convex composite optimization by extending the concept of estimate sequence introduced by Nesterov. This point of view covers the stochastic gradient descent method, variants of the approaches SAGA, SVRG, and has several advantages: (i) we provide a generic proof of convergence for the aforementioned methods; (ii) we show that this SVRG variant is adaptive to strong convexity; (iii) we naturally obtain new algorithms with the same guarantees; (iv) we derive generic strategies to make these algorithms robust to stochastic noise, which is useful when data is corrupted by small random perturbations. Finally, we show that this viewpoint is useful to obtain new accelerated algorithms in the sense of Nesterov.

paragraphs: This paper develops a common mathematical view of gradient-based methods for stochastic convex composite optimization. It extends Nesterov's concept of an estimate sequence so that stochastic gradient descent and variants of SAGA and SVRG can be analyzed within the same framework. The aim is to connect methods that might otherwise require separate convergence arguments.

The framework provides a generic convergence proof and shows that the particular SVRG variant considered adapts to strong convexity. It also yields new algorithms with the same guarantees. This makes the viewpoint constructive: beyond explaining existing approaches, it supplies a route to designing additional methods whose behavior can be justified through the shared analysis.

The authors further derive general strategies for making these algorithms robust to stochastic noise, including small random perturbations corrupting the data. They also use the framework to obtain new accelerated algorithms in Nesterov's sense. The contribution is therefore a unified approach to convergence, adaptation, noise robustness, and acceleration within the stated convex optimization setting.
summary.tldr: An extension of estimate sequences unifies stochastic optimization analyses and yields adaptive, noise-robust, and accelerated algorithm variants.

title: Estimate Sequences for Variance-Reduced Stochastic Composite Optimization

abstract: Adaptive gradient methods such as AdaGrad and its variants update the stepsize in stochastic gradient descent on the fly according to the gradients received along the way; such methods have gained widespread use in large-scale optimization for their ability to converge robustly, without the need to fine-tune parameters such as the stepsize schedule. Yet, the theoretical guarantees to date for AdaGrad are for online and convex optimization. We bridge this gap by providing strong theoretical guarantees for the convergence of AdaGrad over smooth, nonconvex landscapes. We show that the norm version of AdaGrad (AdaGrad-Norm) converges to a stationary point at the $\mathcal{O}(\log(N)/\sqrt{N})$ rate in the stochastic setting, and at the optimal $\mathcal{O}(1/N)$ rate in the batch (non-stochastic) setting – in this sense, our convergence guarantees are “sharp”. In particular, both our theoretical results and extensive numerical experiments imply that AdaGrad-Norm is robust to the unknown Lipschitz constant and level of stochastic noise on the gradient .

Yet, the theoretical guarantees to date for AdaGrad are for online and convex optimization. We bridge this gap by providing strong theoretical guarantees for the convergence of AdaGrad over smooth, nonconvex landscapes. paragraphs: AdaGrad adjusts optimization steps using gradients accumulated during training, reducing the need to hand-design a learning-rate schedule. Although widely used in large-scale learning, its established guarantees had focused on convex or online optimization. This paper analyzes the norm-based variant, AdaGrad-Norm, on smooth nonconvex objectives.

The authors prove convergence to stationary points in both stochastic and deterministic settings. In the stochastic case, the stated rate is O(log(N)/√N); in the batch setting it is the optimal O(1/N) rate under their analysis. These results describe how the method behaves when the objective can contain multiple minima and saddles, rather than assuming convexity.

Theoretical findings and extensive numerical experiments also indicate robustness to an unknown Lipschitz constant and unknown gradient-noise level. That robustness helps explain the appeal of adapting steps from observed gradients. The endpoint guaranteed here is stationarity, which should not be read as a universal guarantee of reaching the global optimum of a nonconvex problem.
summary.tldr: AdaGrad-Norm receives sharp nonconvex stationarity guarantees and evidence of robustness to unknown smoothness and noise.

title: AdaGrad Stepsizes: Sharp Convergence Over Nonconvex Landscapes

abstract: We propose moment-based variational inference as a flexible framework for approximate smoothing of latent Markov jump processes. The main ingredient of our approach is to partition the set of all transitions of the latent process into classes. This allows to express the Kullback-Leibler divergence from the approximate to the posterior process in terms of a set of moment functions that arise naturally from the chosen partition. To illustrate possible choices of the partition, we consider special classes of jump processes that frequently occur in applications. We then extend the results to latent parameter inference and demonstrate the method on several examples.

The main ingredient of our approach is to partition the set of all transitions of the latent process into classes. This allows to express the Kullback-Leibler divergence from the approximate to the posterior process in terms of a set of moment functions that arise naturally from the chosen partition. To illustrate possible choices of the partition, we consider special classes of jump processes that frequently occur in applications. We then extend the results to latent parameter inference and demonstrate the method on several examples.

paragraphs: This paper develops an approximate inference framework for hidden Markov jump processes, whose latent states change through discrete transitions. Its focus is smoothing: estimating the hidden process using observations. The proposed variational approach represents the inference problem through moment functions, providing a structured way to approximate the posterior process.

The central modeling choice is a partition of all possible transitions into classes. From that partition, a corresponding set of moment functions arises. The authors show how to express the Kullback–Leibler divergence from the approximate process to the posterior process using those moments, connecting the chosen transition grouping directly to the variational objective.

The paper considers special classes of jump processes that frequently appear in applications to illustrate possible partitions. It also extends the results to inference about latent parameters and demonstrates the framework on several examples. The contribution is a flexible construction: transition classes determine the moment representation used for approximation, allowing the inference formulation to reflect the structure of the process being modeled.
summary.tldr: Grouping transitions into classes yields moment-based variational objectives for approximate smoothing and parameter inference in Markov jump processes.

title: Moment-Based Variational Inference for Markov Jump Processes

abstract: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (MBRL) offers a promising direction for sample efficient learning, often achieving state of the art results for continuous control tasks. However many existing MBRL methods rely on combining greedy policies with exploration heuristics, and even those which utilize principled exploration bonuses construct dual objectives in an ad hoc fashion. In this paper we introduce Ready Policy One (RP1), a framework that views MBRL as an active learning problem, where we aim to improve the world model in the fewest samples possible. RP1 achieves this by utilizing a hybrid objective function, which crucially adapts during optimization, allowing the algorithm to trade off reward v.s. exploration at different stages of learning. In addition, we introduce a principled mechanism to terminate sample collection once we have a rich enough trajectory batch to improve the model. We rigorously evaluate our method on a variety of continuous control tasks, and demonstrate statistically significant gains over existing approaches.

However many existing MBRL methods rely on combining greedy policies with exploration heuristics, and even those which utilize principled exploration bonuses construct dual objectives in an ad hoc fashion. In this paper we introduce Ready Policy One (RP1), a framework that views MBRL as an active learning problem, where we aim to improve the world model in the fewest samples possible. RP1 achieves this by utilizing a hybrid objective function, which crucially adapts during optimization, allowing the algorithm to trade off reward v.s. exploration at different stages of learning. In addition, we introduce a principled mechanism to terminate sample collection once we have a rich enough trajectory batch to improve the model. We rigorously evaluate our method on a variety of continuous control tasks, and demonstrate statistically significant gains over existing approaches.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning depends on gathering experience that improves a world model while also pursuing reward. Existing approaches can combine greedy policies with exploration heuristics or construct combined objectives in an ad hoc way. Ready Policy One frames this process as active learning: the agent should collect samples that improve its world model as efficiently as possible.

The framework uses a hybrid objective that adapts during optimization. This allows the balance between reward and exploration to change at different stages of learning. It also introduces a principled stopping mechanism for data collection, ending collection once the trajectory batch is sufficiently rich to improve the model. The method therefore addresses both which experience to seek and when enough has been gathered.

Evaluation on a variety of continuous control tasks shows statistically significant gains over existing approaches. These findings support the adaptive objective and collection framework in the evaluated tasks. The broader contribution is to make world-model improvement an explicit organizing goal for exploration, connecting the choice and quantity of collected experience to the learning process.
summary.tldr: Ready Policy One adapts the reward-exploration balance and stops sample collection when trajectories are sufficient to improve its world model.

title: Ready Policy One: World Building Through Active Learning

abstract: In modern supervised learning, many deep neural networks are able to interpolate the data: the empirical loss can be driven to near zero on all samples simultaneously. In this work, we explicitly exploit this interpolation property for the design of a new optimization algorithm for deep learning, which we term Adaptive Learning-rates for Interpolation with Gradients (ALI-G). ALI-G retains the two main advantages of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which are (i) a low computational cost per iteration and (ii) good generalization performance in practice. At each iteration, ALI-G exploits the interpolation property to compute an adaptive learning-rate in closed form. In addition, ALI-G clips the learning-rate to a maximal value, which we prove to be helpful for non-convex problems. Crucially, in contrast to the learning-rate of SGD, the maximal learning-rate of ALI-G does not require a decay schedule. This makes ALI-G considerably easier to tune than SGD. We prove the convergence of ALI-G in various stochastic settings. Notably, we tackle the realistic case where the interpolation property is satisfied up to some tolerance. We also provide experiments on a variety of deep learning architectures and tasks: (i) learning a differentiable neural computer; (ii) training a wide residual network on the SVHN data set; (iii) training a Bi-LSTM on the SNLI data set; and (iv) training wide residual networks and densely connected networks on the CIFAR data sets. ALI-G produces state-of-the-art results among adaptive methods, and even yields comparable performance with SGD, which requires manually tuned learning-rate schedules. Furthermore, ALI-G is simple to implement in any standard deep learning framework and can be used as a drop-in replacement in existing code.

paragraphs: Many deep networks can fit their training data so closely that losses become nearly zero for all samples simultaneously. ALI-G uses this interpolation property to design an optimization algorithm. The aim is to retain stochastic gradient descent's low per-iteration cost and practical generalization while making learning-rate selection easier.

At each iteration, ALI-G computes an adaptive learning rate in closed form and clips it at a chosen maximum. The authors prove that this clipping helps in nonconvex problems. The maximum does not need a decay schedule, reducing the tuning burden associated with manually scheduled SGD. Convergence results cover several stochastic settings, including approximate interpolation with a nonzero tolerance.

Experiments span differentiable neural computers, convolutional architectures, and a bidirectional LSTM across the stated tasks and datasets. The paper reports state-of-the-art results among adaptive methods and performance comparable to SGD with manually tuned schedules. ALI-G is also designed for simple implementation as a drop-in replacement, tying its theoretical use of interpolation to a practical training procedure.
summary.tldr: ALI-G uses interpolation to compute adaptive learning rates, offering convergence guarantees and strong empirical performance without a maximum-rate decay schedule.

title: Training Neural Networks for and by Interpolation

abstract: Deep generative modeling has achieved many successes for continuous data generation, such as producing realistic images and controlling their properties (e.g., styles). However, the development of generative modeling techniques for optimizing discrete data, such as sequences or strings, still lags behind largely due to the challenges in modeling complex and long-range constraints, including both syntax and semantics, in discrete structures. In this paper, we formulate the sequence optimization task as a chance-constrained optimization problem. The key idea is to enforce a high probability of generating valid sequences and also optimize the property of interest. We propose a novel minimax algorithm to simultaneously tighten a bound of the valid chance and optimize the expected property. Extensive experimental results in three domains demonstrate the superiority of our approach over the existing sequence optimization methods.
originalAbstract: Deep generative modeling has achieved many successes for continuous data generation, such as producing realistic images and controlling their properties (e.g., styles). However, the development of generative modeling techniques for optimizing discrete data, such as sequences or strings, still lags behind largely due to the challenges in modeling complex and long-range constraints, including both syntax and semantics, in discrete structures. In this paper, we formulate the sequence optimization task as a chance-constrained optimization problem. The key idea is to enforce a high probability of generating valid sequences and also optimize the property of interest. We propose a novel minimax algorithm to simultaneously tighten a bound of the valid chance and optimize the expected property. Extensive experimental results in three domains demonstrate the superiority of our approach over the existing sequence optimization methods.

paragraphs: Generating a useful sequence involves two demands: it should have desirable properties, and it should obey the rules that make it valid. For discrete structures such as strings, these rules can involve syntax, meaning, and relationships between distant elements. The paper addresses the difficulty of optimizing a property while keeping these complex constraints in view.

The authors formulate sequence generation as chance-constrained optimization. Here, validity is expressed through the probability that the generator produces an acceptable sequence. The objective is to keep that probability high while improving the expected property of interest. Their minimax algorithm tackles both goals together by tightening a bound on the validity probability and optimizing the property.

Experiments across three domains report better performance than existing sequence optimization methods. The contribution is a framework that treats validity as an explicit probabilistic requirement during optimization. A high validity probability does not mean every generated sequence must be valid; that distinction is part of the formulation.
summary.tldr: A generative optimization framework improves sequence properties while explicitly enforcing a high probability of validity.

title: A Chance-Constrained Generative Framework for Sequence Optimization

abstract: Randomly perturbing networks during the training process is a commonly used approach to improving generalization performance. In this paper, we present a theoretical study of one particular way of random perturbation, which corresponds to injecting artificial noise to the training data. We provide a precise asymptotic characterization of the training and generalization errors of such randomly perturbed learning problems on a random feature model. Our analysis shows that Gaussian noise injection in the training process is equivalent to introducing a weighted ridge regularization, when the number of noise injections tends to infinity. The explicit form of the regularization is also given. Numerical results corroborate our asymptotic predictions, showing that they are accurate even in moderate problem dimensions. Our theoretical predictions are based on a new correlated Gaussian equivalence conjecture that generalizes recent results in the study of random feature models.

title: On the Inherent Regularization Effects of Noise Injection During Training

abstract: Minimizing cross-entropy over the softmax scores of a linear map composed with a high-capacity encoder is arguably the most popular choice for training neural networks on supervised learning tasks. However, recent works show that one can directly optimize the encoder instead, to obtain equally (or even more) discriminative representations via a supervised variant of a contrastive objective. In this work, we address the question whether there are fundamental differences in the sought-for representation geometry in the output space of the encoder at minimal loss. Specifically, we prove, under mild assumptions, that both losses attain their minimum once the representations of each class collapse to the vertices of a regular simplex, inscribed in a hypersphere. We provide empirical evidence that this configuration is attained in practice and that reaching a close-to-optimal state typically indicates good generalization performance. Yet, the two losses show remarkably different optimization behavior. The number of iterations required to perfectly fit to data scales superlinearly with the amount of randomly flipped labels for the supervised contrastive loss. This is in contrast to the approximately linear scaling previously reported for networks trained with cross-entropy.

paragraphs: Cross-entropy and supervised contrastive learning offer different ways to train discriminative representations. This paper asks whether those objectives seek fundamentally different geometric arrangements of examples in the encoder’s output space. The question concerns what a minimum-loss representation looks like, separately from how training reaches it.

Under mild assumptions, the authors prove that both losses attain their minimum when each class’s representations collapse to a single vertex of a regular simplex on a hypersphere. In plain terms, examples within a class share a representation, while the class representatives form a symmetric arrangement. Empirical evidence shows this configuration emerging in practice, and approaching it typically accompanies good generalization.

The training dynamics nevertheless differ substantially. For supervised contrastive loss, the iterations needed to fit the data perfectly grow superlinearly with the amount of randomly flipped labels. Thus, sharing a minimum-loss geometry does not imply sharing the same route to that geometry, especially when training labels contain random errors.
summary.tldr: Under mild assumptions, cross-entropy and supervised contrastive loss share a minimum-loss representation geometry but exhibit different optimization behavior under label noise.

title: Dissecting Supervised Contrastive Learning

abstract: While the advent of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) has greatly improved node and graph representation learning in many applications, the neighborhood aggregation scheme exposes additional vulnerabilities to adversaries seeking to extract node-level information about sensitive attributes. In this paper, we study the problem of protecting sensitive attributes by information obfuscation when learning with graph structured data. We propose a framework to locally filter out pre-determined sensitive attributes via adversarial training with the total variation and the Wasserstein distance. Our method creates a strong defense against inference attacks, while only suffering small loss in task performance. Theoretically, we analyze the effectiveness of our framework against a worst-case adversary, and characterize an inherent trade-off between maximizing predictive accuracy and minimizing information leakage. Experiments across multiple datasets from recommender systems, knowledge graphs and quantum chemistry demonstrate that the proposed approach provides a robust defense across various graph structures and tasks, while producing competitive GNN encoders for downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks learn representations by aggregating information from neighboring nodes. The paper studies how to reduce this information leakage while retaining representations that remain useful for the intended prediction task.

The authors propose a framework that locally filters predetermined sensitive attributes through adversarial training. It uses total variation and Wasserstein distances as part of that training. The protection is directed at attributes selected in advance. The theoretical analysis considers a worst-case adversary and characterizes an inherent tradeoff between predictive accuracy and limiting the sensitive information that representations reveal.

Experiments span recommender systems, knowledge graphs, and quantum chemistry. The authors report strong defense against inference attacks with only small losses in task performance, alongside competitive encoders for downstream tasks. These findings support the framework across the tested graph structures and applications, while the tradeoff analysis explains why preserving prediction quality and suppressing leakage must be considered together.
summary.tldr: Adversarial information filtering reduces leakage of predetermined sensitive node attributes while preserving competitive GNN task performance.

title: Information Obfuscation of Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Promoting behavioural diversity is critical for solving games with non-transitive dynamics where strategic cycles exist, and there is no consistent winner (e.g., Rock-Paper-Scissors). Yet, there is a lack of rigorous treatment for defining diversity and constructing diversity-aware learning dynamics. In this work, we offer a geometric interpretation of behavioural diversity in games and introduce a novel diversity metric based on \emph{determinantal point processes} (DPP). By incorporating the diversity metric into best-response dynamics, we develop \emph{diverse fictitious play} and \emph{diverse policy-space response oracle} for solving normal-form games and open-ended games. We prove the uniqueness of the diverse best response and the convergence of our algorithms on two-player games. Importantly, we show that maximising the DPP-based diversity metric guarantees to enlarge the \emph{gamescape} – convex polytopes spanned by agents’ mixtures of strategies. To validate our diversity-aware solvers, we test on tens of games that show strong non-transitivity. Results suggest that our methods achieve at least the same, and in most games, lower exploitability than PSRO solvers by finding effective and diverse strategies.

This paper develops a geometric account of behavioral diversity and a metric based on determinantal point processes, making diversity an explicit part of the learning objective.

summary.tldr: A geometric diversity metric guides game-learning algorithms toward broader strategy sets and lower exploitability in most evaluated games.

title: Modelling Behavioural Diversity for Learning in Open-Ended Games

abstract: Meta-learning can successfully acquire useful inductive biases from data. Yet, its generalization properties to unseen learning tasks are poorly understood. Particularly if the number of meta-training tasks is small, this raises concerns about overfitting. We provide a theoretical analysis using the PAC-Bayesian framework and derive novel generalization bounds for meta-learning. Using these bounds, we develop a class of PAC-optimal meta-learning algorithms with performance guarantees and a principled meta-level regularization. Unlike previous PAC-Bayesian meta-learners, our method results in a standard stochastic optimization problem which can be solved efficiently and scales well.When instantiating our PAC-optimal hyper-posterior (PACOH) with Gaussian processes and Bayesian Neural Networks as base learners, the resulting methods yield state-of-the-art performance, both in terms of predictive accuracy and the quality of uncertainty estimates. Thanks to their principled treatment of uncertainty, our meta-learners can also be successfully employed for sequential decision problems.

paragraphs: Meta-learning extracts useful learning biases from multiple tasks, but those biases can overfit the tasks available during training. This concern is especially relevant when there are few meta-training tasks. The paper analyzes generalization to unseen tasks through the PAC-Bayesian framework and derives new bounds for that setting.

The bounds lead to a class of PAC-optimal algorithms with performance guarantees and a principled form of regularization at the meta-learning level. The resulting optimization is a standard stochastic optimization problem, which the authors describe as efficient and scalable. This connects the theoretical analysis to a training procedure that can be implemented with familiar optimization machinery.

The authors instantiate the PAC-optimal hyper-posterior, PACOH, with Gaussian processes and Bayesian neural networks as base learners. They report state-of-the-art predictive accuracy and uncertainty estimates for the resulting methods. They also demonstrate successful use in sequential decision problems, attributing that applicability to the treatment of uncertainty. The findings combine generalization analysis with empirical evidence across prediction and decision-making.
summary.tldr: PACOH turns PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds into scalable meta-learning algorithms with principled regularization and strong reported uncertainty estimates.

title: PACOH: Bayes-Optimal Meta-Learning with PAC-Guarantees

abstract: Actor-critic (AC) algorithms have been widely used in decentralized multi-agent systems to learn the optimal joint control policy. However, existing decentralized AC algorithms either need to share agents’ sensitive information or lack communication-efficiency. In this work, we develop decentralized AC and natural AC (NAC) algorithms that avoid sharing agents’ local information and are sample and communication-efficient. In both algorithms, agents share only noisy rewards and use mini-batch local policy gradient updates to ensure high sample and communication efficiency. Particularly for decentralized NAC, we develop a decentralized Markovian SGD algorithm with an adaptive mini-batch size to efficiently compute the natural policy gradient. Under Markovian sampling and linear function approximation, we prove that the proposed decentralized AC and NAC algorithms achieve the state-of-the-art sample complexities $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}\ln\epsilon^{-1})$ and $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3}\ln\epsilon^{-1})$, respectively, and achieve an improved communication complexity $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1}\ln\epsilon^{-1})$. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithms achieve lower sample and communication complexities than the existing decentralized AC algorithms.

paragraphs: Decentralized actor-critic learning coordinates multiple agents toward a joint control policy. Existing methods can require sharing sensitive local information or incur substantial communication costs. This paper develops actor-critic and natural actor-critic algorithms that share only noisy rewards while using local mini-batch policy-gradient updates.

For natural actor-critic, the authors additionally develop decentralized stochastic gradient descent for Markovian data with an adaptive mini-batch size. This component computes the natural policy gradient efficiently. Together, the local updates and specialized gradient computation address the amount of data and communication needed during learning.

The theoretical results assume Markovian sampling and linear function approximation. Under those conditions, the sample-complexity bounds are O(ε^-2 log(1/ε)) for actor-critic and O(ε^-3 log(1/ε)) for natural actor-critic, with improved communication complexity of O(ε^-1 log(1/ε)). Numerical experiments also show lower sample and communication requirements than existing decentralized actor-critic methods. The contribution combines finite-time guarantees with a communication design that avoids sharing agents’ local information directly.
summary.tldr: Decentralized actor-critic methods use noisy reward sharing and mini-batch updates to improve sample and communication efficiency under stated approximation assumptions.

title: Sample and Communication-Efficient Decentralized Actor-Critic Algorithms with Finite-Time Analysis

abstract: It would be useful for machines to use computers as humans do so that they can aid us in everyday tasks. This is a setting in which there is also the potential to leverage large-scale expert demonstrations and human judgements of interactive behaviour, which are two ingredients that have driven much recent success in AI. Here we investigate the setting of computer control using keyboard and mouse, with goals specified via natural language. Instead of focusing on hand-designed curricula and specialized action spaces, we focus on developing a scalable method centered on reinforcement learning combined with behavioural priors informed by actual human-computer interactions. We achieve state-of-the-art and human-level mean performance across all tasks within the MiniWob++ benchmark, a challenging suite of computer control problems, and find strong evidence of cross-task transfer. These results demonstrate the usefulness of a unified human-agent interface when training machines to use computers. Altogether our results suggest a formula for achieving competency beyond MiniWob++ and towards controlling computers, in general, as a human would.

The interface matters because it connects machine actions to the same kinds of interactions people perform. Human-computer interaction data can therefore inform how an agent behaves while it learns to complete tasks.

The proposed approach combines reinforcement learning with behavioral priors drawn from actual human interactions. Those priors supply information about human behavior, while reinforcement learning develops task-solving ability. The work centers on making this combination scalable, rather than building the approach around individually designed learning curricula or specialized action spaces for particular tasks.

On MiniWob++, the authors report state-of-the-art results and human-level mean performance across the benchmark's tasks, alongside strong evidence of transfer between tasks. The mean-performance result describes aggregate achievement across this suite. The findings support the usefulness of a shared human-agent interface and suggest a route toward broader computer control; competency beyond MiniWob++ is presented as a prospect.
summary.tldr: Combining reinforcement learning with human interaction priors achieves human-level mean performance on the MiniWob++ computer-control benchmark.

title: A data-driven approach for learning to control computers

abstract: We develop a new, principled algorithm for estimating the contribution of training data points to the behavior of a deep learning model, such as a specific prediction it makes. Our algorithm estimates the AME, a quantity that measures the expected (average) marginal effect of adding a data point to a subset of the training data, sampled from a given distribution. When subsets are sampled from the uniform distribution, the AME reduces to the well-known Shapley value. Our approach is inspired by causal inference and randomized experiments: we sample different subsets of the training data to train multiple submodels, and evaluate each submodel’s behavior. We then use a LASSO regression to jointly estimate the AME of each data point, based on the subset compositions. Under sparsity assumptions ($k \ll N$ datapoints have large AME), our estimator requires only $O(k\log N)$ randomized submodel trainings, improving upon the best prior Shapley value estimators.

paragraphs: This paper estimates how individual training examples contribute to a model's behavior, including a particular prediction. Its target quantity is the average marginal effect: the expected change from adding one example to a training subset drawn from a specified distribution. Under the uniform sampling distribution described in the abstract, this becomes the Shapley value.

The procedure resembles a randomized experiment. The authors draw different subsets of training data, train a separate submodel on each, and measure the behavior of interest. They then use LASSO regression to estimate the examples' effects jointly from which examples appeared in each subset and how the resulting submodels behaved.

The efficiency result assumes sparsity: only k of the N training examples have large average marginal effects, with k much smaller than N. Under that assumption, the estimator needs O(k log N) randomized submodel trainings, improving on prior Shapley estimators. The result makes sparse influence a computational advantage, while keeping the estimated contribution tied to the chosen distribution over training subsets.
summary.tldr: Randomized subset training and LASSO estimate training-example contributions with O(k log N) submodel trainings under a sparse-effects assumption.

title: Measuring the Effect of Training Data on Deep Learning Predictions via Randomized Experiments

abstract: We introduce the unbounded depth neural network (UDN), an infinitely deep probabilistic model that adapts its complexity to the training data. The UDN contains an infinite sequence of hidden layers and places an unbounded prior on a truncation L, the layer from which it produces its data. Given a dataset of observations, the posterior UDN provides a conditional distribution of both the parameters of the infinite neural network and its truncation. We develop a novel variational inference algorithm to approximate this posterior, optimizing a distribution of the neural network weights and of the truncation depth L, and without any upper limit on L. To this end, the variational family has a special structure: it models neural network weights of arbitrary depth, and it dynamically creates or removes free variational parameters as its distribution of the truncation is optimized. (Unlike heuristic approaches to model search, it is solely through gradient-based optimization that this algorithm explores the space of truncations.) We study the UDN on real and synthetic data. We find that the UDN adapts its posterior depth to the dataset complexity; it outperforms standard neural networks of similar computational complexity; and it outperforms other approaches to infinite-depth neural networks.

This paper introduces an unbounded depth neural network, a probabilistic model containing an infinite sequence of hidden layers. An unbounded prior governs the truncation depth, the layer from which the model produces its data.

The contribution treats depth as an inferred quantity alongside weights, providing a gradient-based mechanism for adapting model complexity while representing uncertainty about where the network should be truncated.
summary.tldr: An unbounded-depth probabilistic network learns a distribution over its depth through variational inference and adapts complexity to the data.

title: Variational Inference for Infinitely Deep Neural Networks

abstract: This paper develops the first policy gradient method with global optimality guarantee and complexity analysis for robust reinforcement learning under model mismatch. Robust reinforcement learning is to learn a policy robust to model mismatch between simulator and real environment. We first develop the robust policy (sub-)gradient, which is applicable for any differentiable parametric policy class. We show that the proposed robust policy gradient method converges to the global optimum asymptotically under direct policy parameterization. We further develop a smoothed robust policy gradient method, and show that to achieve an $\epsilon$-global optimum, the complexity is $\mathcal O(\epsilon^{-3})$. We then extend our methodology to the general model-free setting, and design the robust actor-critic method with differentiable parametric policy class and value function. We further characterize its asymptotic convergence and sample complexity under the tabular setting. Finally, we provide simulation results to demonstrate the robustness of our methods.

paragraphs: A policy trained with a simulator may encounter different dynamics in the real environment. Robust reinforcement learning seeks policies that tolerate this model mismatch. This paper develops a policy-gradient approach with global-optimality guarantees and complexity analysis, linking direct policy optimization to this robustness objective.

The authors first derive a robust policy gradient or subgradient applicable to any differentiable parametric policy class. The stronger convergence statement has a narrower scope: under direct policy parameterization, the proposed method approaches a global optimum asymptotically. A smoothed version achieves an epsilon-global optimum with complexity of order epsilon to the power of minus three, describing how the required work grows as the desired accuracy increases.

The approach is then extended to model-free learning through a robust actor-critic method using differentiable policy and value-function classes. Its asymptotic convergence and sample complexity are characterized in the tabular setting. Simulations demonstrate robustness of the proposed methods. The paper therefore combines a broadly applicable gradient construction with guarantees whose particular parameterization and tabular conditions are essential to interpreting their scope.
summary.tldr: The paper develops robust policy-gradient and actor-critic methods, with global-optimality and complexity guarantees under specified settings.

title: Policy Gradient Method For Robust Reinforcement Learning

abstract: One important aspect of understanding behaviors of information cascades is to be able to accurately predict their popularity, that is, their message counts at any future time. Self-exciting Hawkes processes have been widely adopted for such tasks due to their success in describing cascading behaviors. In this paper, for general, marked Hawkes point processes, we present closed-form expressions for the mean and variance of future event counts, conditioned on observed events. Furthermore, these expressions allow us to develop a predictive approach, namely, Cascade Anytime Size Prediction via self-Exciting Regression model (CASPER), which is specifically tailored to popularity prediction, unlike existing generative approaches {–} based on point processes {–} for the same task. We showcase CASPER’s merits via experiments entailing both synthetic and real-world data, and demonstrate that it considerably improves upon prior works in terms of accuracy, especially for early-stage prediction.

paragraphs: Predicting an information cascade’s popularity means estimating how many messages it will accumulate by a chosen future time. The paper approaches this through self-exciting Hawkes processes, which describe cascading activity in which events can stimulate further events. The goal is to support forecasts at different future horizons using the events already observed.

For general marked Hawkes point processes, the authors derive closed-form expressions for the conditional mean and variance of future event counts. These quantities describe the expected amount of future activity and its variability given the cascade’s history. The expressions provide a mathematical foundation for forecasting counts directly from an observed, partially developed cascade.

The authors use these results to construct CASPER, a regression approach specifically designed for popularity prediction. This distinguishes its predictive purpose from existing point-process approaches focused on generative modeling. Experiments with synthetic and real-world data report considerable accuracy improvements over prior work, especially early in a cascade, when the available observations are still limited.
summary.tldr: CASPER uses conditional event-count formulas for Hawkes processes to improve cascade-popularity forecasts, particularly at early stages.

title: Anytime Information Cascade Popularity Prediction via Self-Exciting Processes

abstract: Adversarial training (AT) is a widely recognized defense mechanism to gain the robustness of deep neural networks against adversarial attacks. It is built on min-max optimization (MMO), where the minimizer (i.e., defender) seeks a robust model to minimize the worst-case training loss in the presence of adversarial examples crafted by the maximizer (i.e., attacker). However, the conventional MMO method makes AT hard to scale. Thus, Fast-AT and other recent algorithms attempt to simplify MMO by replacing its maximization step with the single gradient sign-based attack generation step. Although easy to implement, FAST-AT lacks theoretical guarantees, and its empirical performance is unsatisfactory due to the issue of robust catastrophic overfitting when training with strong adversaries. In this paper, we advance Fast-AT from the fresh perspective of bi-level optimization (BLO). We first show that the commonly-used Fast-AT is equivalent to using a stochastic gradient algorithm to solve a linearized BLO problem involving a sign operation. However, the discrete nature of the sign operation makes it difficult to understand the algorithm performance. Inspired by BLO, we design and analyze a new set of robust training algorithms termed Fast Bi-level AT (Fast-BAT), which effectively defends sign-based projected gradient descent (PGD) attacks without using any gradient sign method or explicit robust regularization. In practice, we show that our method yields substantial robustness improvements over multiple baselines across multiple models and datasets.
originalAbstract: Adversarial training (AT) is a widely recognized defense mechanism to gain the robustness of deep neural networks against adversarial attacks. It is built on min-max optimization (MMO), where the minimizer (i.e., defender) seeks a robust model to minimize the worst-case training loss in the presence of adversarial examples crafted by the maximizer (i.e., attacker). However, the conventional MMO method makes AT hard to scale. Thus, Fast-AT and other recent algorithms attempt to simplify MMO by replacing its maximization step with the single gradient sign-based attack generation step. Although easy to implement, FAST-AT lacks theoretical guarantees, and its empirical performance is unsatisfactory due to the issue of robust catastrophic overfitting when training with strong adversaries. In this paper, we advance Fast-AT from the fresh perspective of bi-level optimization (BLO). We first show that the commonly-used Fast-AT is equivalent to using a stochastic gradient algorithm to solve a linearized BLO problem involving a sign operation. However, the discrete nature of the sign operation makes it difficult to understand the algorithm performance. Inspired by BLO, we design and analyze a new set of robust training algorithms termed Fast Bi-level AT (Fast-BAT), which effectively defends sign-based projected gradient descent (PGD) attacks without using any gradient sign method or explicit robust regularization. In practice, we show that our method yields substantial robustness improvements over multiple baselines across multiple models and datasets.

paragraphs: Adversarial training alternates between finding damaging input changes and training a model to withstand them. That optimization can be costly. Fast adversarial training simplifies attack generation to a single gradient-sign step, but the paper identifies weak theoretical support and robust catastrophic overfitting as problems with this shortcut.

The authors reinterpret the commonly used fast method as stochastic gradient optimization of a linearized bi-level problem containing a sign operation. This connects the training procedure to an optimization framework in which one problem depends on another. The discrete sign operation complicates analysis, motivating a new family of methods called Fast Bi-level Adversarial Training, or Fast-BAT.

Fast-BAT is designed and analyzed without using gradient-sign methods or explicit robustness regularization. The authors report effective defense against sign-based projected gradient descent attacks and substantial robustness improvements over several baselines across multiple models and datasets. The contribution links a theoretical reinterpretation of an existing shortcut to new training algorithms with stronger empirical performance in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Fast-BAT uses a bi-level optimization perspective to improve fast adversarial training without gradient-sign methods or explicit robustness regularization.

title: Revisiting and Advancing Fast Adversarial Training Through The Lens of Bi-Level Optimization

abstract: We investigate online Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with adversarially changing loss functions and known transitions. We choose dynamic regret as the performance measure, defined as the performance difference between the learner and any sequence of feasible changing policies. The measure is strictly stronger than the standard static regret that benchmarks the learner’s performance with a fixed compared policy. We consider three foundational models of online MDPs, including episodic loop-free Stochastic Shortest Path (SSP), episodic SSP, and infinite-horizon MDPs. For the three models, we propose novel online ensemble algorithms and establish their dynamic regret guarantees respectively, in which the results for episodic (loop-free) SSP are provably minimax optimal in terms of time horizon and certain non-stationarity measure.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decision-making when losses can change adversarially but the environment's transition rules are known. It evaluates learning through dynamic regret: the performance difference between the learner and a sequence of feasible policies that may change over time. This benchmark permits the comparison policy to adapt as conditions change.

Dynamic regret is therefore a strictly stronger measure than static regret, which compares the learner with one fixed policy. The authors consider three settings: episodic stochastic shortest-path problems without loops, general episodic stochastic shortest-path problems, and infinite-horizon Markov decision processes. These cover different ways that decisions and their consequences can extend through time.

For each setting, the paper develops an online ensemble algorithm and proves a corresponding dynamic regret guarantee. The episodic shortest-path results, including the loop-free case, are minimax optimal in their dependence on the time horizon and a specified measure of nonstationarity. That optimality concerns these particular dependencies; the broader contribution is a set of guarantees that explicitly account for changing comparison policies.
summary.tldr: Online ensemble algorithms obtain dynamic regret guarantees for three MDP settings with known transitions and adversarially changing losses.

title: Dynamic Regret of Online Markov Decision Processes

abstract: We study first-order methods with preconditioning for solving structured convex optimization problems. We propose a new family of preconditioners generated by the symmetric polynomials. They provide the first-order optimization methods with a provable improvement of the condition number, cutting the gaps between highest eigenvalues, without explicit knowledge of the actual spectrum. We give a stochastic interpretation of this preconditioning in terms of the coordinate volume sampling and compare it with other classical approaches, including the Chebyshev polynomials. We show how to incorporate a polynomial preconditioning into the Gradient and Fast Gradient Methods and establish their better global complexity bounds. Finally, we propose a simple adaptive search procedure that automatically ensures the best polynomial preconditioning for the Gradient Method, minimizing the objective along a low-dimensional Krylov subspace. Numerical experiments confirm the efficiency of our preconditioning strategies for solving various machine learning problems.

paragraphs: Gradient methods can be slowed by poorly conditioned optimization problems, where the relevant eigenvalues are unevenly distributed. This paper studies preconditioning for structured convex problems: modifying the optimization geometry to make first-order methods more effective. It proposes a family of preconditioners constructed using symmetric polynomials.

The preconditioners provably improve the condition number by narrowing gaps between the largest eigenvalues, without explicitly knowing the actual spectrum. The authors give a stochastic interpretation through coordinate volume sampling and compare the construction with classical approaches, including Chebyshev polynomials. They incorporate it into both Gradient and Fast Gradient methods and establish improved global complexity bounds.

The paper also proposes an adaptive search procedure for the Gradient Method. It minimizes the objective over a low-dimensional Krylov subspace to automatically obtain the best polynomial preconditioning described by the approach. Numerical experiments on machine learning problems support its efficiency. Together, the results connect a theoretically motivated preconditioner family with a practical way to select preconditioning during optimization.
summary.tldr: Symmetric-polynomial preconditioners improve gradient-method conditioning and complexity without explicit knowledge of the problem’s spectrum.

title: Polynomial Preconditioning for Gradient Methods

abstract: Non-convex optimization plays a key role in a growing number of machine learning applications. This motivates the identification of specialized structure that enables sharper theoretical analysis. One such identified structure is quasar-convexity, a non-convex generalization of convexity that subsumes convex functions. Existing algorithms for minimizing quasar-convex functions in the stochastic setting have either high complexity or slow convergence, which prompts us to derive a new class of stochastic methods for optimizing smooth quasar-convex functions. We demonstrate that our algorithms have fast convergence and outperform existing algorithms on several examples, including the classical problem of learning linear dynamical systems. We also present a unified analysis of our newly proposed algorithms and a previously studied deterministic algorithm.

paragraphs: Non-convex optimization covers many machine learning problems, but that broad category can obscure useful structure. This paper focuses on quasar-convexity, a condition that includes convex functions while also allowing some non-convex ones. Identifying this structure creates an opportunity to obtain stronger optimization results than treating every non-convex objective alike.

The authors develop a class of stochastic optimization methods for smooth quasar-convex functions. Their motivation is that existing stochastic approaches face either high complexity or slow convergence. The proposed methods exploit the specified function structure to obtain fast convergence. The paper also gives a unified analysis covering the new stochastic methods and a previously studied deterministic algorithm.

These results connect the theoretical development to a concrete learning problem rather than leaving it solely as an abstract optimization construction. The scope of the contribution remains tied to smoothness and quasar-convexity: the paper identifies a productive structured setting within non-convex optimization and develops faster methods for it.
summary.tldr: New stochastic methods exploit smooth quasar-convex structure to achieve fast convergence and improve performance on several optimization examples.

title: Accelerated Stochastic Optimization Methods under Quasar-convexity

abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated their powerful generative capability in many tasks, with great potential to serve as a paradigm for offline reinforcement learning. However, the quality of the diffusion model is limited by the insufficient diversity of training data, which hinders the performance of planning and the generalizability to new tasks. This paper introduces AdaptDiffuser, an evolutionary planning method with diffusion that can self-evolve to improve the diffusion model hence a better planner, not only for seen tasks but can also adapt to unseen tasks. AdaptDiffuser enables the generation of rich synthetic expert data for goal-conditioned tasks using guidance from reward gradients. It then selects high-quality data via a discriminator to finetune the diffusion model, which improves the generalization ability to unseen tasks. Empirical experiments on two benchmark environments and two carefully designed unseen tasks in KUKA industrial robot arm and Maze2D environments demonstrate the effectiveness of AdaptDiffuser. For example, AdaptDiffuser not only outperforms the previous art Diffuser by 20.8% on Maze2D and 7.5% on MuJoCo locomotion, but also adapts better to new tasks, e.g., KUKA pick-and-place, by 27.9% without requiring additional expert data. More visualization results and demo videos could be found on our project page.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate plans for offline reinforcement learning, but their planning ability depends on the diversity of their training data. AdaptDiffuser addresses this restriction by letting a planner generate additional training examples and then improve itself using selected examples. The aim is to improve familiar tasks and support adaptation to new ones.

The method uses reward gradients to guide the generation of synthetic expert data for tasks specified by a goal. A discriminator selects high-quality generated data, which is then used to fine-tune the diffusion model. This creates a feedback process linking guided generation, quality selection, and further planner training.

These results support the usefulness of the proposed self-improvement process in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: AdaptDiffuser improves diffusion-based planning by generating reward-guided synthetic data, selecting strong examples, and fine-tuning on them.

title: AdaptDiffuser: Diffusion Models as Adaptive Self-evolving Planners

abstract: It has become standard to solve NLP tasks by fine-tuning pre-trained language models (LMs), especially in low-data settings. There is minimal theoretical understanding of empirical success, e.g., why fine-tuning a model with $10^8$ or more parameters on a couple dozen training points does not result in overfitting. We investigate whether the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK)—which originated as a model to study the gradient descent dynamics of infinitely wide networks with suitable random initialization—describes fine-tuning of pre-trained LMs. This study was inspired by the decent performance of NTK for computer vision tasks (Wei et al., 2022). We extend the NTK formalism to Adam and use Tensor Programs (Yang, 2020) to characterize conditions under which the NTK lens may describe fine-tuning updates to pre-trained language models. Extensive experiments on 14 NLP tasks validate our theory and show that formulating the downstream task as a masked word prediction problem through prompting often induces kernel-based dynamics during fine-tuning. Finally, we use this kernel view to propose an explanation for the success of parameter-efficient subspace-based fine-tuning methods.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a large language model on only a few examples can work surprisingly well despite the model having far more parameters than training points. This paper investigates whether a mathematical description called the Neural Tangent Kernel can help explain that success by describing how predictions change during training.

The kernel framework originally described infinitely wide networks with suitable random initialization. Applying it to pretrained language models therefore requires additional justification. The authors extend the framework to the Adam optimizer and use Tensor Programs to characterize conditions under which kernel dynamics may describe fine-tuning updates.

Experiments across 14 language tasks support the theory. In particular, expressing a task through prompting as a masked word prediction problem often produces kernel-like fine-tuning dynamics. The authors also use this perspective to propose an explanation for why methods that restrict updates to a small parameter subspace can succeed. The result offers a conditional account of fine-tuning behavior, rather than asserting that every language model update follows kernel dynamics.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based analysis explains conditions under which language model fine-tuning behaves predictably, with experiments showing that prompting often encourages these dynamics.

title: A Kernel-Based View of Language Model Fine-Tuning

abstract: Pre-trained language models can be fine-tuned to solve diverse NLP tasks, including in few-shot settings. Thus fine-tuning allows the model to quickly pick up task-specific "skills," but there has been limited study of where these newly-learnt skills reside inside the massive model. This paper introduces the term skill localization for this problem and proposes a solution. Given the downstream task and a model fine-tuned on that task, a simple optimization is used to identify a very small subset of parameters ($\sim$0.01% of model parameters) responsible for ($>$95%) of the model’s performance, in the sense that grafting the fine-tuned values for just this tiny subset onto the pre-trained model gives performance almost as well as the fine-tuned model. While reminiscent of recent works on parameter-efficient fine-tuning, the novel aspects here are that: (i) No further retraining is needed on the subset (unlike, say, with lottery tickets). (ii) Notable improvements are seen over vanilla fine-tuning with respect to calibration of predictions in-distribution (40-90% error reduction) as well as quality of predictions out-of-distribution (OOD). In models trained on multiple tasks, a stronger notion of skill localization is observed, where the sparse regions corresponding to different tasks are almost disjoint, and their overlap (when it happens) is a proxy for task similarity. Experiments suggest that localization via grafting can assist certain forms continual learning.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning gives a language model task-specific abilities, but it is less clear where the relevant changes reside. This paper studies skill localization by identifying a very small subset of parameters whose fine-tuned values preserve most task performance when transferred back into the original pretrained model.

A simple optimization finds subsets containing approximately 0.01% of model parameters that account for more than 95% of fine-tuned performance in this grafting sense. The selected parameters require no further retraining. These findings give an operational meaning to localized skills: a small set of transferred parameter values can recover much of a task’s performance, while relationships between those sets provide information about relationships between tasks.
summary.tldr: Grafting roughly 0.01% of fine-tuned parameters preserves over 95% of task performance and can improve calibration and out-of-distribution prediction.

title: Task-Specific Skill Localization in Fine-tuned Language Models

abstract: This paper introduces a new parameterization of deep neural networks (both fully-connected and convolutional) with guaranteed $\ell^2$ Lipschitz bounds, i.e. limited sensitivity to input perturbations. The Lipschitz guarantees are equivalent to the tightest-known bounds based on certification via a semidefinite program (SDP). We provide a “direct” parameterization, i.e., a smooth mapping from $\mathbb R^N$ onto the set of weights satisfying the SDP-based bound. Moreover, our parameterization is complete, i.e. a neural network satisfies the SDP bound if and only if it can be represented via our parameterization. This enables training using standard gradient methods, without any inner approximation or computationally intensive tasks (e.g. projections or barrier terms) for the SDP constraint. The new parameterization can equivalently be thought of as either a new layer type (the sandwich layer ), or a novel parameterization of standard feedforward networks with parameter sharing between neighbouring layers. A comprehensive set of experiments on image classification shows that sandwich layers outperform previous approaches on both empirical and certified robust accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/acfr/LBDN.

paragraphs: A Lipschitz bound limits how strongly a network’s output can change when its input changes. This paper introduces a way to construct fully connected and convolutional networks with guaranteed bounds measured using Euclidean distance. The guarantee matches the tightest-known bounds obtained through the semidefinite-program certification approach described in the paper.

The main contribution is a smooth mapping from unrestricted parameters to network weights satisfying that certification bound. The mapping is complete: a network meets the specified SDP bound exactly when the parameterization can represent it. This completeness concerns the SDP-certified set. It allows standard gradient-based training without repeatedly projecting weights into the constraint set or adding computationally expensive barrier terms.

The construction can be viewed as a new sandwich layer or as a parameterization of ordinary feedforward networks with sharing between neighboring layers. Image-classification experiments show improvements over previous approaches in both empirical and certified robust accuracy. The practical significance is that enforcing the stated sensitivity guarantee becomes part of the network’s parameterization itself.
summary.tldr: A complete, smooth parameterization enables standard gradient training of networks that satisfy specified SDP-based Lipschitz bounds.

title: Direct Parameterization of Lipschitz-Bounded Deep Networks

abstract: Imitation learning addresses the challenge of learning by observing an expert’s demonstrations without access to reward signals from environments. Most existing imitation learning methods that do not require interacting with environments either model the expert distribution as the conditional probability p(a|s) (e.g., behavioral cloning, BC) or the joint probability p(s, a). Despite the simplicity of modeling the conditional probability with BC, it usually struggles with generalization. While modeling the joint probability can improve generalization performance, the inference procedure is often time-consuming, and the model can suffer from manifold overfitting. This work proposes an imitation learning framework that benefits from modeling both the conditional and joint probability of the expert distribution. Our proposed Diffusion Model-Augmented Behavioral Cloning (DBC) employs a diffusion model trained to model expert behaviors and learns a policy to optimize both the BC loss (conditional) and our proposed diffusion model loss (joint). DBC outperforms baselines in various continuous control tasks in navigation, robot arm manipulation, dexterous manipulation, and locomotion. We design additional experiments to verify the limitations of modeling either the conditional probability or the joint probability of the expert distribution, as well as compare different generative models. Ablation studies justify the effectiveness of our design choices.

paragraphs: Imitation learning trains a policy from expert demonstrations without requiring reward signals. Behavioral cloning predicts an action given a state, which is simple but can generalize poorly. Modeling states and actions together can improve generalization, yet the paper identifies slow inference and manifold overfitting as difficulties with relying on that joint distribution.

Diffusion Model-Augmented Behavioral Cloning combines the two views of expert behavior. A diffusion model learns the expert distribution, while the policy is trained with both the usual behavioral cloning loss and a diffusion-based loss representing the joint distribution. The policy therefore receives guidance about the demonstrated action at a state and about how state-action combinations fit expert behavior overall.

Experiments report better performance than baselines across continuous control tasks involving navigation, robot arms, dexterous manipulation, and locomotion. Additional experiments examine the limitations of conditional-only and joint-only modeling and compare generative models. Ablations support the proposed design choices, providing evidence that combining the two training signals is useful across the evaluated control settings.
summary.tldr: DBC combines behavioral cloning with a diffusion-based training signal to improve imitation learning across several continuous control domains.

title: Diffusion Model-Augmented Behavioral Cloning

abstract: The combination of Monte Carlo tree search and neural networks has revolutionized online planning. As neural network approximations are often imperfect, we ask whether uncertainty estimates about the network outputs could be used to improve planning. We develop a Bayesian planning approach that facilitates such uncertainty quantification, inspired by classical ideas from the meta-reasoning literature. We propose a Thompson sampling based algorithm for searching the tree of possible actions, for which we prove the first (to our knowledge) finite time Bayesian regret bound, and propose an efficient implementation for a restricted family of posterior distributions. In addition we propose a variant of the Bayes-UCB method applied to trees. Empirically, we demonstrate that on the ProcGen Maze and Leaper environments, when the uncertainty estimates are accurate but the neural network output is inaccurate, our Bayesian approach searches the tree much more effectively. In addition, we investigate whether popular uncertainty estimation methods are accurate enough to yield significant gains in planning.

paragraphs: Planning systems often combine neural network predictions with a search over possible actions. When those predictions are wrong, search can be misdirected. This paper asks whether knowing how uncertain the predictions are can help a planner decide where further search is most valuable.

The authors develop a Bayesian planning approach and a tree-search algorithm based on Thompson sampling. They prove a finite-time Bayesian regret bound, describing performance over a limited search horizon rather than only in the long run. They also provide an efficient implementation for a restricted family of posterior distributions and introduce a tree-based variant of Bayes-UCB.

Experiments in ProcGen Maze and Leaper show substantially more effective search when network predictions are inaccurate but their uncertainty estimates are accurate. That condition is central: the finding supports using reliable uncertainty to guide planning, rather than establishing that uncertainty-aware search always helps. The paper also investigates whether commonly used uncertainty estimation methods are accurate enough to deliver meaningful planning gains.
summary.tldr: Bayesian tree search can improve planning when uncertainty estimates reliably identify weaknesses in neural network predictions.

title: A Bayesian Approach to Online Planning

abstract: Graph embeddings have emerged as a powerful tool for understanding the structure of graphs. Unlike classical spectral methods, recent methods such as DeepWalk, Node2Vec, etc. are based on solving nonlinear optimization problems on the graph, using local information obtained by performing random walks. These techniques have empirically been shown to produce “better” embeddings than their classical counterparts. However, due to their reliance on solving a nonconvex optimization problem, obtaining theoretical guarantees on the properties of the solution has remained a challenge, even for simple classes of graphs. In this work, we show convergence properties for the DeepWalk algorithm on graphs obtained from the Stochastic Block Model (SBM). Despite being simplistic, the SBM has proved to be a classic model for analyzing the behavior of algorithms on large graphs. Our results mirror the existing ones for spectral embeddings on SBMs, showing that even in the case of one-dimensional embeddings, the output of the DeepWalk algorithm provably recovers the cluster structure with high probability.
