paragraphs: Graph embeddings turn nodes into numerical representations that reveal graph structure. DeepWalk learns these representations from local information collected through random walks. Its empirical success is difficult to explain mathematically because learning involves a nonconvex optimization problem, whose solutions are harder to characterize than those of classical spectral approaches.

The paper establishes convergence properties for DeepWalk on graphs generated by the Stochastic Block Model. This model provides a simplified setting with an underlying cluster structure, making it possible to study whether the learned representation recovers the organization that generated the graph. The analysis concerns DeepWalk's output, connecting its optimization procedure to a meaningful structural result.

The authors prove that even a one-dimensional embedding can recover the cluster structure with high probability in the studied setting. These guarantees parallel existing results for spectral embeddings on block models. Their significance is theoretical: a method supported by empirical evidence also receives a cluster-recovery guarantee under this specific graph model.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that DeepWalk can recover cluster structure with high probability, even in one dimension, on Stochastic Block Model graphs.

title: Convergence Guarantees for the DeepWalk Embedding on Block Models

abstract: The $\ell_0$-constrained mean-CVaR model poses a significant challenge due to its NP-hard nature, typically tackled through combinatorial methods characterized by high computational demands. From a markedly different perspective, we propose an innovative autonomous sparse mean-CVaR portfolio model, capable of approximating the original $\ell_0$-constrained mean-CVaR model with arbitrary accuracy. The core idea is to convert the $\ell_0$ constraint into an indicator function and subsequently handle it through a tailed approximation. We then propose a proximal alternating linearized minimization algorithm, coupled with a nested fixed-point proximity algorithm (both convergent), to iteratively solve the model. Autonomy in sparsity refers to retaining a significant portion of assets within the selected asset pool during adjustments in pool size. Consequently, our framework offers a theoretically guaranteed approximation of the $\ell_0$-constrained mean-CVaR model, improving computational efficiency while providing a robust asset selection scheme.

paragraphs: Sparse portfolio optimization combines an investment objective with a restriction on how many assets can be selected. The paper studies a mean-CVaR model with an explicit asset-count constraint. This formulation is NP-hard, and conventional combinatorial approaches can require substantial computation. The authors propose an alternative model that can approximate the original formulation with arbitrary accuracy.

The construction first expresses the asset-count constraint through an indicator function, then handles that function using a tailed approximation. To solve the resulting model, the authors introduce a proximal alternating linearized minimization algorithm with a nested fixed-point proximity algorithm. Both algorithms have convergence guarantees, providing theoretical support for the proposed iterative solution process.

Thus, the approach addresses both computational demands and continuity in asset selection. Its stated contribution is a theoretically guaranteed approximation with improved computational efficiency and a robust selection scheme, rather than a claim about realized investment returns.
summary.tldr: The proposed portfolio model approximates an asset-count-constrained mean-CVaR problem while supporting efficient optimization and continuity in asset selection.

title: Autonomous Sparse Mean-CVaR Portfolio Optimization

abstract: In the Generalized Mastermind problem, there is an unknown subset $H$ of the hypercube 0,1$^d$ containing $n$ points. The goal is to learn $H$ by making a few queries to an oracle which given a point $q$ in 0,1$^d$, returns the point in $H$ nearest to $q$. We give a two-round adaptive algorithm for this problem that learns $H$ while making at most $\exp(\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d \log n}))$. Furthermore, we show that any $r$-round adaptive randomized algorithm that learns $H$ with constant probability must make $\exp(\Omega(d^{3^{-(r-1)}}))$ queries even when the input has poly$(d)$ points; thus, any poly$(d)$ query algorithm must necessarily use $\Omega(\log \log d)$ rounds of adaptivity. We give optimal query complexity bounds for the variant of the problem where queries are allowed to be from 0,1,2$^d$. We also study a continuous variant of the problem in which $H$ is a subset of unit vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and one can query unit vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$. For this setting, we give a $O(n^{\lfloor d/2 \rfloor})$ query deterministic algorithm to learn the hidden set of points.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover a hidden set of binary strings through queries. Each query is itself a binary string, and an oracle returns the closest hidden string. The challenge is to discover every hidden point while limiting both the number of queries and the rounds in which later queries can depend on earlier answers.

For n hidden points in dimension d, the authors give a two-round algorithm using at most exp(Õ(√(d log n))) queries. They also prove a lower bound for randomized algorithms with a fixed number of adaptive rounds. Even when the hidden set has polynomial size, any algorithm using polynomially many queries needs at least order log log d rounds.

The paper also studies how changing the allowed queries changes the problem. It obtains optimal query-complexity bounds when query coordinates may include 2 alongside 0 and 1. For a continuous version involving unit vectors, it gives a deterministic algorithm using O(n^{floor(d/2)}) queries. These results characterize tradeoffs between query power, adaptivity, and discovery cost.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes query algorithms and adaptivity limits for recovering hidden point sets from nearest-point answers.

title: Learning Multiple Secrets in Mastermind

abstract: Recently various optimization problems, such as Mixed Integer Linear Programming Problems (MILPs), have undergone comprehensive investigation, leveraging the capabilities of machine learning. This work focuses on learning-based solutions for efficiently solving the Quadratic Assignment Problem (QAPs), which stands as a formidable challenge in combinatorial optimization. While many instances of simpler problems admit fully polynomial-time approximate solution (FPTAS), QAP is shown to be strongly NPhard. Even finding a FPTAS for QAP is difficult, in the sense that the existence of a FPTAS implies P = NP. Current research on QAPs suffer from limited scale and computational inefficiency. To attack the aforementioned issues, we here propose the first solution of its kind for QAP in the learn-to-improve category. This work encodes facility and location nodes separately, instead of forming computationally intensive association graphs prevalent in current approaches. This design choice enables scalability to larger problem sizes. Furthermore, a Solution AWare Transformer (SAWT) architecture integrates the incumbent solution matrix with the attention score to effectively capture higher-order information of the QAPs. Our model’s effectiveness is validated through extensive experiments on self-generated QAP instances of varying sizes and the QAPLIB benchmark.

paragraphs: The quadratic assignment problem is a difficult combinatorial optimization problem involving facilities and locations. The paper emphasizes its strong computational hardness: a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme would imply P equals NP. Against that background, the authors focus on learned methods that improve existing solutions, addressing the limited scale and computational inefficiency of prior approaches.

Their design encodes facility nodes and location nodes separately, avoiding the computationally intensive association graphs used in existing methods. This representation supports larger problem sizes. The Solution AWare Transformer, or SAWT, then incorporates the current solution matrix into its attention scores, allowing its representation of the problem to depend explicitly on the assignment being improved.

This solution-aware attention is intended to capture higher-order information relevant to quadratic assignment. Experiments on generated instances of different sizes and the QAPLIB benchmark validate the model’s effectiveness. The contribution is a scalable learned improvement approach supported by experiments; the computational-hardness discussion explains why efficient solution methods remain valuable without suggesting that the underlying complexity barrier has disappeared.
summary.tldr: SAWT improves quadratic-assignment solutions using separate facility and location encodings and attention conditioned on the current assignment.

title: Learning Solution-Aware Transformers for Efficiently Solving Quadratic Assignment Problem

abstract: Diffusion models have exhibit exceptional performance in text-to-image generation and editing. However, existing methods often face challenges when handling complex text prompts that involve multiple objects with multiple attributes and relationships. In this paper, we propose a brand new training-free text-to-image generation/editing framework, namely Recaption, Plan and Generate (RPG), harnessing the powerful chain-of-thought reasoning ability of multimodal LLMs to enhance the compositionality of text-to-image diffusion models. Our approach employs the MLLM as a global planner to decompose the process of generating complex images into multiple simpler generation tasks within subregions. We propose complementary regional diffusion to enable region-wise compositional generation. Furthermore, we integrate text-guided image generation and editing within the proposed RPG in a closed-loop fashion, thereby enhancing generalization ability. Extensive experiments demonstrate our RPG outperforms state-of-the-art text-to-image models, including DALL-E 3 and SDXL, particularly in multi-category object composition and text-image semantic alignment. Notably, our RPG framework exhibits wide compatibility with various MLLM architectures and diffusion backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/YangLing0818/RPG-DiffusionMaster

The difficulty is compositional: producing the requested elements while preserving how they fit together. Recaption, Plan and Generate, or RPG, addresses this using a multimodal language model to organize the generation process.

The multimodal model acts as a global planner, breaking a complex image request into simpler generation tasks assigned to image subregions. These findings support the value of coordinating generation through explicit regional planning. The contribution is a framework that organizes existing model capabilities around complex requests, with generation and editing participating in the same process.
summary.tldr: RPG uses multimodal language models to plan regional diffusion tasks, improving complex text-to-image composition without additional training.

title: Mastering Text-to-Image Diffusion: Recaptioning, Planning, and Generating with Multimodal LLMs

abstract: In-memory computing (IMC) has emerged as a promising solution to address both computation and data-movement challenges, by performing computation on data in-place directly in the memory array. IMC typically relies on analog operation, which makes analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) necessary, for converting results back to the digital domain. However, ADCs maintain computational efficiency by having limited precision, leading to substantial quantization errors in compute outputs. This work proposes RAOQ (Reshape and Adapt for Output Quantization) to overcome this issue, which comprises two classes of mechanisms including: 1) mitigating ADC quantization error by adjusting the statistics of activations and weights, through an activation-shifting approach (A-shift) and a weight reshaping technique (W-reshape); 2) adapting AI models to better tolerate ADC quantization through a bit augmentation method (BitAug), complemented by the introduction of ADC-LoRA, a low-rank approximation technique, to reduce the training overhead. RAOQ demonstrates consistently high performance across different scales and domains of neural network models for computer vision and natural language processing (NLP) tasks at various bit precisions, achieving state-of-the-art results with practical IMC implementations.

paragraphs: In-memory computing performs operations directly where data is stored, addressing both computation and data movement. Its analog outputs must be converted back to digital values using analog-to-digital converters. Limited converter precision helps maintain efficiency but introduces substantial output quantization error. RAOQ targets this specific source of error through quantization-aware training.

The method combines two kinds of intervention. A-shift and W-reshape adjust activation and weight statistics to reduce converter-induced error. BitAug then helps models tolerate the quantization that remains. ADC-LoRA, a low-rank approximation technique, reduces the training overhead associated with adaptation. The design therefore addresses both the production of quantization error and the model’s sensitivity to it.

Experiments span neural networks of different sizes, computer vision and natural-language tasks, and multiple bit precisions. The authors report consistently strong performance and state-of-the-art results with practical in-memory computing implementations. The findings show the value of matching model training to the output-precision constraints of the computing hardware.
summary.tldr: RAOQ adjusts model statistics and trains for quantization tolerance to improve neural-network performance on limited-precision in-memory hardware.

title: Reshape and Adapt for Output Quantization (RAOQ): Quantization-aware Training for In-memory Computing Systems

abstract: Data pruning – the combinatorial task of selecting a small and representative subset from a large dataset, is crucial for mitigating the enormous computational costs associated with training data-hungry modern deep learning models at scale. Since large-scale data collections are invariably noisy, developing data pruning strategies that remain robust even in the presence of corruption is critical in practice. Existing data pruning methods often fail under high corruption rates due to their reliance on empirical mean estimation, which is highly sensitive to outliers. In response, this work proposes Geometric Median (GM) Matching, a novel k-subset selection strategy that leverages the Geometric Median (GM) , a robust estimator with an optimal breakdown point of 1/2; to enhance resilience against noisy data. Our method iteratively selects a $k$-subset such that the mean of the subset approximates the GM of the (potentially) noisy dataset, ensuring robustness even under arbitrary corruption. We provide theoretical guarantees, showing that GM Matching enjoys an improved $\mathcal{O}(1/k)$ convergence rate, outperforming $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{k})$ scaling of uniform sampling, even under arbitrary corruption. Extensive experiments across image classification and image generation tasks demonstrate that GM Matching consistently outperforms existing pruning approaches, particularly in high-corruption settings; making it a strong baseline for robust data pruning.

paragraphs: Data pruning selects a small representative subset to reduce the cost of training on a large dataset. Noise makes this selection harder, especially when a method relies on the empirical mean, which can be strongly influenced by outliers. GM Matching replaces that vulnerable target with the geometric median, a robust estimator with a breakdown point of one half.

The method iteratively chooses a subset of k examples whose mean approximates the geometric median of the potentially corrupted dataset. The distinction between target and subset is useful: the selected subset still has a mean, but that mean is matched to a robust reference. The authors prove an O(1/k) convergence rate, improving on uniform sampling's O(1/√k) rate, including in their analysis of arbitrary corruption.

Experiments on image classification and image generation show consistent improvements over the compared pruning approaches, particularly at high corruption rates. The result connects robustness in the selection target with practical performance on noisy data. The geometric median's stated breakdown point also matters when interpreting robustness; arbitrary corruption does not imply tolerance of an unrestricted corrupted fraction.
summary.tldr: GM Matching selects subsets whose means approximate a geometric median, improving theoretical convergence and empirical pruning performance on noisy data.

title: Geometric Median (GM) Matching for Robust k-Subset Selection from Noisy Data

abstract: We propose a new approach for unsupervised alignment of heterogeneous datasets, which maps data from two different domains without any known correspondences to a common metric space. Our method is based on an unbalanced optimal transport problem with Gromov-Wasserstein marginal penalization. It can be seen as a counterpart to the recently introduced joint multidimensional scaling method. We prove that there exists a minimizer of our functional and that for penalization parameters going to infinity, the corresponding sequence of minimizers converges to a minimizer of the so-called embedded Wasserstein distance. Our model can be reformulated as a quadratic, multi-marginal, unbalanced optimal transport problem, for which a bi-convex relaxation admits a numerical solver via block-coordinate descent. We provide numerical examples for joint embeddings in Euclidean as well as non-Euclidean spaces.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to align two heterogeneous datasets when no correspondences between their points are known. The objective is to place both datasets in a common metric space, giving them a shared representation based on distances. The proposed formulation uses unbalanced optimal transport with Gromov–Wasserstein penalties on its marginals.

The authors establish that their objective has a minimizer. They also characterize its connection to embedded Wasserstein distance: as the penalty parameters grow without bound, the corresponding minimizers converge to a minimizer of that distance. This gives the formulation a precise limiting relationship to another alignment objective and positions it as a counterpart to joint multidimensional scaling.

For computation, the model is rewritten as a quadratic, multi-marginal, unbalanced transport problem. A bi-convex relaxation can then be solved numerically through block-coordinate descent, which updates groups of variables in turn. Numerical examples demonstrate joint embeddings in both Euclidean and non-Euclidean spaces. The work thus combines an existence result and a limiting characterization with a computational route through a relaxed version of the problem.
summary.tldr: An optimal-transport formulation aligns datasets without known correspondences, with existence and convergence results plus a solver for a relaxed problem.

title: Joint Metric Space Embedding by Unbalanced Optimal Transport with Gromov–Wasserstein Marginal Penalization

abstract: Multi-objective learning under user-specified preference is common in real-world problems such as multi-lingual speech recognition under fairness. In this work, we frame such a problem as a semivectorial bilevel optimization problem, whose goal is to optimize a pre-defined preference function, subject to the constraint that the model parameters are weakly Pareto optimal. To solve this problem, we convert the multi-objective constraints to a single-objective constraint through a merit function with an easy-to-evaluate gradient, and then, we use a penalty-based reformulation of the bilevel optimization problem. We theoretically establish the properties of the merit function, and the relations of solutions for the penalty reformulation and the constrained formulation. Then we propose algorithms to solve the reformulated single-level problem, and establish its convergence guarantees. We test the method on various synthetic and real-world problems. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in finding preference-guided optimal solutions to the multi-objective problem.

paragraphs: Multi-objective learning must account for several goals, while a user may also have preferences about the trade-offs among them. This paper formalizes the task as optimizing a predefined preference function while requiring model parameters to be weakly Pareto optimal. That requirement rules out solutions for which every objective could be strictly improved together.

The authors express this as a semivectorial bilevel optimization problem and then simplify how its constraints are handled. A merit function converts the multiple-objective constraints into one constraint with an easy-to-evaluate gradient. A penalty reformulation then turns the problem into a single-level form suitable for the proposed optimization algorithms.

The theory establishes properties of the merit function, relationships between solutions of the constrained and penalty formulations, and convergence guarantees for the algorithms. Tests on synthetic and real-world problems demonstrate effectiveness in finding solutions guided by the specified preferences. The contribution is a route from a difficult nested optimization formulation to a more directly solvable problem, while retaining an explicit connection to the original multi-objective requirements.
summary.tldr: The method reformulates preference-guided Pareto optimization into a single-level problem with first-order algorithms and convergence guarantees.

title: Efficient First-Order Optimization on the Pareto Set for Multi-Objective Learning under Preference Guidance

abstract: Deep learning methods have made significant progress in regular rainfall forecasting, yet the more hazardous tropical cyclone (TC) rainfall has not received the same attention. While regular rainfall models can offer valuable insights for designing TC rainfall forecasting models, most existing methods suffer from cumulative errors and lack physical consistency. Additionally, these methods overlook the importance of meteorological factors in TC rainfall and their integration with the numerical weather prediction (NWP) model. To address these issues, we propose Tropical Cyclone Precipitation Diffusion (TCP-Diffusion), a multi-modal model for forecasting of TC precipitation given an existing TC in any location globally. It forecasts rainfall around the TC center for the next 12 hours at 3 hourly resolution based on past rainfall observations and multi-modal environmental variables. Adjacent residual prediction (ARP) changes the training target from the absolute rainfall value to the rainfall trend and gives our model the capability of rainfall change awareness, reducing cumulative errors and ensuring physical consistency. Considering the influence of TC-related meteorological factors and the useful information from NWP model forecasts, we propose a multi-model framework with specialized encoders to extract richer information from environmental variables and results provided by NWP models. The results of extensive experiments show that our method outperforms other DL methods and the NWP method from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF).

paragraphs: TCP-Diffusion forecasts rainfall around an existing tropical cyclone anywhere globally. Given past rainfall and environmental information, it predicts the next 12 hours at three-hour intervals. The paper addresses cumulative forecasting errors, physical consistency, and the need to incorporate cyclone-related meteorology together with information from numerical weather prediction.

Its adjacent residual prediction approach changes the training target from absolute rainfall to rainfall changes. The authors describe this as giving the model awareness of rainfall trends, reducing accumulated errors and ensuring physical consistency. Specialized encoders also extract information from environmental variables and numerical weather forecasts, allowing these different inputs to contribute to the diffusion model.

Extensive experiments show better performance than the compared deep learning approaches and the ECMWF numerical weather prediction method. The contribution combines a change-focused prediction target with several sources of meteorological evidence. Its stated scope is rainfall forecasting around a cyclone that already exists, and the results support this combination for the evaluated tropical cyclone precipitation forecasting task.
summary.tldr: TCP-Diffusion combines rainfall-change prediction, environmental variables, and numerical forecasts to predict precipitation around existing tropical cyclones.

title: TCP-Diffusion: A Multi-modal Diffusion Model for Global Tropical Cyclone Precipitation Forecasting with Change Awareness

abstract: Medical multi-modal learning requires an effective fusion capability of various heterogeneous modalities. One vital challenge is how to effectively fuse modalities when their data quality varies across different modalities and patients. For example, in the TCGA benchmark, the performance of the same modality can differ between types of cancer. Moreover, data collected at different times, locations, and with varying reagents can introduce inter-modal data quality differences ($i.e.$, $\textbf{Modality Batch Effect}$). In response, we propose ${\textbf{A}}$daptive ${\textbf{M}}$odality Token Re-Balan${\textbf{C}}$ing ($\texttt{AMC}$), a novel top-down dynamic multi-modal fusion approach. The core of $\texttt{AMC}$ is to quantify the significance of each modality (Top) and then fuse them according to the modality importance (Down). Specifically, we access the quality of each input modality and then replace uninformative tokens with inter-modal tokens, accordingly. The more important a modality is, the more informative tokens are retained from that modality. The self-attention will further integrate these mixed tokens to fuse multi-modal knowledge. Comprehensive experiments on both medical and general multi-modal datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of $\texttt{AMC}$.

paragraphs: Combining medical data sources is difficult when their usefulness varies across patients and diseases. Differences in collection time, location, or reagents can also create quality differences between modalities, described here as a Modality Batch Effect. The paper proposes Adaptive Modality Token Re-Balancing, or AMC, to make fusion responsive to those differences.

AMC first assesses the importance and quality of each input modality, then uses that assessment to control the tokens entering fusion. More important modalities retain more informative tokens. Uninformative tokens are replaced with inter-modal tokens, and self-attention integrates the resulting mixture. This gives the initial quality assessment a direct role in determining what information the fusion stage receives.

Experiments on medical and general multimodal datasets demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness and generalizability. The central contribution is an adaptive connection between modality quality and token allocation. Rather than assuming that a modality contributes equally across all inputs, the framework changes the representation supplied to fusion according to its assessed importance for the particular input.
summary.tldr: AMC adapts multimodal fusion by retaining more informative tokens from higher-quality modalities and replacing uninformative ones.

title: Modalities Contribute Unequally: Enhancing Medical Multi-modal Learning through Adaptive Modality Token Re-balancing

abstract: A key challenge in training Large Language Models (LLMs) is properly aligning them with human preferences. Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) uses pairwise comparisons from human annotators to train reward functions and has emerged as a popular alignment method. However, input datasets in RLHF can be unbalanced due to adversarial manipulation or inadvertent repetition. Therefore, we want RLHF algorithms to perform well even when the set of alternatives is not uniformly distributed. Drawing on insights from social choice theory, we introduce robustness to approximate clones, a desirable property of RLHF algorithms which requires that adding near-duplicate alternatives does not significantly change the learned reward function. We first demonstrate that the standard RLHF algorithm based on regularized maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) fails to satisfy this property. We then propose the weighted MLE, a new RLHF algorithm that modifies the standard regularized MLE by weighting alternatives based on their similarity to other alternatives. This new algorithm guarantees robustness to approximate clones while preserving desirable theoretical properties.

The collection of alternatives can become unbalanced through accidental repetition or deliberate manipulation. This paper asks whether adding nearly identical alternatives can distort the reward function, even though those additions contribute little genuinely different choice.

This adjustment guarantees robustness to approximate clones while retaining desirable theoretical properties. The contribution makes resistance to duplication an explicit requirement of reward learning, with a corresponding algorithmic guarantee. Its focus is the effect of repeated or nearly repeated alternatives on learned rewards, a specific source of imbalance in preference datasets.
summary.tldr: Weighting alternatives by similarity makes reward learning robust to near-duplicate choices that can distort standard RLHF reward estimation.

title: Clone-Robust AI Alignment

abstract: The Max-$k$-Cut problem is a fundamental combinatorial optimization challenge that generalizes the classic $\mathcal{NP}$-complete Max-Cut problem. While relaxation techniques are commonly employed to tackle Max-$k$-Cut, they often lack guarantees of equivalence between the solutions of the original problem and its relaxation. To address this issue, we introduce the Relax-Optimize-and-Sample (ROS) framework. In particular, we begin by relaxing the discrete constraints to the continuous probability simplex form. Next, we pre-train and fine-tune a graph neural network model to efficiently optimize the relaxed problem. Subsequently, we propose a sampling-based construction algorithm to map the continuous solution back to a high-quality Max-$k$-Cut solution. By integrating geometric landscape analysis with statistical theory, we establish the consistency of function values between the continuous solution and its mapped counterpart. Extensive experimental results on random regular graphs and the Gset benchmark demonstrate that the proposed ROS framework effectively scales to large instances with up to $20,000$ nodes in just a few seconds, outperforming state-of-the-art algorithms. Furthermore, ROS exhibits strong generalization capabilities across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, underscoring its effectiveness for large-scale optimization tasks.

summary.tldr: ROS combines continuous relaxation, graph neural network optimization, and sampling to produce scalable Max-k-Cut solutions with function-value consistency.

title: ROS: A GNN-based Relax-Optimize-and-Sample Framework for Max-$k$-Cut Problems

abstract: The exact minimum width that allows for universal approximation of unbounded-depth networks is known only for ReLU and its variants. In this work, we study the minimum width of networks using general activation functions. Specifically, we focus on squashable functions that can approximate the identity function and binary step function by alternatively composing with affine transformations. We show that for networks using a squashable activation function to universally approximate $L^p$ functions from $[0,1]^{d_x}$ to $\mathbb R^{d_y}$, the minimum width is $\max\\{d_x,d_y,2\\}$ unless $d_x=d_y=1$; the same bound holds for $d_x=d_y=1$ if the activation function is monotone. We then provide sufficient conditions for squashability and show that all non-affine analytic functions and a class of piecewise functions are squashable, i.e., our minimum width result holds for those general classes of activation functions.

paragraphs: Universal approximation asks whether a network family can approximate an entire class of functions arbitrarily well. This paper studies the minimum required width when network depth is unrestricted. Its focus is on squashable activations: functions that can approximate both the identity and a binary step through alternating composition with affine transformations.

For these activations, the authors establish a minimum width of max{d_x, d_y, 2} for approximating L^p functions from the d_x-dimensional unit cube to d_y-dimensional real outputs, except for the scalar-input, scalar-output case. When both dimensions equal one, the same formula holds if the activation is monotone. The exception and added condition are part of the theorem's scope.

The paper also gives sufficient conditions for squashability, showing that every non-affine analytic function and a class of piecewise functions qualify. This extends exact minimum-width results beyond ReLU and its variants. The contribution concerns representational capacity with unrestricted depth: it identifies how narrow networks can be while retaining the stated approximation ability.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes exact universal-approximation width bounds for broad classes of squashable activations, with a qualified scalar-case exception.

title: Minimum Width for Universal Approximation using Squashable Activation Functions

abstract: Diffusion models, widely recognized for their success in generative tasks, have not yet been applied to clustering. We introduce Clustering via Diffusion (CLUDI), a self-supervised framework that combines the generative power of diffusion models with pre-trained Vision Transformer features to achieve robust and accurate clustering. CLUDI is trained via a teacher–student paradigm: the teacher uses stochastic diffusion-based sampling to produce diverse cluster assignments, which the student refines into stable predictions. This stochasticity acts as a novel data augmentation strategy, enabling CLUDI to uncover intricate structures in high-dimensional data. Extensive evaluations on challenging datasets demonstrate that CLUDI achieves state-of-the-art performance in unsupervised classification, setting new benchmarks in clustering robustness and adaptability to complex data distributions.

paragraphs: CLUDI uses diffusion models to tackle clustering: organizing data into groups without supervised class labels. Its goal is to use the generative model’s ability to produce variation to help identify structure in high-dimensional data.

The teacher uses stochastic diffusion sampling to generate diverse cluster assignments, and the student learns to turn those varied assignments into stable predictions. Randomness therefore has a specific training role: it provides an augmentation strategy through alternative assignments, giving the student varied signals from which to learn a consistent grouping.

The authors report state-of-the-art unsupervised classification performance across challenging datasets, along with improvements in robustness and adaptability to complex distributions. These empirical findings support the combination of varied teacher outputs and stable student predictions. The methodological contribution is to make diffusion-generated variation part of the clustering learning process, connecting a generative tool with the task of discovering groups.
summary.tldr: CLUDI trains a student to stabilize diffusion-generated cluster assignments, achieving strong reported clustering results with pretrained visual features.

title: Clustering via Self-Supervised Diffusion

abstract: Blind Speech Separation (BSS) aims to separate multiple speech sources from audio mixtures recorded by a microphone array. The problem is challenging because it is a blind inverse problem, i.e., the microphone array geometry, the room impulse response (RIR), and the speech sources, are all unknown. We propose ArrayDPS to solve the BSS problem in an unsupervised, array-agnostic, and generative manner. The core idea builds on diffusion posterior sampling (DPS), but unlike DPS where the likelihood is tractable, ArrayDPS must approximate the likelihood by formulating a separate optimization problem. The solution to the optimization approximates room acoustics and the relative transfer functions between microphones. These approximations, along with the diffusion priors, iterate through the ArrayDPS sampling process and ultimately yield separated voice sources. We only need a simple single-speaker speech diffusion model as a prior, along with the mixtures recorded at the microphones; no microphone array information is necessary. Evaluation results show that ArrayDPS outperforms all baseline unsupervised methods while being comparable to supervised methods in terms of SDR. Audio demos and codes are provided at: https://arraydps.github.io/ArrayDPSDemo/ and https://github.com/ArrayDPS/ArrayDPS.

paragraphs: ArrayDPS separates overlapping voices recorded by multiple microphones without requiring information about the microphone arrangement. The challenge is that several unknowns must be resolved together: the individual voices, the room’s acoustic effects, and the relationships between microphone recordings. The method combines the recordings with a diffusion model trained to represent single-speaker speech.

Its starting point is diffusion posterior sampling, which uses a generative prior alongside evidence from measurements. Here, the likelihood connecting candidate speech sources to recorded mixtures is not directly tractable. ArrayDPS therefore solves a separate optimization problem to approximate room acoustics and relative transfer functions between microphones. These estimates are used together with the speech prior throughout the sampling process.

The reported evaluation shows better separation than all tested unsupervised baselines and performance comparable to supervised methods on SDR, a separation-quality measure. The contribution is an unsupervised separation procedure that can work across microphone arrays without requiring their geometry, while still exploiting relationships among their recordings.
summary.tldr: ArrayDPS combines a speech diffusion prior with estimated room acoustics to separate voices without microphone-array information.

title: ArrayDPS: Unsupervised Blind Speech Separation with a Diffusion Prior

abstract: The empirical evidence indicates that stochastic optimization with heavy-tailed gradient noise is more appropriate to characterize the training of machine learning models than that with standard bounded gradient variance noise. Most existing works on this phenomenon focus on the convergence of optimization errors, while the analysis for generalization bounds under the heavy-tailed gradient noise remains limited. In this paper, we develop a general framework for establishing generalization bounds under heavy-tailed noise. Specifically, we introduce a truncation argument to achieve the generalization error bound based on the algorithmic stability under the assumption of bounded $p$th centered moment with $p\in(1,2]$. Building on this framework, we further provide the stability and generalization analysis for several popular stochastic algorithms under heavy-tailed noise, including clipped and normalized stochastic gradient descent, as well as their mini-batch and momentum variants.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization can encounter gradient noise with unusually large fluctuations. Empirical evidence motivates heavy-tailed noise as a more appropriate description of some training behavior than standard bounded-variance assumptions. Much existing theory examines convergence of optimization error, while this paper focuses on generalization: how training translates into performance beyond the observed sample.

The authors develop a framework based on algorithmic stability, which connects sensitivity to changes in training data with generalization error. A truncation argument makes this analysis possible under a bounded pth centered moment assumption, with p greater than one and at most two. This explicitly accommodates moment assumptions weaker than bounded variance when p is below two.

The framework yields stability and generalization analyses for clipped and normalized stochastic gradient descent, including mini-batch and momentum variants. Its contribution is theoretical coverage of these optimization methods under the stated heavy-tail assumption. By examining stability rather than only optimization convergence, the work addresses a separate question: how the learning procedure’s response to its data can control the gap between training and generalization.
summary.tldr: A truncation-based stability framework establishes generalization bounds for stochastic optimizers under bounded heavy-tail moment assumptions.

title: Stability and Generalization of Nonconvex Optimization with Heavy-Tailed Noise

abstract: Recent advances have demonstrated that coded aperture snapshot spectral imaging (CASSI) systems show great potential for capturing 3D hyperspectral images (HSIs) from a single 2D measurement. Despite the inherent spectral continuity of scenes captured by CASSI, most existing reconstruction methods are restricted to fixed, discrete spectral outputs, thereby precluding continuous spectral reconstruction or spectral super-resolution. To address this challenge, we propose Phy-CoSF, which synergizes deep unfolding networks with implicit neural representations, establishing a new paradigm for continuous spectral reconstruction and super-resolution in CASSI. Specifically, we propose a two-phase architecture that bridges discrete-wavelength training with continuous spectral rendering, enabling the synthesis of high-fidelity HSIs at arbitrary target wavelengths. At the core of our framework lies the continuous spectral fields (CoSF) module, embedded within each unfolding stage as a dynamic prior, which comprises a triple-branch cross-domain feature mixer for comprehensive spatial–frequency–channel feature fusion, alongside a spectral synthesis head that generates spectral intensities by querying continuous wavelength coordinates. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that Phy-CoSF not only achieves continuous modeling at arbitrary spectral resolutions but also outperforms many state-of-the-art methods in both reconstruction fidelity and spectral detail preservation.

paragraphs: Snapshot spectral imaging compresses a three-dimensional hyperspectral scene into a single two-dimensional measurement. Reconstruction methods commonly recover a fixed set of wavelength bands, even though scene spectra are continuous. Phy-CoSF addresses this mismatch by learning a representation that can be queried at target wavelengths rather than producing only a predetermined spectral grid.

The architecture combines deep unfolding networks with implicit neural representations. Its two-phase design connects training at discrete wavelengths to continuous spectral rendering. Within each unfolding stage, a continuous spectral fields module acts as a dynamic prior. Three branches mix spatial, frequency, and channel information, while a synthesis head predicts spectral intensities from continuous wavelength coordinates.

This design supports both reconstruction and spectral super-resolution through the same continuous representation. Experiments demonstrate modeling at arbitrary spectral resolutions and improvements over many state-of-the-art methods in reconstruction fidelity and preservation of spectral detail. The findings support representing wavelength as a continuous query coordinate when recovering spectral information from compressed measurements, while retaining the reconstruction structure supplied by the unfolding network.
summary.tldr: Phy-CoSF reconstructs hyperspectral images through continuous wavelength queries, enabling flexible spectral resolution from snapshot measurements.

title: Phy-CoSF: Physics-Guided Continuous Spectral Fields Reconstruction and Spectral Super-Resolution for Snapshot Compressive Imaging

abstract: Observational studies are a key resource for causal inference but are often affected by systematic biases. Prior work has focused mainly on detecting these biases, via sensitivity analyses and comparisons with randomized controlled trials, or mitigating them through debiasing techniques. However, there remains a lack of methodology for uncovering the underlying mechanisms driving these biases, e.g., whether due to hidden confounding or selection of participants. In this work, we show that the relationship between bias magnitude and the predictive performance of nuisance function estimators (in the observational study) can help distinguish among common sources of bias. We validate our methodology through extensive synthetic experiments and a real-world case study, demonstrating its effectiveness in revealing the mechanisms behind observed biases. Our framework offers a new lens for understanding and characterizing bias in observational studies, with practical implications for improving causal inference.

This paper asks a different diagnostic question: what process produced the bias, such as hidden confounding or the way participants were selected into the study?

The proposed method examines the relationship between bias magnitude and the predictive performance of nuisance-function estimators within the observational study. These estimators are auxiliary components of the causal analysis. The authors show that the way bias relates to their predictive performance can help distinguish common bias sources, turning that relationship into evidence about the mechanism behind an observed discrepancy.

Extensive synthetic experiments and a real-world case study support the method’s effectiveness at revealing bias mechanisms. The contribution adds a diagnostic perspective to causal inference: identifying that an estimate is biased and understanding why it is biased become separate analytical goals. The stated finding is that this relationship can help characterize common mechanisms, providing information relevant to improving observational causal analyses.
summary.tldr: Relationships between bias magnitude and nuisance-estimator predictive performance can help identify the mechanisms producing bias in observational studies.

title: Uncovering Bias Mechanisms in Observational Studies

abstract: Edge-cloud collaborative inference is crucial for LLM-powered edge devices, as on-device models often lack the required reasoning capability, while cloud-only inference can be costly and slow under strict latency and token/API budgets. However, existing edge-cloud collaboration methods typically route input tasks based on their estimated difficulty. These static, coarse heuristics overlook subtask dependencies, missing opportunities for parallel execution and budget-adaptive routing. To this end, we propose HybridFlow, a resource-adaptive edge-cloud inference framework that enables parallel execution of interdependent subtasks. Specifically, we build a dependency-aware DAG for each input task, facilitating concurrent execution of subtasks once their dependencies are resolved, thereby reducing end-to-end latency. Additionally, we propose a dynamic benefit–cost utility model, optimizing the trade-off between accuracy, token/API cost, and latency in real-time. This dynamic routing minimizes unnecessary cloud usage while preserving reasoning quality. Across GPQA, MMLU-Pro, AIME24, and LiveBench-Reasoning, HybridFlow improves the cost-accuracy trade-off, reducing latency and cloud API usage while maintaining competitive accuracy.

paragraphs: HybridFlow addresses how an edge device should share language-model work with the cloud. Local models can lack the reasoning capability a task requires, while cloud inference consumes time and API or token budgets. Routing an entire task using a fixed difficulty estimate misses opportunities to distribute its parts according to their dependencies and the resources currently available.

The framework represents each task as a directed acyclic graph of subtasks. A subtask becomes eligible to run once its dependencies are resolved, allowing eligible work to proceed concurrently. A dynamic benefit–cost model then guides routing by considering accuracy, latency, and token or API costs in real time.

Evaluations on GPQA, MMLU-Pro, AIME24, and LiveBench-Reasoning report a better cost–accuracy trade-off, reduced latency, and lower cloud API usage while maintaining competitive accuracy. The contribution combines scheduling with resource-aware routing: identifying which work can run together and deciding where that work should execute. The reported gains concern this joint coordination of subtasks under resource constraints.
summary.tldr: HybridFlow schedules dependent subtasks and dynamically routes them between edge and cloud models to improve cost, latency, and accuracy trade-offs.

title: HybridFlow: Resource-Adaptive Subtask Routing for Efficient Edge-Cloud LLM Inference

abstract: Recent advances in large language models have enabled deep research systems that generate expert-level reports through multi-step reasoning and evidence-based synthesis. However, evaluating such reports remains challenging: report quality is multifaceted, making it difficult to determine what to assess and which criteria to use; LLM-based judges may miss errors that require domain expertise to identify; and because deep research relies on retrieved evidence, report-wide claim verification is also necessary. To address these issues, we propose DEER, a benchmark for evaluating expert-level deep research reports. DEER systematizes evaluation criteria with an expert-developed taxonomy (7 dimensions, 25 subdimensions) operationalized as 101 fine-grained rubric items. We also provide task-specific Expert Evaluation Guidance to support LLM-based judging. In addition to rubric-based assessment, we propose a claim verification architecture that verifies both cited and uncited claims and quantifies evidence quality. Experiments show that current systems produce structurally plausible, evidence-citing reports, but still struggle to fully satisfy expert-level user requests and achieve logical completeness. Beyond performance comparisons, DEER makes system strengths and limitations interpretable and provides diagnostic signals for improvement.

paragraphs: A research report can look convincing, include citations, and still fail to answer an expert's request completely. DEER addresses the difficulty of evaluating such reports across multiple aspects of quality. It also tackles two related problems: automated judges can overlook errors requiring specialist knowledge, and claims need checking throughout a report, including passages without citations.

The benchmark organizes expert-developed criteria into seven dimensions and 25 subdimensions, implemented through 101 detailed rubric items. It supplies task-specific expert guidance to help language-model judges apply those criteria. A separate claim-verification architecture checks both cited and uncited claims and measures the quality of their supporting evidence.

Experiments find that current research systems can produce reports with plausible organization and visible evidence references, yet still struggle to meet expert-level requests fully and maintain logical completeness. DEER makes these distinctions explicit rather than compressing report quality into surface plausibility. Its contribution is both an evaluation benchmark and a source of diagnostic feedback that helps explain system strengths and weaknesses.
summary.tldr: DEER combines expert rubrics and report-wide claim verification to reveal gaps behind apparently convincing AI research reports.

title: DEER: A Benchmark for Evaluating Deep Research Agents on Expert Report Generation

abstract: This paper studies the theoretical foundations of guidance mechanisms in continuous-time score-based diffusion models. We adopt Doob’s $h$-transform as a principled framework for characterizing ideal guided diffusion processes and analyze the discrepancy between ideal and approximate guidance. Our analysis provides explicit error bounds and yields probabilistic guarantees on satisfying prescribed constraints, which are particularly important for safety-critical planning. We further show that the Doob-based formulation induces a stochastic optimal control problem, enabling practical guidance design without additional model training. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework on 2D navigation and 7-DOF Franka joint-trajectory generation tasks.

paragraphs: This paper develops theoretical foundations for guiding continuous-time score-based diffusion models in planning tasks. Guidance is used to steer generation toward prescribed constraints, making its accuracy especially relevant when plans have safety requirements. The authors use Doob’s h-transform to characterize an ideal guided diffusion process and provide a reference for analyzing practical guidance.

The analysis examines the discrepancy between that ideal process and approximate guidance. It supplies explicit error bounds and probabilistic guarantees for satisfying prescribed constraints. These guarantees describe constraint satisfaction in probabilistic terms; they do not amount to unconditional certainty that every generated plan satisfies every constraint. The distinction ties safety claims to the analyzed approximation.

The formulation also induces a stochastic optimal control problem, creating a route to practical guidance design without additional model training. Demonstrations cover two-dimensional navigation and joint-trajectory generation for a seven-degree-of-freedom Franka robot. The contribution links an ideal mathematical description, quantifiable approximation error, and implementable planning guidance within one framework, giving the reported applications a theoretical basis for evaluating constraint satisfaction.
summary.tldr: A Doob’s h-transform framework connects training-free diffusion planning guidance with approximation bounds and probabilistic constraint-satisfaction guarantees.

title: Training-Free Guided Diffusion for Planning: A Unified Framework via Doob’s h-Transform with Safety Guarantees

abstract: Navigating under non-stationary environment shifts poses a critical challenge for a Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) agent deployed in the wild. Yet, existing Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods for VLN largely treat online adaptation as transient, isolated updates, leading to catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer. To overcome these issues, we propose Inter-Domain BridgE with Historical Assets (IDEA), a novel TTA framework that transforms adaptation into the accumulation and composition of assets. Specifically, IDEA introduces soft prompts optimized via a Fisher-guided weighting scheme to capture the transferable knowledge. These optimized prompts are then augmented with domain coordinates to form a dynamic asset library. Leveraging this library, IDEA constructs a cross-domain bridge by projecting the target domain onto the convex hull of historical knowledge. These designs form a complementary loop: the evolving library underpins bridge construction, while the bridge provides superior initialization to accelerate asset optimization. Extensive experiments across REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE benchmarks demonstrate the consistent superiority of IDEA over existing methods, showcasing its ability to enable training-free adaptation via asset sharing.

paragraphs: Vision-language navigation agents encounter environments whose properties change over time. Updating separately for each new environment can discard useful knowledge or transfer unsuitable knowledge from previous settings. IDEA treats adaptation results as reusable assets, allowing experience from earlier domains to contribute to later navigation.

The framework optimizes soft prompts using Fisher-guided weighting to capture transferable information. It stores these prompts together with domain coordinates in a growing library. For a new target domain, it constructs a bridge by projecting the target onto the convex hull of historical knowledge. This uses combinations of stored assets to provide a better initialization for subsequent prompt optimization.

The library and bridge reinforce one another: accumulated prompts improve initialization, and newly optimized prompts expand the available assets. Experiments on REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE report consistent superiority over existing methods. The paper also reports training-free adaptation through asset sharing, alongside its prompt-optimization procedure. The broader finding is that retaining and composing adaptation results can make online adjustment more useful across changing environments.
summary.tldr: IDEA stores and combines domain-specific prompts so navigation agents can reuse earlier adaptations when environments change.

title: Turning Adaptation into Assets: Cross-Domain Bridging for Online Vision-Language Navigation

abstract: Multistate mechanisms underlie many of the complex functions observed in natural proteins. The ability to rationally design multistate proteins would have transformative implications for many areas of biotechnology, yet lies beyond the capabilities of existing deep learning frameworks for protein design. To address this gap, we introduce SwitchCraft, a versatile and programmatic framework for designing state-switching proteins based on backpropagation through compositional design constraints parameterized by structure prediction models. In silico evaluations demonstrate success on a wide range of state-switching functional primitives, from allosteric regulation of motifs to discrimination of bound ligand identities. Using these primitives, we demonstrate an in silico strategy for de novo design of fluorescent biosensors to arbitrary small molecule analytes. These results position SwitchCraft at the inception of a powerful paradigm for higher-order functional protein design. Code is available at https://github.com/bjing2016/switchcraft.

paragraphs: Many natural protein functions depend on switching between multiple states. Designing that behavior requires coordinating several structural conditions, rather than targeting just one structure. SwitchCraft provides a programmatic framework for specifying and optimizing such state-switching behavior through combinations of design constraints.

The framework uses structure prediction models to parameterize these constraints and backpropagates through them during design. This makes the desired relationships between states part of the optimization process. Computational evaluations cover functional building blocks including allosteric regulation of motifs and discrimination between the identities of bound ligands.

The authors then combine these building blocks into an in silico strategy for designing fluorescent biosensors from scratch for arbitrary small-molecule analytes. The stated evidence is computational: the abstract reports in silico success rather than experimental validation of functioning proteins. Within that scope, the work demonstrates how compositional constraints can extend protein design toward coordinated, multistate functions and provide a basis for designing more complex sensing behaviors.
summary.tldr: SwitchCraft uses compositional constraints and structure-model gradients to design state-switching proteins, with computational demonstrations including biosensor design.

title: SwitchCraft: A Programmatic Framework for Designing State-Switching Proteins

abstract: Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) has become a fundamental framework for learning discrete representations in image modeling. However, VQ-VAE models must tokenize entire images using a finite set of codebook vectors, and this capacity limitation restricts their ability to capture rich and diverse representations. In this paper, we propose ArcCosine Additive Margin VQ-VAE (ArcVQ-VAE), a novel vector quantization framework that introduces a spherical angular-margin prior (SAMP) for the codebook of a conventional VQ-VAE. The proposed SAMP consists of Ball-Bounded Norm Regularization, which constrains all codebook vectors within a time-dependent Euclidean ball, and ArcCosine Additive Margin Loss, which encourages greater angular separability among latent vectors. This formulation promotes more discriminative and uniformly dispersed latent representations within the constrained space, thereby enabling codebook vectors to capture richer information and leading to improved codebook utilization. Experimental results on standard image reconstruction and generation tasks show that ArcVQ-VAE outperforms baseline models in terms of reconstruction accuracy, representation diversity, and sample quality.

paragraphs: A vector-quantized variational autoencoder represents images using entries from a finite codebook. Because that codebook must support many different visual patterns, its limited capacity can restrict the richness of the learned representation. ArcVQ-VAE focuses on how the available vectors are arranged and used, seeking to encode more diverse information within the constrained representation space.

The proposed spherical angular-margin prior combines two mechanisms. Ball-Bounded Norm Regularization keeps codebook vectors inside a Euclidean ball whose size changes over time. An ArcCosine Additive Margin Loss encourages latent vectors to be more separated in angle. Together, these mechanisms promote representations that are distinguishable and more uniformly dispersed.

This geometric organization is intended to improve codebook utilization and allow its entries to carry richer information. On standard image reconstruction and generation tasks, the authors report improvements over baseline models in reconstruction accuracy, representation diversity, and generated sample quality. The findings connect better use of a finite codebook with gains in both representing existing images and generating new ones.
summary.tldr: ArcVQ-VAE organizes discrete image representations using norm constraints and angular separation, improving codebook use and image reconstruction and generation results.

title: ArcVQ-VAE: A Spherical Vector Quantization Framework with ArcCosine Additive Margin

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are widely used, but how parameter sparsity affects the expressivity of relational (RGNNs) and temporal (TGNNs) variants is poorly understood. The Strong Expressive Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (SELTH) posits the existence of sparse GNNs that preserve Weisfeiler-Leman (WL) expressivity on static graphs. We generalize this existence result to a probabilistic statement for multi-relational and temporal domains via the relational WL (RWL). We prove that sufficiently parameterized RGNNs contain sparse subnetworks that maintain 1-RWL expressivity and derive a lower bound on the probability that a random pruning yields such a subnetwork. We show that common TGNNs and cross-graph message passing schemes admit RGNN reformulations such that they inherit these guarantees and, moreover, that the expressivity of a sparse RGNN is connected to its optimization behavior under common update regimes. Experiments instantiate the bound, compare it to empirical probabilities on synthetic data, and study how pre-training expressivity relates to optimization and prediction quality metrics on temporal and molecular benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper asks when a graph neural network can lose many parameters while retaining its ability to distinguish graph structures. Earlier expressive lottery-ticket results concerned static graphs. The authors extend that perspective to networks handling multiple relationship types and temporal information, using relational Weisfeiler–Leman expressivity as the standard for what the network can distinguish.

The main result establishes that sufficiently parameterized relational graph neural networks contain sparse subnetworks preserving 1-RWL expressivity. It also gives a lower bound on the probability of finding such a subnetwork through random pruning. The parameterization condition matters: the result does not say that arbitrary pruning of any network will preserve its expressive capabilities.

The authors show that common temporal networks and cross-graph message-passing schemes can be reformulated as relational networks, allowing them to inherit the guarantees. They also connect sparse-network expressivity with optimization under common update regimes. Experiments compare the probability bound with synthetic observations and examine relationships between initial expressivity, optimization, and prediction quality on temporal and molecular tasks.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditional expressivity guarantees and random-pruning probability bounds for sparse relational and temporal graph networks.

title: A Unifying Relational Perspective on Expressive Lottery Tickets

abstract: Data selection during supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can critically change the behavior of large language models (LLMs). Although existing work has studied the effect of selecting data based on heuristics such as perplexity, difficulty, or length, the reported findings are often inconsistent or context-dependent. In this work, we systematically study the role of data difficulty in fine-tuning from both empirical and theoretical perspectives, and find that there is no universally optimal difficulty level; rather, its effectiveness depends on the dataset size. We show that for a fixed data budget, there exists an optimal data difficulty for SFT, and that this optimal difficulty shifts toward harder data as the data budget increases. To explain this phenomenon, we conduct controlled synthetic experiments that reveal a simple underlying mechanism: the interplay between the (in-distribution) generalization gap and the extrapolation gap. We further support this mechanism through a theoretical analysis using PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds. Overall, our results clarify how data size and difficulty jointly affect the trade-off between generalization and extrapolation in SFT, providing guidance for difficulty-based data selection under certain model and data conditions.

paragraphs: Choosing easy or difficult examples for supervised fine-tuning can change a language model’s behavior, but previous findings do not point to a consistently best choice. This paper examines data difficulty jointly with dataset size. Its central finding is that the usefulness of a difficulty level depends on how much training data is available.

For a fixed data budget, the authors find an optimal difficulty level, which shifts toward harder examples as the budget grows. Controlled synthetic experiments connect this pattern to two competing gaps: generalization within the training distribution and extrapolation beyond it. Selecting difficulty therefore changes a balance between learning effectively from the available examples and extending beyond their distribution.

The paper supports this explanation with a theoretical analysis using PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds. Its practical implication is that difficulty-based selection should account for dataset size rather than treating difficulty as an isolated quality score. The authors frame this guidance under certain model and data conditions, so the result does not establish one selection rule that is optimal for every fine-tuning setting.
summary.tldr: The paper finds that optimal fine-tuning difficulty shifts toward harder examples as data budgets grow under the studied model and data conditions.

title: Data Difficulty and the Generalization–Extrapolation Tradeoff in LLM Fine-Tuning

abstract: Continual learning is a long-standing challenge in robot policy learning, where a policy must acquire new skills over time without catastrophically forgetting previously learned ones. While prior work has extensively studied continual learning in relatively small behavior cloning (BC) policy models trained from scratch, its behavior in modern large-scale pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models remains underexplored. In this work, we find that pretrained VLAs are remarkably resistant to forgetting compared with smaller policy models trained from scratch. Simple Experience Replay (ER) works surprisingly well on VLAs, sometimes achieving zero forgetting even with a small replay data size. Our analysis reveals that pretraining plays a critical role in downstream continual learning performance: large pretrained models mitigate forgetting with a small replay buffer size while maintaining strong forward learning capabilities. Furthermore, we find that VLAs can retain relevant knowledge from prior tasks despite performance degradation during learning new tasks. This knowledge retention enables rapid recovery of seemingly forgotten skills through finetuning. Together, these insights imply that large-scale pretraining fundamentally changes the dynamics of continual learning, enabling models to continually acquire new skills over time with simple replay.

paragraphs: A robot learning new skills over time can lose competence on tasks it previously mastered. Much earlier work examined this problem in small policies trained from scratch. This paper studies large pretrained vision-language-action models and finds that their continual-learning behavior differs substantially: they are more resistant to forgetting than the smaller policies considered.

Simple experience replay, which revisits stored examples from earlier tasks, works particularly well with these pretrained models. In some cases, even a small replay dataset yields zero forgetting. The analysis identifies pretraining as a critical factor, allowing models to retain earlier capabilities with a small buffer while still learning new tasks effectively.

The researchers also distinguish reduced task performance from complete loss of relevant knowledge. Models can preserve information about earlier tasks even when their visible performance declines, enabling rapid recovery through fine-tuning. These findings suggest that large-scale pretraining changes both how forgetting appears and how much machinery is needed to manage it, making simple replay effective in the studied settings.
summary.tldr: Pretrained vision-language-action models show strong resistance to forgetting, with simple replay sometimes preserving all measured prior performance.

title: Pretrained Vision-Language-Action Models are Surprisingly Resistant to Forgetting in Continual Learning

abstract: Large Language Models with Chain-of-Thought reasoning capabilities represent valuable intellectual property, yet existing black-box watermarking methods often trade robustness for reasoning fidelity by perturbing final answers or relying on fragile trigger patterns. We propose BiCoT, a watermarking framework that embeds ownership signals into the internal geometry of reasoning traces by aligning high-saliency structural anchors with a private signature subspace while regularizing ordinary control tokens to preserve semantic capacity. This design couples the watermark with reasoning-relevant representations, making removal difficult without disrupting the features that support coherent reasoning. To enable verification under model theft and representation drift, we introduce Robust Subspace Registration(RSR), a Top-$k$ logprob-based black-box verifier that uses sentinel tokens to calibrate systematic shifts in the output distribution. Experiments show that BiCoT preserves reasoning fidelity across diverse complex reasoning tasks while achieving robust detection under fine-tuning, quantization, model-level perturbations, and adaptive output-level attacks across in-domain and out-of-distribution settings.

paragraphs: BiCoT aims to identify ownership of reasoning language models while preserving their reasoning quality. Existing black-box watermarking approaches can interfere with final answers or depend on fragile triggers. This paper embeds the ownership signal in the internal geometry associated with reasoning traces, tying it to representations involved in producing coherent reasoning.

The method aligns structurally important anchors with a private signature subspace and regularizes ordinary control tokens to preserve their capacity to carry meaning. The design makes watermark removal difficult without disturbing reasoning-relevant features. For verification, Robust Subspace Registration uses top-k token log probabilities and sentinel tokens. These sentinels help calibrate systematic changes in output distributions caused by model modification or representation drift.

The experiments report preserved reasoning fidelity and robust watermark detection across complex reasoning tasks. Detection remains effective under tested fine-tuning, quantization, model perturbations, and adaptive output attacks, including both familiar and out-of-distribution settings. The results support coupling ownership evidence to reasoning representations and calibrating its detection after changes to the model.
summary.tldr: BiCoT embeds ownership signals in reasoning representations and verifies them through token probabilities while preserving reasoning quality in reported tests.

title: Echoes within the Reasoning: Stealthy and Effective Watermarking via Chain of Thought

abstract: LLM-powered coding agents are reshaping the development paradigm. However, existing evaluation systems, neither traditional tests for humans nor benchmarks for LLMs, fail to capture this shift, excluding problems that require both human reasoning to guide solutions and AI efficiency for implementation. We introduce CentaurEval, a unified, ecologically valid benchmark for measuring human-in-the-loop value in coding. CentaurEval’s core innovation is its "Collaboration-Necessary" problem templates, which are intractable for standalone LLMs or humans, but solvable through effective collaboration. CentaurEval dynamically instantiates tasks from 45 templates, providing a standardized IDE for humans and a reproducible 450-task toolkit for LLMs. We benchmark 45 participants against 5 LLMs under 4 levels of human intervention. Results show that while LLMs or humans alone achieve poor pass rates (0.67% and 18.89%), human–AI collaboration significantly improves to 31.11%. Our analysis reveals an emerging co-reasoning partnership, challenging the traditional human-tool hierarchy by showing that strategic breakthroughs can originate from either humans or AI.

paragraphs: CentaurEval asks how much human involvement adds to coding agents. Traditional human tests and standalone AI benchmarks miss tasks where a person’s reasoning and an AI system’s implementation efficiency must work together. The benchmark therefore centers on problem templates designed to make collaboration necessary, placing joint problem-solving at the center of evaluation.

Tasks are generated dynamically from 45 templates. Human participants use a standardized development environment, while a reproducible toolkit provides 450 tasks for evaluating language models. The study compares 45 participants and five models across four levels of human intervention. This setup allows the authors to examine how different amounts of participation affect results on a shared family of coding problems.

Reported pass rates are 0.67% for models alone, 18.89% for humans alone, and 31.11% for collaboration. These results show a substantial benefit from working together on the benchmark’s deliberately demanding tasks. The analysis also finds that strategic breakthroughs can originate from either partner, supporting a view of collaborative coding in which both humans and AI contribute reasoning as well as execution.
summary.tldr: CentaurEval measures human–AI coding collaboration and finds higher success together, with strategic contributions coming from both partners.

title: CentaurEval: Benchmarking Human-in-the-Loop Value in Agentic Coding

abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly deployed as autonomous collaborators, where agents interact freely rather than execute fixed, pre-specified workflows. In such settings, effective coordination cannot be fully designed in advance and must instead emerge through interaction. However, most prior work enforces coordination through fixed roles, workflows, or aggregation rules, leaving open the question of how well self-organizing teams perform when coordination is unconstrained. Drawing on organizational psychology, we study whether self-organizing LLM teams achieve strong synergy, where team performance matches or exceeds the best individual member. Across human-inspired and frontier ML benchmarks, we find that—unlike human teams—LLM teams consistently fail to match their expert agent’s performance, even when explicitly told who the expert is, incurring performance losses of up to 41.1% on ML benchmarks. Decomposing this failure, we show that expert leveraging, rather than identification, is the primary bottleneck. Conversational analysis reveals a tendency toward integrative compromise—averaging expert and non-expert views rather than appropriately weighting expertise—which increases with team size and correlates negatively with performance. Interestingly, this consensus-seeking behavior improves robustness to adversarial agents, suggesting a trade-off between alignment and effective expertise utilization. Our findings reveal a significant gap in the ability of self-organizing multi-agent teams to harness the collective expertise of their members.
